#3173. Bending Spoons (BSP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Acquisitions drove revenue higher, but organic growth tells a much quieter story.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:14PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Bending Spoons (BSP -1.68%) reported financial results for the third quarter of 2026, highlighting the integration of large-scale enterprise software assets and the expansion of its global acquisition pipeline. Management reported significant growth in total revenue and adjusted operating income driven by the consolidation of recent acquisitions including Airtable and Vimeo. The company stated it has secured $8.35 billion in financing since the start of the quarter to support its M&A strategy, including a debut bond issuance and private placements from investors such as Berkshire Hathaway. Management indicated that it is focusing on transforming acquired businesses by rewriting codebases and implementing proprietary AI-driven operational tools to improve productivity and monetization.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Bending Spoons' Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your first speaker today, James Cordwell, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

James Cordwell: Thank you, and hello, everyone. Welcome to Bending Spoons' Q3 2026 Earnings Call. With us today to discuss our results are Luca Ferrari, Co-Founder and CEO; and Enrico Martinelli, Co-CFO. For the Q&A portion of the call, we'll also be joined by Davide Scarpazza, Co-CFO; and Francesco Patarnello, Co-Founder and Head of M&A. But before we begin, let me cover the safe harbor statement. Some of the information you'll hear today will consist of forward-looking statements, including those regarding our outlook, objectives, initiatives and pending transactions. These statements reflect our current understanding and expectations and are subject to a variety of risks and uncertainties. Actual events and results may differ materially.

For more information, please refer to our registration statement on Form F-1 including the risk factors described there. We assume no obligation to update any forward-looking statements. During the call, we'll discuss both GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures. You can find the definitions of our non-GAAP financial measures, together with reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures in our Q3 2026 earnings release, which is available on the Bending Spoons' Investor Relations website at investors.bendingspoons.com. Unless we say otherwise, all comparisons refer to year-over-year results. And now over to you, Luca.

Luca Ferrari: Thanks, James. In Q3, revenue increased 125% to $780 million. Operating income increased 34% to $172 million, representing a margin of 22%. Adjusted operating income increased 130% to $424 million, representing a margin of 54%. Organic revenue growth was 3%. Growth trends across most of our businesses were broadly consistent with Q2. At AOL, the transition to advertising stack reduced its contribution to organic growth by approximately 1 percentage point relative to Q2. Growth at WeTransfer remained strong, both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter, but a tougher comparable meant it contributed less to organic growth than in the prior quarter. I will now discuss progress across the three stages of our playbook: acquire, transform and optimize and reinvest.

The first stage is acquire. During the quarter, we announced the acquisitions of Airtable and Miro for a combined enterprise value of $2.65 billion. These acquisitions have now closed, and we have deployed Spooner teams to both, to build on the work done by the pre-acquisition teams. At Miro, we are currently focused on deepening our understanding of the business and developing our road map. At Airtable, we have announced our initial priorities and begun implementing them. These priorities are to improve the core offering, invest in AI and enable people and agents to collaborate with appropriate controls. Since acquisition, we have already shipped 60 product improvements.

We recently upgraded Omni, Airtable's built-in AI assistant and launched Canvas, which allows users to build custom apps on their data. Yesterday, we announced the agreement to acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for an enterprise value of $3.68 billion. Mailchimp generated $1.27 billion in revenue in the 12 months to October 31 by helping customers plan, execute and optimize their e-mail marketing campaigns. We see opportunities to improve the technology, product and monetization through our platform and are attracted by the business's scale and revenue predictability. The second stage of our playbook is transform and optimize. And for this call, I will focus on AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo.

Based on the work done in Q3 and prior quarters, all 3 are positioned to accelerate growth in Q4. At AOL, planned subscription pricing and packaging adjustments were substantially completed by the end of Q3. By that point, most of the technological separation from Yahoo! was also behind us. Old desktop properties had migrated to a new instance of the advertising stack and mobile traffic has since transitioned. The disruption to advertising performance was broadly in line with expectations and the gap in impression pricing relative to Yahoo!'s stack had largely closed by mid-September. In October, we completed the rewrite of the iOS and Android apps, enabling us to start working on more significant product improvements.

Operating on our own technologies has enabled test across advertising and user experience with several experiments showing increases in engagement and advertising yield. At Eventbrite, we have shipped more than 70 product improvements in the 7 months since we acquired the business, and we continue to upgrade the business' technological infrastructure. Revenue also returned to year-over-year growth in October. Our primary focus has been on helping creators reach and better monetize larger audience, simplifying event management and improving technical reliability. Eventbrite events can now be discovered through ChatGPT and creators can automate ticket pricing changes using predefined rules. We have also strengthened waiting rooms to handle surges in ticket demand and introduced additional checks to combat bot purchases.

Alongside these improvements, we have introduced new monetization methods, including post-checkout advertising and a dedicated step for ticket add-ons. Turning to Vimeo. In Q3, bookings from both new and renewing customers grew year-over-year in each of the self-serve and enterprise segments. Trends in the OTT segment have been more challenging, but an overhauled checkout flow has lifted conversion for customers in early testing. Overall technical performance continues to improve, with medium video trans-coding volume decreasing by 40% between the start and the end of the quarter. New bookings per sales representative reached an all-time high in Q3 as we improved the team structure and invested in technology to support operations.

More recently, we launched our free tier offering, unlimited storage for public videos, removing the previous 1 gigabyte cap. Alongside our commitments not to place advertising against uploaded videos or use them to train AI models, this offering is designed to make Vimeo a more attractive place for filmmakers to share their work. AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo are still in their initial transformation phase, but we continue to improve our businesses well beyond the first year of ownership. For instance, in Q3, Meetup's revenue grew more than 20%, supported by Meetup+, the subscription offering for attendees.

Our objective is to compound per share earnings and free cash flow as rapidly as possible over the long term. We, therefore, assess each of our business primarily against our original return expectations. Remini has performed exceptionally well by this measure. Brightcove, after our somewhat disappointing start, has recently shown encouraging progress. Even with the benefit of hindsight, we would make both acquisitions again. We allocate Spooners where we see the most attractive prospective returns, and our platform enables us to regularly reallocate them as these opportunities evolve. During the quarter, we added over 80 net new Spooners to our team, taking our core team to 753 full-time equivalents as of the end of Q3.

We have also continued to expand our use of AI to improve productivity. Today, 98% of our pull requests are written in full or in apart by AI. Since the start of the year, pull requests per Spooner software engineer have more than quadrupled while inference cost per pull request has roughly halved. These improvements reflect in part our investment in a proprietary harness to select models based on task requirements and inference cost. Beyond coding, we recently rolled out Diagram, a proprietary AI-powered design tool tailored to our workflows. With Diagram, every Spooner can develop a new user experience or slide deck from only a few natural language prompts, drastically reducing the design resources required.

We consider Diagram clearly better in our context than the third-party tools we were previously using. The third stage of our playbook is reinvest. As discussed last quarter, the pace at which we can reinvest and drive all 3 acquisitions is governed by three potential constraints: the availability of targets, our access to capital and our operational capacity. Hiring in AI are expanding our operational capacity. Those Spooners are currently our scarcest resource. Since the start of Q3, we have secured $8.35 billion in financing through debt and equity transactions and expanded revolving credit facilities.

Our debut bond issuance opened a new source of capital while the Berkshire Hathaway private placement and the placement announced yesterday have further strengthened our financial position. After deducting the funds expected to be used for the Mailchimp acquisition and upon closing of the placement, we have more than $4 billion of available liquidity to support further acquisitions. Enrico will now discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Enrico Martinelli: Thank you, Luca, and hello, everyone. For Q3, total revenue was $780 million, up 125%. Of this total, $38 million was attributable to Airtable, which was consolidated into our financials from September 4. Organic revenue growth was 3%. Similar to Q2, the strongest contributions to organic growth came from WeTransfer and Tractive. To provide some incremental detail the 2026 and 2025 acquisitions cohorts each grew revenue 6% year-over-year. The 2024 cohort, 8%; and the 2023 cohort, 10%. These figures reflect revenue-weighted growth and where applicable, include comparisons to pre-acquisition periods. This growth was partly offset by weakness at Remini, which reduced organic growth by 2 percentage points.

We expect Remini to continue to face revenue pressure due to its historically relatively low retention rates, dependence on viral spikes for user acquisition and increased competition in the AI image generation market. So its impact on overall organic growth will be moderated by its declining size within our overall portfolio. Q3 operating income totaled $172 million, increasing 34%; and adjusted operating income reached $424 million, increasing 130%. Airtable contributed $10 million to adjusted operating income. Operating income as a percentage of revenue was 22%, down from 37% in Q3 '25. Adjusted operating income margin was 54%, expanding 1 percentage point compared to Q3 2025.

Operating income as a percentage of revenue declined despite the improvement in adjusted operating income margin, primarily due to a $149 million increase in amortization of intangible assets. This increase reflected the businesses we acquired over the past year and the finalization of purchase price allocations for AOL, Eventbrite, Tractive and Vimeo. Finalizing these allocations resulted in a $65 million catch-up charge relating to prior periods. Transaction-related expense and other items not indicative of ongoing operating performance also pressured the operating income as a percentage of revenue, the former due to the acquisitions of Airtable and Miro and the latter due to the IPO-related costs.

The expansion in adjusted operating income margin was primarily driven by a 275 basis point decline in advertising expense as a percentage of revenue. This reduction is both a function of our strategy to select acquisition targets that are not highly reliant on paid advertising for user acquisition and the result of our work to eliminate inefficient expenditure. This improvement was partly offset by the impact of changes in portfolio mix on certain items within cost of revenue. IT infrastructure expense and other cost of revenue, both increased, while distribution and payment processing expense declined, all measured as a percentage of revenue. Together, these cost of revenue items reduced adjusted operating income margin by 125 basis points.

Interest expense was $107 million, rising 163% year-over-year, but broadly stable sequentially as outstanding debt in the quarter was consistent with Q2. Other expense was $17 million, primarily reflecting currency exchange losses, and we recognized an income tax benefit of $43 million. This benefit included the partial release of a valuation allowance associated with the finalized purchase price allocation for Vimeo. Diluted earnings per share was $0.13, down 3%; and adjusted earnings per share was $0.42, up 98%. Turning now to cash flow and our financial position. In Q3, net cash from operating activities totaled $261 million. We also received $1.09 billion in net proceeds from our IPO. We paid $1.21 billion for acquisitions, net of cash acquired.

Capital expenditure was $5 million. We also repaid $297 million under our revolving credit facilities and made $206 million in scheduled principal repayments of long-term debt. At quarter end, the carrying amount of long-term debt was $4.91 billion. Net debt fell by $187 million during the quarter to $4 billion at the end of Q3. Leverage ratio stood at 2.1x. Available liquidity totaled $3.36 billion, including cash and amounts available under committed term loan and revolving credit facilities. After quarter end, we paid $1.36 billion for Miro. We secured $4.46 billion from term loan add-ons, our first bond issuance, the Berkshire Hathaway private placement, the reinvestment by certain Miro shareholders and other borrowings.

These transaction amounts are gross of fees and associated costs. Given effect to these transactions, available liquidity at quarter end would have been $6.46 billion. The private placement announced yesterday would add $1.3 billion upon closing. The Mailchimp acquisition would reduce liquidity by $3.31 billion, net of Intuit's reinvestment. Had both pending transactions also closed at quarter end, available liquidity would have been $4.45 billion. Now to guidance. For Q4, we expect revenue to be in the range of $984 million to $1 billion. This represents organic revenue growth of 5% at the midpoint.

We expect adjusted operating income to be in the range of $470 million to $490 million, which represents an adjusted operating income margin of 48% at the midpoint. The implied sequential decline in this margin reflects the incorporation of the Airtable and Miro cost bases into our financials. We expect margins, excluding these businesses to expand both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter. For the full financial year of 2026, this outlook implies revenue of between $3.07 billion and $3.09 billion, an increase from our prior guidance of $2.78 billion to $2.82 billion. It also implies full year 2026 adjusted operating income of $1.58 billion to $1.6 billion, an increase from the previously provided outlook of $1.46 billion to $1.51 billion.

Both increases reflect a stronger outlook for businesses included in our prior guidance and contributions from Airtable and Miro. This guidance is based on the set of businesses we own today and doesn't incorporate any contribution from future acquisitions. Specifically, it includes a full quarter contribution from Airtable and Miro's contribution from October '26, but no contribution from the pending Mailchimp acquisition. With that, we are ready to start the Q&A portion of the call.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And now, we're going to take our first question, and the question comes from the line of Eric Sheridan from Goldman Sachs.

Eric Sheridan: Maybe 2, if I can. On the organic revenue piece, in terms of some of the acquired assets you have, once an acquired asset, maybe runs into either operational headwinds or slows from a growth perspective, how are you thinking about philosophically either reinvesting back in that business to stimulate organic revenue growth or optimize for margin or cash flow? And maybe if I could just ask a quick follow-up after that.

Luca Ferrari: This is Luca, Co-Founder, CEO. Thank you for the question. So our investment, whether it's R&D or sales and marketing is completely independent of organic revenue growth. We, at all times, ask ourselves the question of where that talent, that money would yield the highest possible returns and invest accordingly. So there could be a case where a business is declining and incremental investment would yield substantial uplift in free cash flows in the long run. We would -- assuming we have the resources, we would make that investment. In other cases, if we don't think we can influence that decline, we wouldn't. And the very same concept applies for a fast-growing business.

There are fast-growing businesses where growth, at least to the best of our knowledge, cannot be necessarily accelerated by further investments, at least not profitably and vice versa. And more generally, everything we do, whether at the individual business level and even more so when looking at Bending Spoons as a whole is aimed at compounding earnings and free cash flows per share as rapidly as possible with a multi-decade view. So organic revenue growth is not an indicator that really comes into play in those considerations.

Eric Sheridan: Great. And against the current capital markets environment, how is your view continuing to evolve in terms of the utilization of debt as opposed to the utilization of equity as either a source of capital or being issued in parallel to facilitating certain transactions on the M&A front?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. Still me, still Luca. So basically, we start from the same objective of generating as much value in terms of earnings and free cash flows on a per share basis over the next 10 or 20 years and solve backward, and that applies to our financing as well. Now typically, if you look at our historical performance, we have delivered very high returns, I'd like to say, exceptional returns on our investments in acquisitions. And we have no reason right now to doubt that we'll continue to deliver outstanding returns going forward. So those returns have generally been substantially higher than the cost of our debt.

And therefore, it's always been, in our view, wise to prioritize using debt as long as we kept our exposure at very prudent levels, which you could translate into a cap to leverage ratio, for example, and we assess this in a more sophisticated way internally. But as a rule of thumb, keeping leverage ratio in the 2 to 3 range, typically, we believe, results in a highly prudent posture. Of course, we reinvest all of our free cash flows into acquisitions because that's the highest return opportunity, at least it has been consistently so far, and we believe it will continue to be given just how rich our pipeline for acquisitions is.

Equity remains a very useful type of financing in -- when at least one of the following 2 criteria are met. Of course, the valuation needs to be decent enough that the cost of acquisition is not tremendous and in excess of our returns. But assuming valuation is in the range of acceptable, then it boils down to either it being useful to keep leverage ratio lower.

We naturally delever pretty quickly, but sometimes we want to lower it faster than we would by simply operating the business or, and it's really 2 phases of the same coin, to be able to go after a larger target that we couldn't really reach not in the short term through the investment of our free cash flows and incremental debt alone. So we always redeploy free cash flows. We always raise incremental debt while keeping leverage at prudent levels.

And then time and again, we might go back to the equity markets if we think that doing so helps either further improve our risk profile or grow faster on a per share basis, which is what you have seen recently. While the IPO naturally, we had to issue equity to get it done, and that helps with access to the debt markets, too. But after that, we raised a little bit of money from Berkshire Hathaway. Yesterday, we announced a PIPE for another $1.3 billion. And a couple of the recent acquisitions, the seller reinvested a small percentage of the overall consideration into newly issued Bending Spoons stock.

So we are not shy when it comes to using equity as long as we believe that, that helps us compound value for our shareholders even faster.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question, and it comes from the line of Kirk Materne from Evercore ISI.

Kirk Materne: With Airtable, Miro and now Mailchimp, you all are definitely moving further into enterprise-oriented businesses. Can you just talk about how the way you apply the Bending Spoons playbook maybe changes a little bit as you go into enterprise versus what's worked in consumer. They have longer customer relationships, implementation sales motions. I'm just kind of curious how you guys think about that. It might be more nuanced than anything more dramatic, but I'd love to just hear your thoughts on that as you've now done 3 in a row in that area?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. So I would say Mailchimp actually, I wouldn't call it enterprise, although it serves I believe, about 1 million customers. So there's a little bit of everything in there, but primarily, it's, let's say, SMEs, and it's almost fully self-serve. So there is -- the sales motion is very limited, almost nonexistent at the scale of the entire business. And so it's actually closer to our more typical acquisitions from the past than Airtable and Miro, both of which have primarily enterprise customers and a sales-led go-to-market motion.

Now what we have found over time is that the biggest differences in customer behavior and optimal tactics and approaches are driven by whether a business is primarily self-serve versus sales-led and not so much whether it's consumer or B2B. We find that self-serve consumer behaves actually quite similarly to self-serve, let say, SMEs, whereas the big differences come when you switch from self-serve to having to deal with customers through human beings and negotiations and procurement departments.

Both can be optimized in very -- in excellent ways, but they require different skill set, different approaches and to some extent, different underlying technologies, which is why, by the way, precisely to approach perfection in sales-led enterprise we have invested quite aggressively, particularly this year in developing not just insights and expertise, but also underlying proprietary tooling. We developed -- we created a dedicated team of engineers and product managers and they have been hard at work to create tools that make our salespeople more efficient. We had some excellent results better than at least personally, I expected. For example, at Vimeo, we managed to achieve the highest level of new bookings per salesperson in Vimeo's history.

And this is important because Vimeo clearly is not in an up-and-coming explosive growth kind of phase where that would happen naturally, quite the opposite, right? And that was achieved at the same time as we actually got to the maximum level of absolute new bookings. So this is not the product of a shrinkage in the sales force where we only kept the highest performing salespeople. Naturally, the proprietary technologies we put to work are not the only reason. There's a lot of work on organization and processes and the approach.

But it is reassuring and encouraging as we keep working on becoming really good at this as I believe we have proven to be at the self-serve side of the equation.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question. And the question comes from the line of Alec Brondolo from Wells Fargo.

Alec Brondolo: Perhaps 2 for me. First, on AOL. As you noted in the prepared remarks, there was a price increase taken during the quarter. Could you just speak to how the user base responded to that price increase, the level of churn, if any, relative to your expectations? And then secondly, with regards to the 5% organic revenue growth guidance in the fourth quarter, could you perhaps just unpack that a little bit? I think that Airtable and Miro are going to be included in that. They're obviously growing a little bit faster. So how much of that acceleration -- sequential acceleration is the inclusion of Airtable and Miro relative to the rest of the portfolio improving?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. So yes, AOL, like every one of our businesses, we experimented extensively with all sorts of monetization changes well beyond mere pricing, but pricing being one of the things. We have done this the entire time since the acquisition closed in January. And we have identified several changes in configurations that based on our testing, yield substantial improvements in revenue trajectory. We did begin deploying one of these configurations at scale recently with high expectations given our extensive testing of nice revenue uplift, modest one-off churn and no impact on, let's say, long-term ongoing churn levels.

So the expected result is to see an improvement in revenue levels at no cost in terms of revenue quality after the short-lived transitional period where, of course, churn spikes a little bit. We've really just very recently deployed that at scale. So the impact of that applies almost not at all in Q3, although very slightly does, and it will apply from Q4 and onward for most of 2027 as well. That's our expectation. Now regarding the Q4 5 percentage points in organic growth at the midpoint of the range, we expect most of our businesses to continue performing along similar lines.

The main changes sequentially vis-a-vis Q3 would be we expect AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo to each do better than their past trajectories. So those would have a nice impact there, I think more so AOL and Vimeo. At Eventbrite, we have not touched prices or almost -- monetization almost at all with the exception of a little bit of advertising work. And so we expect growth to be a little bit slower, but still positive, which is new after a couple of years of declines for Eventbrite. So I believe an excellent result. We'll be able to report more on that in the next couple of quarters as all the numbers come in, but we're quite positively impressed.

And so again, AOL and Vimeo will probably do most of the heavy lifting vis-a-vis Q3 and then, of course, being able to account for both Airtable and Miro for the full quarter will help. We think they will contribute approximately 1 percentage point to guidance.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question. And the question comes from the line of Omar Dessouky from Bank of America.

Omar Dessouky: So I think many people have seen the videos online of Meta's new AI agent and Gemini's searching your inbox for subscriptions that you paid for, but you don't use. And in the past, you haven't really bothered to cancel them because you're either not aware of it or you don't want to take the effort to log in and cancel that unused subscription. Wondering if you've seen those videos. Obviously, it's not clear how widespread that's happening. But has Bending Spoons estimated the percentage of payers that don't use the apps across its portfolio on at least a monthly basis, but still pay for them. And if so, what have you found?

For example, like what percentage of payers don't use the apps on a monthly basis? And have you recently seen any uptick in the pace of cancellations? And the second part of the question is, would you say your consumer subscriptions will be unaffected or experience limited impact as a result of AI agents informing the consumers of their subscription inventory?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you for the question. I've not seen the videos, but of course, I understand the concept you're describing. So I think it's a reasonable concern for an investor to have. I would certainly recommend people to embed a little bit of a buffer for adverse events in general, and this could be one of those. Now I'll give you a number of facts that I believe seem to indicate this to be a reason for very limited concern. First of all, only about 1/3 of our revenues from consumer subscriptions.

Second of all, we actually looked very closely last week in anticipating the question, product by product, and we could not find even the slightest impact on any important indicator, whether it's gross retention, net retention and any other indicator of business health across the entire portfolio. So, so far, we feel very confident saying 0 impact whatsoever. It's also worth noting that products meant to help customers manage their subscriptions, including canceling subscriptions they are presumably not using that have been launched. I remember at least 2 separate such products being launched by startups over the past 5 or 6 years. I never followed closely.

But to my knowledge, they never saw any commercial success, which I think indicates that probably consumers in general, they don't think they have this problem. I mean I'm sure there's 10 billion people out there. So certainly someone does. But that, to me, seems to indicate that this is not something people feel they need help with. It's also worth noting that I can only speak when it comes to this about our products, but we make notifications and cancellations extremely easy. So we notify our customers on their payments. And of course, credit card providers do so, and you can find it on your bank account summary.

And we make cancellation extremely easy, generally a couple of clicks across most of our products, at least after we've owned them for a while. Sometimes when we buy them, previous owners were not as thoughtful and customer-friendly, but we always make sure to transition to very friendly cancellation procedures within the first year or so. So it's -- at least for our product, it's very hard to believe people would find that it's difficult to cancel. They can also contact customer support. They just need to say, I want to cancel and we basically cancel, no questions asked.

And last but not least, we try pretty hard to make sure our products are great and worth using and paying for. And they're certainly not perfect, but I believe they're in almost every case, very, very good, and we try to make them better by the day. So is this a potential risk? I would say I would be responsible if I said it's impossible this ever impacts Bending Spoons. Based on what we see and all these factual considerations, we find it hard to believe this would be a major headwind at some point, although it's reasonable to expect that at some point, in at least some cases, we may see a little bit of deterioration.

And when that happens, we'll let you know. But again, so far, absolutely no signal whatsoever.

Operator: And now, we'll take our next question, and it comes from the line of Bryan Smilek from JPMorgan.

Bryan Smilek: Luca, curious, can you just help us better understand the ad road map at Eventbrite across post checkout and first-party ad revenue more broadly? I guess like how do you think about modulating ad load over time and the potential subscription opportunity in a more meaningful way at Eventbrite?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you for the question. So I'm a little bit wary of stealing the team's thunder when it comes -- like we like our teams to give them a lot of autonomy and be able to communicate and announce their own plans and achievements. But what I can say is that we see a significant opportunity at Eventbrite on both advertising and subscriptions monetization. For example, we recently introduced post-checkout ads. And for those of you who have not used Eventbrite or maybe are not as well versed with the sort of things, it means that after a potential attendee purchases a ticket, there is, of course, a page there for summary.

We now display advertising, and that's led to a nice uplift in advertising revenue, had absolutely no impact on engagement or retention or any other metric you want to keep healthy. We have also helped -- and this is part of advertising, but slightly different. We've also helped event organizers advertise more and more effectively on Eventbrite because as an event organizer, you may want to spend a little bit of money to make sure your event is more prominently displayed on the platform. We have 80 million people come to Eventbrite every month to look for things to do.

And so being more prominently displayed can make a huge difference in how many tickets you sell and often lead to a good return on investment. And so we made some changes there to the user experience for our event organizers, and that led to a very noticeable uplift in how much they spend, and we believe it's also good for them based on what we've been able to see so far.

So that also so far has been successful, and we believe it's only the beginning of things we can do to improve that offering, not just its presentation, but substantially the value it can deliver also by adding sophistication in how we -- in what events we show to whom. And so we want to make that advertising investment more and more accretive for our event organizers. When it comes to subscriptions, we have introduced 2 different subscription -- well, it's really multiple versions really because we tested a huge variety of things. But to keep it relatively simple, we tested 2 types of subscriptions, one for consumers for attendees and one for the organizers themselves.

For the attendees, they now have the possibility of purchasing an ongoing subscription to -- so that all fees by Eventbrite are waived for their ticket purchases. And this is interesting for people who purchase frequently on Eventbrite. We have users who go to multiple events each month, and this is a good deal for them. And this is showing nice penetration and retention. And again, it has had so far in all of our experiments, no detrimental impact on all the things you care about, such as engagement and retention and satisfaction of attendees. And the one for organizers instead offers advanced marketing features.

In particular, it offers e-mail marketing automations, which is funny because now we announced the acquisition of Mailchimp, but I promise we started this before we knew that was a possibility. And also, it enables SMS campaigns, which is something that wasn't available before. And so far, reception by organizers has been very positive because it doesn't -- these are not necessary tools. So the subscription is perceived to be in no way intrusive or limiting of what they can do on the platform if they want to be, let's say, less sophisticated or ambitious with their events.

But for those who want to try to go a little bit further, then it can be pretty good value for money based on what we've seen so far. And all of these areas, we think, are just scratching the surface. And hopefully, over the next multiple years, we can bring our offering to the next level.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question, and the question comes from the line of Stefan Slowinski from BNP Paribas.

Stefan Slowinski: I've got 2. First one is on Mailchimp more specifically. I just wanted to double-click on that acquisition. We've seen over the past few years Intuit, first, investing a lot in the product and trying to get the product right and then more recently, significant cost cutting to shift to more of a kind of cash strategy for the company. So it's a business that's already seen a lot of product investment and cost cutting. And so just wondering kind of what gives you the confidence that you can get the returns that you need from that business? Where do you see the opportunity?

And why are you paying maybe slightly above the 2.5x revenues that maybe you paid for previous acquisitions? That's the first question.

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. It's a wise observation. So just a quick accuracy pointer. So historically, we have paid anywhere between -- in most cases, anywhere between 1 and 6x revenue for our acquisitions. So it's really a pretty wide range. And yes, if you -- I believe if you average for acquisitions 2023 through 2025, it's probably like 2.5x. But if you shift that window, it can easily fluctuate, easily by a point or so. So this is -- it's true.

This is close to that average, but a little bit above our more recent range, partly because we think as we scale -- as we have talked about multiple times before, as we scale, it's reasonable to expect returns to moderate a little bit. Now they have been absolutely astronomical in the past. We have no reason to think that there will be anything less than outstanding going forward. But even then, it's reasonable to expect a little bit of compression. And this could be -- it's hard to tell whether this is a trend or just one deal, but we do expect slightly inferior returns from this deal than some other deals, but still amazing.

I mean, returns, I think most companies would feel for, to be clear. Now -- specifically to, let's say, product investment and then cost reduction, a lot of the acquisitions we have done in the past, you could argue similar things. When we bought Evernote, there had been a tremendous amount of investment in the product. And yet I believe we -- demonstrably, if you look at what we have done over the past few years, we managed to bring it to a whole new level. I think even the people who hate us for having increased prices would generally agree that the product has improved by leaps and bounds.

And so -- and I could go on and on and most of our acquisitions were -- had been in both phases or at least one of those phases, and that has not prevented us from doing better. We have no reason to believe that we will not be able to improve performance at Mailchimp substantially going forward or else we wouldn't have offered this price. We're very excited about the acquisition. We see substantial opportunity to improve both revenue and cost. And we also like a few other things about it. First, of course, the scale. We talked about it in the past.

One disadvantage of our model is that those integrations, which are as deep as it gets technologically, people-wise, and those transformations, which also are sometimes dramatic, they take a lot of operational effort, and we don't have an infinite number of people. But thankfully, we find that the number of tuners we need to deploy to take care of those things does not scale anywhere linearly with revenue potential of an acquisition. And so larger scale acquisitions are much preferable. So of course, Mailchimp checks that box with flying colors. We believe it's -- the earnings will be predictable because this is such a long-standing business. We have a couple of decades' worth of data.

We've been able to study cohort behavior across all sorts of situations. COVID, of course, for digital business is super relevant , situations where competition intensified tremendously. Now the market has been relatively stable for quite a few years, but there was a period after Mailchimp really a trailblazer in e-mail marketing automation that a lot of competitors joined and many had plenty of financing and we were aggressive on marketing. So we went through all those periods and studied our users and customers behaved, which has given us a lot of confidence in our ability to know what's going to happen going forward.

We also found that gross retention of customers has been incredibly resilient across all of these events for a decade, which also, in our experience, is a great sign of resilience for our business going forward. And a few other things, I'll keep it short. But -- and in terms of improvements, we believe that, thanks to our platform, our access to talent, our proprietary technologies, our expertise, our data, we will be able to, as I mentioned earlier, substantially boost revenue and cost trajectories, resulting in a nice expansion in earnings. All considered, again, we expect returns to be excellent. And we look forward to seeing this acquisition complete sometime in the first part of 2027.

Stefan Slowinski: Great. Just a follow-up, I guess, on the pace of M&A heading into next year. You've just done 3 deals here, Mailchimp pending. So just wondering whether it's access to talent and hiring of Spooners or just the need to digest these deals, whether we should see that pace of M&A slow in the first half of next year?

Luca Ferrari: So in 2026, we should see 5 deals being completed for Bending Spoons. Last year, we did 6. I think the previous year, it was 5. Again in '23, it was 1. So it goes up and down a little bit. I'd say the pace this year has been roughly in line with our historical average.

I would still consider 2027 (sic) [ 2026 ] above average in terms of overall the overall amount of complexity that we have digested or are in the process of digesting primarily -- not so much because of the scale of these businesses, although that also plays a part, but primarily because businesses like Airtable and Miro, but also Vimeo have substantial go-to-market organizations and those add yet another dimension of complexity and larger headcount. And so certainly, it's been a -- as I've said before, it's certainly been a challenging year operationally. We are absolutely happy with our results so far and very confident in how things will play out going forward.

But you're right in asking how we're doing operationally. I think we still have a substantial buffer for things we can buy and integrate. We have also been able to greatly improve our ability to scale our operations through -- by pulling levers that we intend to continue pulling going forward. For example, we have invested a lot in our proprietary technologies this year with AI being a major tailwind to improve scalability. In the earnings release, you may have noticed, we showed a graph that displays how we have roughly quadrupled productivity for Spooners software engineers. If we -- similar improvements happened for other roles, too. And we believe there's plenty to go there. So we intend to continue.

I did mention earlier the work we did with proprietary technologies supporting our salespeople at Vimeo, where we saw major improvement in productivity as well. So we intend to continue investing aggressively in our technological platform to keep unlocking new productivity. We do keep enjoying scale economies that get unlocked with each next level of revenue. These are quite substantial. We do have the opportunity to remove resources from businesses that have become too small to matter given the new large acquisitions and the growth in many of our existing businesses.

And even though maybe those resources in an ideal world would be valuable at those businesses, if they don't really move the needle one way or another at the group level, then we will move them to be able to tackle larger acquisitions or more interesting opportunities. And we have worked hard to expand our access to talent. October was our best year (sic) [ month ] ever in terms of both job applications and new hires. This year, we opened offices in Spain and Poland. We expanded our office in the U.K. We have plans to keep expanding our footprint, potentially opening offices in the U.S. next year. We are doing some preliminary work there.

So there are plenty of things -- plenty of tailwinds when it comes to keeping our operational leverage going up and up. So overall, I'd say we feel pretty good about 2027, whether that enables 6 acquisitions or 3 or 8 is really hard to tell because it depends also on the particular deals with deals like Mailchimp being a little bit easier for us to digest than deals like Airtable where there is a massive sales force. So overall, good to -- for every investor, to keep in mind, operational capacity is a potential bottleneck, and it certainly -- it comes up time and again as a bottleneck. I would say right now, we feel reasonably good about it.

Operator: Now we're going to take our next question, and it comes from the line of Mark Shmulik from Bernstein.

Mark Shmulik: One specifically on advertising. I know this quarter, you kind of rebuilt and migrated some of that AOL ad tech stack. Any kind of learnings that you've seen in kind of applying the playbook to kind of an ad style business? I know we touched a little bit about Eventbrite as well, but just any more color just how that playbook is working on the advertising side?

Luca Ferrari: Thanks. Yes. So I mean, the overall message is positive. I'll give you first the -- let's say, the challenges that we had to overcome and then some of the promising signs. So last quarter, we did say that we plan to transition AOL's various properties to a new instance of the advertising stack fully controlled by us, fully enabled by proprietary tooling and that we expected that to cause disruption.

Well, partly -- I guess, you could always introduce a bug, but partly when you have to establish new contracts with the, in this case, 50-plus advertising networks and just let the their respective algorithms adapt to what's ultimately the very same product, but for them, it's, in a way, a completely new thing. It's a new instance. They don't recognize it as more of the same. We knew from experience that, that could cause some disruption. We did see some disruption, which, by the way, impacted our rate of organic revenue growth in the quarter. Had we seen no disruption whatsoever, we would have posted maybe 1 percentage points higher or 1 or 2. Disruption was short-lived.

We're now back to the pre-transition impression pricing. So all good as planned. And by the way, kudos to the team because I think managing that complexity and such a transition in just a few months, I think it's absolutely stunning. I mean, a truly exceptional feat of engineering and business management. In any case, as we did that, we also started launching a number of experiments with the advertising placement frequency, hopefully, starting next year, also new formats, which was not impossible before, but it was more cumbersome now that we control the whole thing. We can use our A/B testing tools and of course, expand them and improve them to better manage advertising-related experiments.

And we have already found several changes that appear to be improving advertising yields quite noticeably. Again, it's early. I don't want to promise the moon, but we feel pretty good about our ability to substantially improve AOL's advertising revenue, and this would apply to other businesses with programmatic revenues from advertising. Of course, assuming that market levels for the pricing of impressions are flat because like all advertising businesses, part of that, you can control by improving your displays and part of how you optimize those through technology and partly, it's also -- it just depends on how the market is doing.

But assuming markets are stable, then we feel pretty good about being able to bolster AOL's advertising revenue going forward.

Mark Shmulik: And I guess just one quick follow-up to that. So kind of based on the experiences there and kind of the most recent acquisition in Mailchimp, relative to kind of your plans going in about the addressable market in kind of advertising-based businesses, do you feel like better or worse, kind of the same relative to kind of before you went into this one?

Luca Ferrari: Better. I mean we -- partly, I believe it's -- our culture is one where we are, at the same time, acutely self-critical and aware of our shortcomings and gaps in skill set. But at the same time, we're just very competitive, and we have a belief that through great talent and huge amounts of hard work and a scientific approach to things we can become world-class at things given enough time. So we never doubted that we could do well with advertising and of course, having overcome a few initial challenges, we feel even better at that. But so it remains an area where we are confident we can excel.

Now it's -- we won't buy businesses that depend on advertising just to show off. We will, if anything, assign some discount to those acquisitions slightly because we are -- we can't be as confident in our abilities as we would be for, say, a self-serve subscription business. But we -- if the right opportunity comes up and currently, we estimate about 15% of our addressable market to be advertising revenue. So small, but significant, we will certainly do that. I mean we're not going to shy away simply because it's not our core expertise. Ultimately, everything we do well today, we didn't at some point. You need to do to learn.

And so we'll keep those things -- we'll keep an eye on those opportunities. And if we can buy them while applying even more conservative assumptions and delivering expected returns in line with the other opportunities, we'll go for them, and then we'll be talking about them with you guys.

Operator: Dear participants, now we're going to take our final question for today. And it comes from the line of Lloyd Walmsley from Mizuho.

Lloyd Walmsley: I wanted to follow up on the M&A question. It seems like you're moving faster with acquisitions. You're doing bigger ones. You've raised a bit more equity. Do you think you're on a trajectory where over the next few years, you may be deploying more than this sort of $4 billion to $5 billion level annually of sort of new capital into M&A? And the follow-up would just be if you can just talk a little bit more about your relationship with Berkshire Hathaway. They've clearly become a significant investor, but any other areas of cooperation or anything you would like to share about that relationship a bit would be great?

Luca Ferrari: Thank you. I'll start with the latter question. Well, I mean, we have known Berkshire for a few years, and you have to ask them. But as far as I'm concerned, we have a wonderful trusting partnership. I think we see eye to eye and essentially the core idea of trying to compound value for shareholders as efficiently as possible without being swayed by market trends. Of course, we want to be open-minded, listen question, but not follow them simply because everybody is doing certain things, being willing to be contrarian if we feel that we know what we're doing, not focusing too much on promotion and staying focused on substance and execution. And of course, we admire Berkshire tremendously.

Partly, when we started Bending Spoons, those out there who have been following us for a long time already know this, but we -- many companies have very product-specific missions like they want to develop -- solve a problem. In our case, we just wanted to try to build an all-time great company, one of the best of our generation. And of course, we are inspired by companies that become institutions like Berkshire Hathaway. And so if we could build something even remotely of that caliber, would be just amazing. And so partnering with them can only help. We don't have any agreement with Berkshire that they will necessarily invest more or necessarily support any hypothetical new acquisition.

But hopefully, both parties, I believe, are in this because they think that's a possibility at least. So it's good for us to have them on board, extending our relationship, strengthening our relationship. And then if in the future, we find ourselves in a situation where a substantial equity injection on a short notice, maybe when the markets are paralyzed, Berkshire has a history of being able to move quickly in those situations. If we find ourselves in such a scenario, then, of course, we would call them, and they'll be the decision makers there. But it's good to know that we have that line open, let's put it that way.

When it comes to capital deployment, look, it's very difficult for me to know how much capital we'll deploy because it depends on -- the one thing I'm most confident in is our operational performance. So actually, in my mind, the range of operating profits in the next couple of years is actually fairly narrow from our existing portfolio. But then we depend on whether the markets for debt, how open are they, what cost is there. We depend on the availability of targets. Having said that, I think we see probably the richest pipeline we have ever seen. So I don't think that finding targets is likely to be a significant bottleneck to deploying capital within reason, of course.

And we are better positioned to raise capital today than we ever have been because we are now a public company. We'll be extending our track record as a public company, hopefully, in a very successful way. It's up to us, but we're confident there. We have recently tapped the bond markets, which is possibly the largest pool of capital available to us. We have done a couple of pipes, which is also a nice useful instrument going forward and strengthened relationships with most of the largest public market investors in the world. We recently saw our credit ratings improved with both Moody's, Ba3 and S&P, BB-, and got rated by Fitch for the first time with a BB.

So we think that going forward, we have better access to capital than ever before, assuming the markets are within a range of normal or semi-normal conditions. As we mentioned in our prepared remarks, on a pro forma basis, we would now have well over $4 billion we could deploy. And clearly, this does not include any free cash flows we'll be generating going forward. On a run rate basis, we are generating over $1 billion, and it's increasing quite rapidly. And of course, it does not -- that $4-plus billion does not include any incremental debt we can raise on our expanding operating profits.

So clearly, in terms of capital available, we could deploy more than $4 billion, $5 billion next year. I would still encourage investors to be cautious. We feel that $5 billion on average yearly is a reasonable assumption. Perhaps you want to sprinkle a little bit of a few mega deals on top. I think it's reasonable to expect that occasionally, we'll find a bigger target that would substantially skew the average when calculated over multiple years. But outside of those less usual transactions, I think a $5 billion deployment yearly seems a relatively conservative, but realistic assumption.

Operator: Thank you. There are no further questions for today. I would now like to hand the conference over to the management team for any closing remarks.

Luca Ferrari: Well, thank you, everybody, for attending. We don't take it for granted. We wish you a wonderful day.

#3172. Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse said the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

Reuters’ findings may provide an opportunity for Google’s agentic offering, now called Tasks (formerly Spark), which it made free (with usage limits, like Muse) this week.

#3171. One Month and a Half-Million-Plus Folds Later, Our Machine Is Still Testing the iPhone Duo

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apple's folding phone is showing unmistakable signs of wear, but it hasn't broken yet.

Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo folding phone came out a month ago. Every day since then, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, a dedicated machine inside CNET’s lab has been folding and unfolding it over and over again. For science.

How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? As of Friday, Nov. 20, we’re up to more than 565,000 folds and the Duo hasn’t broken yet. The hinge has shown signs of potential failure, however. Our technicians, as well as the cameras and sensors that are part of our testing rig, continue to monitor the situation and collect data.

I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations in our lab in Louisville, Kentucky. My team and I designed and built this proprietary machine to test foldable phones like Apple’s and its Samsung rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (which we’ve also started testing). I’ve worked on the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone.

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

My team of engineers and testing experts has been watching the iPhone Duo open and close, over and over, for the past few weeks to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review as well as her one-month-later follow-up. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube weekdays from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

#3170. Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The messaging app similarly limited screenshots because of Microsoft Recall last year.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do

Just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal said its protections don’t currently work on MacOS.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

#3169. Bitcoin Fell More Than 20% in November. History Says This Happens Next.

The world’s top cryptocurrency could face a lot more selling pressure.

Bitcoin's (BTC -7.54%) price has declined by over 20% in November. At just under $60,000, it's trading more than 50% below its all-time high of about $126,000 from last October. Let's see what caused that decline -- and what its historical performance suggests could happen next.

A year ago, many investors expected the Fed to cut interest rates in 2026. Lower rates would presumably weaken the U.S. dollar, making blue chip cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin more attractive, and spark a rotation from conservative, higher-yielding investments into riskier ones.

Long-term catalysts also supported Bitcoin. Its spot-price exchange-traded funds (ETFs), initially approved in early 2024, were attracting more retail and institutional investors. It was also attracting more attention from corporations and governments as a hedge against the debasement of fiat currencies. Investors also expected its next halving -- which halves the rewards for mining Bitcoin every four years -- to exacerbate its scarcity in 2028.

But in 2026, those tailwinds dissipated as the Iran war exacerbated inflation and prompted the Fed to raise its rates for the first time in three years in September. The Democratic sweep in the U.S. midterms also increased the likelihood of tighter restrictions on the crypto market. Those challenges curbed the market's appetite for cryptocurrencies, and Bitcoin's price plummeted.

Past performance never guarantees future gains, but Bitcoin has a solid record of bouncing from steep peak-to-trough declines. However, each drawdown shook out many investors.

As of this writing, Bitcoin has declined 53% from its all-time high. Therefore, investors shouldn't be surprised if it sinks even lower over the next year before stabilizing. An 80% drop from $126,000 would reduce its price to about $25,000.

That would be a painful pullback -- especially for investors who bought Bitcoin in late 2025 -- but its historical performance suggests it could bounce back sharply after it bottoms out. Every time Bitcoin crashed, it set new all-time highs within a few years.

I'm not saying that's guaranteed to happen this time, but plenty of catalysts -- including interest rate cuts and its next halving -- could drive the bulls back to Bitcoin. While it could certainly get worse before it gets better, I believe Bitcoin will be trading much higher in just a few years.

#3168. Google Gemini Partners With Watch Duty to Clear Static From Firefighter Radio

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

After spending months training with firefighters in the field, the app uses Google Gemini to decode distorted radio signals in real time.

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home

On Friday, Google’s Gemini team announced the results of a new partnership with the wildfire-tracking app Watch Duty, after Gemini engineers spent six months embedded with Watch Duty’s first responders. The results cut vital new wildfire dispatch translations down to seconds and helped improve radio communications, which can be rough on the front lines of a new fire.

The Gemini AI improvements got a real-world test during Washington state’s Railroad Fire in July 2026, when Watch Duty issued what it calls its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert. The alert stemmed from a nearly unintelligible, static-filled 911 call that the Gemini tool transcribed in under 30 seconds. That kind of assistance can help Watch Duty send alerts to affected communities more quickly and enable first responders to update maps more accurately and make better-informed decisions.

“This is something the tool also has the capability to do if reports of flooding are communicated via radio,” said Dave Merritt, co-founder and chief technology officer of Watch Duty. “Across disasters, we hear feedback every day that first responders are using Watch Duty for additional situational awareness, especially for disasters that span multiple counties.”

Watch Duty reporters are active and retired first responders who can manually monitor up to 20 different feeds, though static and rapid-fire jargon can make them difficult to follow.

Gemini workers used more than 20,000 hours of Watch Duty radio recordings to train the AI tool to recognize firefighting terms that aren’t in the average dictionary or books that AIs are typically trained on.

Google says the tool is not designed to replace human decision-making in life-or-death situations.

“This tool takes on the demanding work of listening, freeing Watch Duty’s volunteers to focus on what matters most: confirming fires and getting warnings to people while they can still act,” said Stephanie Chew, Google project team lead.

The project was completed at no cost thanks to a Google.org fellowship, and the resulting Watch Duty app features are free to use.

From the data collected, Gemini engineers and Watch Duty identified several measures of success.

One metric was the word error rate, which fell by around 15% after the AI model was implemented. Another sign of success was a jump in Watch Duty volunteers’ satisfaction with their radio transcription tools, from around 35% to 92%.

The Gemini tool continues to analyze approximately 200 hours of radio speech traffic from 400 feeds per day. The tool was made to handle more than 10,000 radio feeds if necessary.

The integration could pave the way for broader use across public safety. The platform’s built-in scalability could eventually bring similar audio-clearing tools to local fire departments, 911 call centers and Coast Guard operations, where clear communication is critical under pressure.

#3167. I Didn’t Know Southwest Points Could Be This Valuable
