By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:39PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Post (POST +2.23%) reported fourth quarter and full-year results for fiscal 2026, meeting Adjusted EBITDA expectations despite headwinds from increased freight and diesel costs. Management reported that the company is focusing on execution in fiscal 2027, with earnings momentum expected to build in the second half of the year as pricing actions and productivity initiatives offset inflation timing. The company completed several divestitures during the year, including the Crystal Farms business and the 8th Avenue pasta business, while simultaneously integrating the remaining pet food and private label assets. Management indicated that the company maintains significant financial flexibility, with a focus on prioritizing debt reduction while remaining opportunistic regarding share repurchases and potential acquisitions.

Operator: Welcome to the Post Holdings Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call and Webcast. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Daniel O'Rourke, Investor Relations for Post. Please go ahead.

Daniel O'Rourke: Good morning. Thank you for joining us today for Post's Fourth Quarter Fiscal 2026 Earnings Question-and-answer Session. This call is being recorded, and an audio replay will be available on our website at postholdings.com. During today's call, we may make forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties that should be carefully considered by investors as actual results could differ materially from these statements. These forward-looking statements are current as of the date of this call, and management undertakes no obligation to update these statements. The press release and written management remarks that support today's call are posted on our website in the Investors section. This call will discuss certain non-GAAP measures.

For a reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to the nearest GAAP measure, see our press release issued yesterday and posted on our website. I'm joined this morning by Nico Catoggio, our President and CEO; Matt Mainer, our CFO and Treasurer. With that, I'll turn the call over to Nico for some opening remarks.

Nicolas Catoggio: Thanks, Daniel. Good morning, everyone. Before we discuss the quarter, I want to briefly acknowledge the announcement we made yesterday regarding Rob. Our thoughts are with Rob and his family. He has been an exceptional leader, colleague and friend, and he has our full support as he takes the time he needs to focus on his health. Jeff Zadoks will serve as Interim Chairman during Rob's leave, and we have a strong and experienced Board and management team in place. Turning to the quarter. Let me briefly highlight a few things from our prepared remarks. We finished Q4 with adjusted EBITDA modestly ahead of our expectations despite higher-than-anticipated freight and diesel costs.

Importantly, volume trends were generally in line with our expectations. The incremental pressure we experienced in the quarter was primarily cost driven and does not change our view of the trajectory of the business. As we look to fiscal 2027, our outlook remains consistent with what we communicated last quarter, and we are focused on executing against the key drivers of our plan. The back half weighting primarily reflects the timing of inflation and our pricing response, not changing our expectations for the businesses. We continue to expect food service growth, together with the benefit of pricing and productivity initiatives to increasingly offset inflationary pressures as we move through the year.

Our credit profile remains strong and give us meaningful flexibility to deploy capital where we see the greatest opportunity to create long-term shareholder value. Overall, we remain confident in our outlook. Fiscal 2027 is about execution, and we believe delivering against the key drivers of our plan will build earnings momentum as we move through the year and position the business well for growth in fiscal 2028. With that, let's open the call for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our first question from Andrew Lazar with Barclays.

Andrew Lazar: Sending my best to Rob as well. Two questions, if I could. First, Nico, maybe regarding Pet Food and the relaunch, I guess I was under the impression maybe that the brands would start to see quite a bit more progress on share towards the end of fiscal '26. And it just seems like that's sort of been getting pushed out with continued distribution losses and Post still lost quite a bit of share with volume well below the category again in fiscal 4Q. So what's, I guess, really going on there? And what informs the visibility that things will start to stabilize moving forward? And can additional footprint optimization that you mentioned help profitability this coming fiscal year?

Or is it really more impactful for '28? And then I've just got a follow-up.

Nicolas Catoggio: Thanks, Andrew. Let me start by acknowledging that stabilizing our pet business or pet brands has been a bit more challenging than we anticipated. And part of it is the category has been a bit more challenging. I mean we talk a lot about the dynamic between dog and specifically dry dog and cat with our portfolio skewing towards dry dog. And then on top of that, the category promotional dynamics changed quite a bit. When we entered the category, less than 10% of the volume in the category was promotional volume. We're up to 25%, around 25% now. So it's a different category.

So in that environment, we are focusing, I would say, less on the year-over-year because there's so much noise. As an example, on Nutrish, we were heavily promoting last year to sustain the brand. We are not doing that this year. So we're focusing on a few things. One is how is our base volume doing, base volume being base velocity and distribution, not promotional volume and how we're doing sequentially. And we are seeing encouraging signs on both. So our base velocity on Nutrish, for example, our base volume Nutrish has improved month after month for the last 5 months. So 4 months ago, we were around 20% down.

The last 4 weeks, we are closer to mid- to high single digits in our base volume. So it's encouraging. Most importantly, we're focusing on our household penetration, and we're seeing stable household penetration across all our brands. And we focus on our overall market share. Can we stay around that 3% that we have had now for 4, 5 months? And if the answer is yes, then that gives us the confidence to focus on cost out and footprint optimization. Our expectation right now is that we will remain at that 3% market share, maybe a bit more, a bit less month after month for 2027. So we expect sequentially stable volumes quarter after quarter.

And with that, we're focusing now on cost out and footprint optimization. Anything that we do with footprint optimization beyond kind of what we produce where and optimizing that is probably more F '28.

Andrew Lazar: Got it. Okay. And then quite a few food companies have significant debt refinancing coming up in the next year or 2 and have signaled more divestiture activity to accelerate deleveraging. Post mentioned in the prepared remarks, it has the financial flexibility for M&A. Have you started to see or expect to see more activity recently as others contemplate their own portfolio optimization moves? Or have you not seen much of that yet?

Matt Mainer: Andrew, it's more of the latter. I'm not seeing it yet. I think it's more of we see what you talked about, and we want to make sure we have flexibility to take action if we see something that's attractive relative to share repurchases or again, it's a high bar given our multiple, but also given where interest rates are today. But we definitely preserve that flexibility if there is an attractive opportunity.

Operator: We will take our next question from Matt Smith with Stifel.

Matthew Smith: If we think about the higher cost environment, which sounds like it moved up sequentially through your fourth quarter. As you look through the year in fiscal '27, kind of what's the expected level of input cost inflation, the phasing of the year-over-year inflation? And then your expectation for pricing in the second half? Do you expect to recapture all of the impact of inflation? And within the outlook range, how are you thinking about elasticities? And I'm sure that's different by business unit, but any idea you can give us on how you think about volumes in reaction to the pricing would be helpful.

Matt Mainer: Yes. Obviously, a lot of factors have got embedded in our guidance range you just talked about there, Matt. I think starting with inflation, we talked about it last quarter, and we saw some additional inflation in Q4 around diesel prices and freight and packaging impacts. So maybe a little higher than we talked about last quarter, but still in that overall mid-single-digit inflationary range with some categories being obviously higher than that, like freight and fuel charges.

When we think about pricing, I don't want to be too specific, but we have targeted pricing actions in place in certain areas of the portfolio today that are taking effect -- we see additional inflation on the commodity side hitting later in the year. And again, we will address that with pricing in the back half of the year. So I don't want to get into too many specifics. Obviously, elasticities vary from category and also within our business segments, even brands within there, depending on our position. So we really don't have an elasticity I can give you that's for Post consolidated, but certainly have that factored into our guidance range.

Matthew Smith: And as a follow-up, you have a nut butters cost optimization program as well. Do you expect to start to see savings from that program in the second half of the year? Or is that, again, because it's footprint-oriented more fiscal '28?

Matt Mainer: Yes. Majority of that's in fiscal '28, likely get about 1/4 of it in fiscal '27. So again, that's an action that was started towards the end of fiscal '26. So it's about a year journey to get to closure and actually having a benefit.

Nicolas Catoggio: But I would expect that to be very good. Most of it is F '28.

Operator: We will take our next question from David Palmer with Evercore ISI.

David Palmer: First and most importantly, I'm thinking of and praying for Rob and his family. Secondly, I wanted to ask about foodservice. It's always an interesting area, and there's a lot going on. It looks like egg prices are at historic lows. You're dealing with freight costs as well, and you're seeing some AI influences away. Could you talk about the key dynamics going on for the industry and for you that are driving your expectations? We went below $125 million on EBITDA this last quarter. I'm just trying to think about how we should be thinking about the quarterly cadence of EBITDA for that segment through the year.

Matt Mainer: Sure. So maybe starting with the last piece there. We did obviously say we see Q1 in a similar territory as Q4 -- and really, the driver there is a couple of things. You alluded to both. But in Q4, we saw some inflationary pressures mainly around freight and packaging that impacted the quarter. Additionally, we talked about we got back to a normalized supply, got back to a normalized inventory really at the end of Q3. So didn't have any ability to really arbitrage some of those lower egg markets anymore. What they are doing at historic lows and they put a little pressure on volumes on the egg side just as an alternative to customers that can switch.

That's a much smaller subset of our business, but that's put a little bit of volume pressure. We see that as transitory. As we step back and look at the overall industry, there is a vast oversupply, we believe, in terms of what's driving that -- those historically low shell eggs. We don't think that is actually something that can be sustained. So we expect that transitory piece to take care of itself sooner rather than later. The other piece is on the freight and packaging side on the inflation. As we mentioned, we actually have pricing that will hit market in Q2. So we're addressing that with pricing.

So I think sequentially, you should see improvement in Q2, and then we would expect some growth in the back half of the year and we get back on track on the volume side as well.

David Palmer: Are you seeing any dynamics either in the industry? It feels like the fast food industry is getting a little bit better lately. And/or is there a diminishing appetite for value-added or even liquid eggs given what's going on with cracked eggs lately? Any dynamics there that are also maybe weighing on the recent EBITDA that you have to kind of work through in '27? And I'll pass it on.

Matt Mainer: Yes. I don't -- we don't see any changes to the fundamental value proposition of the business, still very strong demand. We see a lot of opportunity for the business. We've just got some near-term headwinds, one on the cost side, one on a little bit of a competitive alternative, but still see good demand there and the value proposition, as a reminder, is taking labor out of the operator system. That's obviously a very expensive piece. So no change to the underlying expectations.

Operator: We will take our next question from Tom Palmer with JPMorgan.

Thomas Palmer: When thinking across the guidance range, I know you don't guide for top line, but when you think about the guidance range, how much of an improvement do you need or do you embed at least when thinking about next year's guidance versus the growth rates that we've been seeing here in the back half of the year?

Matt Mainer: Yes. I mean, again, we're not a volume-driven business and a top line-driven business, more focused on bottom line. So don't have a guide for top line. Obviously, cereal category and pet categories where we play right now are still having declines just in terms of category dynamics, so I wouldn't expect outperforming that. Foodservice, we would expect some growth. But again, that's a cost-plus model. So you got to be careful with the top line modeling just because it's -- as prices come down in terms of our grain-based model, that could decline sales and vice versa if they increase. And then I think that really covers the bulk of the portfolio.

So not giving you a lot of help there, but I don't think it's really a top line-driven exercise for us in terms of beyond the pricing impact.

Thomas Palmer: Okay. No, understood. I was really just trying to understand if mid- to high single-digit declines would kind of impair that outlook or if it can absorb it. The year is back half weighted, and I know you've highlighted costs versus pricing as kind of a key driver. Are there other reasons for the back half weighting that we should be keeping in mind?

Matt Mainer: No, that's really the key driver. We talked about it last quarter with our preliminary outlook. The only thing that has changed is we saw some acceleration of some inflationary pockets that we will address or are addressing with pricing. And then we're seeing more inflation showing up by midyear on the commodity side, and we will react to that. Our expectation is with pricing in the second half. So that's really just the phasing of that. It's not a change in overall expectations. It's just a change in timing.

Nicolas Catoggio: I would add one thing in PCB specifically, there's a lot that is going to happen in cost out in pet and there's a full pipeline of very concrete initiatives. Many of them actually hit in the second half of the year as well. So that's outside of anything footprint related also just productivity and cost savings and those tend to be more back half than [indiscernible].

Operator: [Operator Instructions] We will take our next question from Marc Torrente with Wells Fargo.

Marc Torrente: Wishing the best for Rob as well. On PCB were quite strong. I think there were some one-timers in there, but what drove the upside in the quarter on the underlying -- it looks like mix back into it was positive on the core piece. What were the other puts and takes there? And then any other color on progress on the 8th Avenue integration and synergy realization to date?

Nicolas Catoggio: You help me with that one because I was going to say -- so PCB had a really good quarter in general. So -- and you mentioned both. So first, if you remember, we've been talking about as we compare our volume performance with the category, we're running a couple of percentage points below the category. Half of that has been Malt-O-Meal exclusion. The other half was intentional was we changed our assortment in the food channel to better align kind of the promotional bundles, but also drive some price realization. In a quarter where there's the category promotional activity is normal, let's say, like Q4 was, then you get the full benefit of our mix.

And so PCB had a really outstanding mix in Q4. And mix, I mean, everything that you can think of mix. Our premium portfolio performed extremely well. We gained -- continue gaining market share with our premium portfolio. That helps a lot. And then our pack mix within the brands actually was really, really strong. Again, that is essentially the initiative that we work on throughout the year. The other one is 8th Avenue. 8th Avenue is performing extremely well, not only the synergies, the business performance was very, very solid in Q4. So we exited the year with a run rate ahead of what we estimated as synergies.

We are probably closer to $20 million of synergies run rate by now, we -- again, that's excluding the peanut butter footprint that's on top of.

Marc Torrente: Okay. I appreciate that. And then you touched on this earlier a little bit. Just on capital allocation. First, it sounds like you still feel well positioned to be opportunistic on M&A. But then absent M&A, you're leaning more into debt paydown. Maybe just how aggressive will you be there? And how does that balance with ongoing share repurchases?

Matt Mainer: Sure. So again, it's not to say we won't do share repurchases. But I think I don't really want to put an absolute number on the split between the 2, but I think favor would be definitely more than 50% of capital allocation towards debt versus share repurchases would be our starting point. And obviously, that can fluctuate if we see interest rates pull back and start to improve. And there's a number of other factors, including our own multiple that goes into that equation.

But just a nod to, hey, we've got to take some actions to address debt maturities and just reduce some of the overall debt out there given what we're seeing in terms of refinancing rates these days.

Operator: We will take our next question from Rob Dickerson with U.S. Bancorp BTIG.

Robert Dickerson: And all my best to Rob, of course, and his family. So look, I just kind of bigger picture right now, the company is basically almost back to the EBITDA margin around 20% kind of pre-COVID, let's say, we still say that. And I realize this kind of business model overall, a little less top line driven, more like you just said, kind of bottom line profit driven. When we look at that advertising line, it looks like it did decline maybe like 25% last year, like I think it's almost like 40% over the past 2 years. And I'm just kind of curious what's driving that?

Like is that kind of more the push model, let's say, isn't -- like hasn't really been that effective. So like why waste the money, why not just capture the profit? And then just kind of curious like how you're thinking about just advertising in general as we kind of go through '27 vis-a-vis costs, et cetera?

Nicolas Catoggio: Yes. So as you think about advertising, most of the decline has been in pet. Some of that has been advertising, so moved from the advertising line to net sales. We just decided to use a different marketing mix and do things that hit net sales versus advertising. And some of was essentially, we were not getting the return on some of the advertising spend. So in pet, we are now focused on Nutrish. We are sustaining the support for Nutrish. And the rest of the brands, we are essentially supporting more with kind of above-the-line tactics, promotions or consumer promotions, but more targeted things.

In grocery, the support -- so we are also focusing on fewer brands, but we are sustaining the support, and that's still, Honey Bunches of Oats, Oreo O's, those brands are getting full support and nothing has changed. What has changed is the way we are supporting the brands. We are 100% digital. We reduced -- we increased the working A&C, reduced the nonworking A&C, so we are more efficient. So -- but we haven't reduced the support for the brands, the actual support for the brands, and we feel really good about those brands. In those ones, we get really good returns on our advertising spend.

Operator: We will take our next question from Carla Casella.

Carla Casella: I'm wondering if you have further divestiture opportunities like you've done with cheese and with pasta from the 8th Avenue. And then you've divested some businesses, you've exited some private or lower-margin business. What are your thoughts on the manufacturing base, whether there's more opportunity to consolidate or would you enter into some other private brand business to help fill manufacturing space?

Matt Mainer: Yes. So I think just in terms of divestitures, we've said this across our portfolio, we're open to opportunities depending on valuation. So I think no definitive path there, but we'd certainly evaluate every opportunity in front of us.

Nicolas Catoggio: So we're always open again and opportunistic on all ideas. I have to say though, with all the footprint work that we have been doing, once that's done, we will be operating at a pretty high capacity utilization. So it's not that we will have a lot of capacity to go after opportunities. So -- but we're always open and we're always considering whether that's select private label opportunities, co-man opportunities. We are always considering those and having the conversations, but we will not have a lot of capacity.

Carla Casella: Okay. Great. And then do you -- how much do you do today of private brand? And do you see that changing over time? And would you go into other categories where you haven't done private brand, but you already manufacturer?

Nicolas Catoggio: I would actually say in PCB, probably 20% to 25% of our business is private label, private brands. And it varies a little bit by category. In categories like peanut butter, we have a higher percentage of our businesses, private label and granola are the same. And then we are selectively exploring those opportunities. We have some private label private brand business in Weetabix. We have some as we have been talking in this is within Bob Evans. So we are -- again, we are probably more than any other CPG always open to the idea of actually producing private label. But around -- right now, I would say it's around 20% to 25% of our business.

Operator: Thank you. At this time, there are no further questions in the queue. This concludes today's Post Holdings Fourth Quarter and Fiscal Year 2026 Earnings Conference Call and Webcast. Please disconnect your line at this time, and have a wonderful day.

#3148. With Mortgage Rates Rising, Should You Hibernate Until Spring?

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

#3144. PepsiCo Has Raised Its Dividend by a Total of 37% Over the Last 5 Years. I Predict $10,000 Invested in It Today Will Pay This Much in Dividends Over the Next Decade.

The beverage and snack powerhouse’s stock may be underperforming, but its quarterly payouts keep on coming.

By James Brumley – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:40PM EST

On Wall Street, the experts regularly remind us that past performance is no guarantee of future results. However, when not much about a company is changing, it can be a pretty good indication of what the future likely holds.

With that as the backdrop, what does PepsiCo (PEP +1.54%) stock's past performance tell us about how this ticker will perform? Specifically, how much dividend income might a $10,000 stake in the company bought today generate over the course of, say, the next 10 years?

Here's what we know: Since this point in 2021, PepsiCo has increased its quarterly dividend from $1.075 per share to $1.48 per share. That's an annualized growth rate of 6.6%. Assuming the beverage company maintains that pace of increases -- and that's plenty plausible -- by mid-2036, its quarterly payout should be $2.80 per share.

Figuring out how much dividend income a $10,000 position in PepsiCo will produce in the meantime isn't quite as simple, but still certainly calculable. En route from $1.48 per share per quarter now to $2.80 per share then, assuming equal-sized annual hikes, each share will produce a total of $85.60 in dividend payments in the meantime. And since $10,000 will purchase about 70 shares at its current price near $142, a position of this size should pay out about $5,992 in dividend income over this stretch, then about $784 per year at that point.

Don't forget that PepsiCo shares are also likely to deliver some price appreciation of their own in the meantime, too. While it's certainly no growth stock, those gains would bolster your total returns.

Also, if you don't actually need these cash payments to cover your expenses during this stretch, reinvesting any dividends you collect along the way would leave you with a measurably bigger stake in this income holding. In fact, over the past 10 years, reinvesting PepsiCo's dividend payments would have built a position that's 36% bigger than the one you'd be holding had you not reinvested these payments in more shares of the ticker paying them. That would raise the annual dividend payment for a new $10,000 position opened today to a little over $1,000 by that time.

#3142. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3141. Every AI Agent Needs An Owner

Jesse Stockall is Chief Architect, Flexera.

​AI agents have officially moved from controlled pilots into everyday enterprise workflows. While this shift unlocks increased productivity, it risks creating a new layer of technology sprawl. Agents can access data, trigger actions and consume resources with limited human involvement. That makes them fundamentally different from much of the software enterprises are accustomed to managing.​

Enterprises spent the first phase of generative AI asking, “What can we automate?” As agents move into production, architects now have to answer a harder set of questions: Who is accountable for them? What are they allowed to do? What should the business be willing to spend on them?​

Negative consequences are not inherent to AI agents themselves, but they can emerge when organizations deploy agents faster than they establish the visibility and accountability needed to manage them. With key provisions of the EU AI Act having taken effect in August 2026, governance expectations around AI are also becoming increasingly concrete.​

Beyond determining whether an agent can be connected, organizations must understand how they will identify, govern, observe and ultimately retire each agent. Every AI agent needs an owner because ownership provides the operating model for enforcing standards, governing costs, accounting for actions and scaling agents responsibly within enterprise architecture.​

Here are a few key steps for building sound agentic architecture:​

Autonomy makes accountability essential. An owner is more than the person who built the agent: they are accountable for its purpose, compliance with enterprise standards, access to systems and data, authority to act, outputs, costs and retirement.​

Ownership should follow the agent throughout its lifecycle and remain tied to an accountable person or team, just as the agent itself is tied to a distinct identity. Ninety-five percent of enterprises worldwide now have at least one company-funded agent-enabled workflow in production, with the average organization running roughly 11 across different functional areas. As that number grows, informal ownership will become increasingly difficult to sustain. If nobody can identify who is responsible for an agent after deployment, the organization does not truly control that agent.​

Every cost, resource, license and action should be visible and attributable to an accountable user, whether human or autonomous.​

Enterprises cannot assign accountability for agents they do not know exist, making a complete view of where agents are deployed and who is responsible for them essential. This challenge will only grow as agent adoption accelerates. Gartner forecasted that the average global Fortune 500 company could have more than 150,000 AI agents in use by 2028, up from fewer than 15 in 2025.

Foundational questions all architects should be able to answer are:

• What agents are running across the enterprise?

• What permissions have they been granted?

AI activity can span models, SaaS applications, infrastructure, agents and employees. Every autonomous action must be traceable to its originating agent and accountable owner, with an audit trail and a clear path to rollback.

Multi-agent systems, in which one agent delegates work to specialized subagents, have become a real architectural pattern. Companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI both have systems that support multi-agent architectures where a “manager” agent coordinates work across multiple specialized agents.

Traditional access controls answer an important question: “What can this system reach?” Agentic architecture also must answer another one: “What is this agent actually allowed to do once it gets there?”

Agents need enforceable boundaries beyond basic access control: limits on the actions they may execute autonomously, human approval thresholds for higher-risk actions, cost and budget thresholds, and shutdown mechanisms when behavior falls outside defined standards or expectations.

Agent architecture must therefore govern more than access. It must set standards for how and when agents may act, make their decisions about how and when to act, ensure actions are traceable to an accountable owner, and enforce limits on what those actions may cost.

Cost should not sit outside agentic architecture as a reporting exercise conducted after deployment. Instead, it should remain a constraint an agent is designed to operate within.

An agent that delivers $100,000 of business value may justify substantial consumption, while an agent performing a low-value administrative task may not. Organizations therefore need cost attribution by agent and use case, visibility into consumption and enforceable budget thresholds. Because one workflow can consume models, tokens, infrastructure, SaaS resources and licenses across the technology stack, those costs must be assigned to an accountable human or non-human user rather than left in disconnected reports.

For architects, the goal should be to make an agent’s economic activity as visible and attributable as its technical activity, with both tied to an accountable owner. AI optimization should maximize return rather than simply minimize spend. Mission-critical applications and agents may warrant different spending limits based on their business importance, but those limits should be explicit, measurable and governed.

The lesson from cloud and SaaS is that governance becomes much harder once adoption is already widespread. Enterprises have an opportunity now to avoid repeating that pattern with AI agents.

Agents should enter the technology estate with ownership, visibility, standards, controls and economic accountability already attached. Before an agent enters production, you should be able to answer four questions:

3. How will its actions be traced and reviewed?

4. What is it worth spending on, and where will that cost be assigned?

The enterprises that scale agents successfully will not necessarily be the ones that deploy the most. They will be the ones whose architectures make every agent, resource, cost and action visible, attributable and controllable from the start.​​

Atmos Rewards offers six communities, each with its own travel perks and opportunities to earn bonus points

Atmos Rewards is the airline loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. One of its newer features is Atmos Communities, which offer additional rewards and benefits tailored to different travel interests.

There are six communities, including two reserved for Alaska and Hawaii residents. The other four are open to members regardless of where they live. But don’t get caught up in the community names. The best choice for you may depend more on your travel plans than the groupings suggest.

Here’s how to decide which Atmos Community best fits your travel patterns.

Atmos Communities are like groups within the Atmos Rewards program that offer additional benefits based on different travel interests.

They’re free to join for Atmos Rewards members. Four communities are available to all members, while community Club 49 is reserved for Alaska residents and community Huaka’i by Hawaiian is reserved for Hawaii residents.

You can belong to only one community at a time and switch communities once per calendar year. Consider your upcoming travel plans before choosing.

Joining a community is easy: Log in to your Atmos Rewards account and navigate to “Account overview.” Select “Join a Community,” browse the options and click the “Join” button under the one you choose.

Each Atmos Community has a list of 10 destinations where members can earn bonus points and status points. Although the destinations differ by community, the rewards structure is the same.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, members can earn up to 10,000 bonus points and 10,000 status points by visiting qualifying destinations.

Here’s how many points you’ll earn as you reach each milestone:

Visit one destination, earn 100 status and bonus points.

Visit two destinations, earn 200 status and bonus points.

Visit three destinations, earn 300 status and bonus points.

Visit four destinations, earn 400 status and bonus points.

Visit five destinations, earn 500 status and bonus points.

Visit six destinations, earn 750 status and bonus points.

Visit seven destinations, earn 1,000 status and bonus points.

Visit eight destinations, earn 1,250 status and bonus points.

Visit nine destinations, earn 2,500 status and bonus points.

Visit 10 destinations, earn 3,000 status and bonus points.

The first member of each community to visit all 10 qualifying destinations during the challenge period will also earn 100,000 bonus points.

New lists of qualifying destinations for each community take effect on Jan. 1, 2028.

Here’s a closer look at the six communities, their benefits and the destinations eligible for bonus points.

Global Locals is geared toward frequent international travelers. Benefits include:

Earn 10% more status points toward Atmos elite status on flights that begin and/or end outside the U.S., including award flights.

Earn 1 status point for every 25 points transferred to Atmos Rewards from Bilt or Marriott Bonvoy.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these 10 Oneworld Alliance hubs count toward bonus points and status points. Qualifying layovers also count toward the destination challenge, so you don’t necessarily need to make these cities your final stop.

If you frequently travel internationally or have any upcoming flights through any of these airports, including qualifying layovers, Global Locals might be a fit for you.

If you have the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, you’ll earn 3 Atmos points per $1 spent on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, dining and foreign transactions. The last bonus category can be especially useful for frequent international travelers.

This community has a similar setup to Global Locals, but most of its bonus destinations are in the U.S. Here’s what you can get:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

This community would be an excellent choice if your upcoming travels include several of these airports, even if dining isn't the main reason for your trips. If dining out is one of your favorite activities, check out the best credit cards for restaurants.

Active Escapes focuses on airports in outdoor-oriented destinations that are all in the U.S., save one. Benefits here are:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

While these airports are gateways to national parks and other natural attractions, you don’t have to be an outdoor enthusiast to benefit. Like before, don’t let the heading sway you. Rather, consider the destinations before you decide.

Families On the Go might appeal to you if you redeem Atmos Rewards for your children. Benefits include:

Get 20% of your points back on eligible award flights for kids 12 and under after you complete your trip.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these destinations qualify for bonus points and status points:

This community may be especially valuable if you regularly book award flights for children 12 and under. Even if you don't travel with kids, it could be worth considering if its qualifying airports align better with your travel plans than those of other communities.

Exclusively for Alaska residents, Club 49 offers rewards that are focused on travel to, from and within the state:

Two free checked bags when traveling to or from Alaska on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines.

Three free checked bags when traveling within Alaska on Alaska Airlines.

Two Travel Now discounts per year for 30% off one-way refundable Y-class fares on Alaska Airlines, booked within four days of departure for travel to, from or within Alaska.

Ship cargo within Alaska for $49 plus tax (weight, size and content limits apply).

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Baggage benefits don’t combine with other free checked bag allowances, such as those that come with some Alaska credit cards. However, they apply to everyone traveling on the same reservation.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus offers:

While this community is only for Alaskans, you might decide one of the other communities more closely matches your travel plans — especially if you already have an Alaska credit card with free baggage benefits. However, if you ship a lot of cargo or think you’ll use the Travel Now discounts, those are special benefits that may sway you to choose Club 49.

Hawaii residents have their own community just for them: Huaka’i by Hawaiian. It offers benefits focused on interisland travel:

Two free checked bags on neighbor island flights on Hawaiian Airlines, including sports equipment like surfboards and golf bags.

Quarterly fare discounts of 10% off one neighbor island booking, or 20% off for eligible Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® and Atmos™ Rewards Visa® cardholders.

Earn 50% more points and status points on flights between Hawaiian islands beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

The 10 destinations eligible for bonus points through Dec. 31, 2027 are:

Seven destinations are in Hawaii, with one on the mainland and two international cities. If you live in Hawaii and like to hop between islands, this community is a strong choice.

Don’t be persuaded by the names of the communities. Look a little deeper, because there’s a lot of overlap between destination lists. Compare the options against your upcoming travel plans.

You can change communities once per calendar year, so you aren’t locked in to your initial choice indefinitely. However, switching communities resets your destination-challenge progress, but you’ll retain any points you’ve already earned.

If your home airport (or one you visit frequently) is already on a community’s list, you may have an easier time earning points. Also consider whether a particular community benefit, such as free checked bags or points back on award flights for kids, outweighs the destination challenge.

Finally, pay attention to airport codes. For example, Tokyo’s Narita (NRT) and Haneda (HND) appear on different community lists. New York’s qualifying airport is JFK, while it is DCA in Washington, D.C. If you have a choice between airports, check which one qualifies for your community’s challenge.

#3138. Why Intuit Stock Crashed Today

Investors are selling Intuit -- but the stock looks cheap.

By Rich Smith – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:44PM EST

Intuit (INTU -11.18%) stock tumbled 8.3% through 12:15 p.m. ET Friday despite beating earnings estimates last night.

Analysts forecast that Intuit would earn only $2.70 per share on $4.31 billion in sales in its fiscal Q1 2027. Intuit actually earned $2.91 per share (pro forma) on $4.35 billion in sales.

CEO Sasan Goodarzi called the results "solid," with revenue rising 12% year over year, led by the Global Business Solutions division with 15% growth. Consumer revenue underperformed at 7% growth, and the company's Mailchimp marketing platform saw revenue decline 1%.

(Don't worry about that last bit, though, because Intuit -- perhaps disappointed by the business's performance -- now says it is selling Mailchimp to Bending Spoons (BSP -1.34%) for approximately $3.7 billion, paid $3.3 billion in cash plus $368 million in Bending Spoons stock.)

As regards earnings, the "$2.91" was only non-GAAP. Actual earnings, calculated under generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP), for the quarter were only $2.59 -- but still up 63% year over year.

Intuit did give investors GAAP guidance on what to expect for the rest of its fiscal 2027, but the news wasn't quite as good. Revenue is forecast between $23.1 billion and $23.4 billion -- no more than 9% growth, again led by Global Business Solutions. Earnings per share are expected to grow less quickly than in Q1 -- but still pretty quick, rising about 23% to $20.24 per share.

Assuming Intuit hits that mark, at its current $284 share price, the stock would be trading at only 14 times current-year earnings -- quite cheap for a 23% grower.

The bad news is that most analysts doubt Intuit can keep growing at this rate long-term. Average analyst forecasts are closer to 13.5% growth. Between the growth rate and the 1.8% dividend yield, though, I still see Intuit stock as at worst fairly priced -- and probably a bit of a bargain.

#3137. Systems Of Record, Systems Of Action And The Parts Of The Enterprise That Still Don't Have A System

Kunal Chopra is the CEO of Certivo, an AI-powered compliance system of record for global manufacturers.

​I’ve spent most of my career building enterprise software, and the pattern I keep returning to is simple: A business function matures when it gets a system. Before that, it runs on people, spreadsheets and inboxes. After that, it can be measured, scaled and audited. AI is now changing what a system can do, which makes it worth asking which functions still don’t have one.

A system brings that knowledge into one place everyone can rely on. It defines what data counts, who owns it and what happens next, so a company can run the same process a thousand times without depending on the one person who remembers how it’s done. Few systems fully achieve a single source of truth, but the ones that come closest become the foundation the rest of the business is built on.

Geoffrey Moore popularized the term “systems of record” in a 2011 white paper for AIIM, describing the transactional systems companies had relied on for decades. A system of record is the authoritative source of truth for a domain. Other teams trust it because it agrees with itself.​

CRM holds customers, contacts and opportunities, while ERP holds orders, inventory and financials. SCM manages suppliers, purchase orders and logistics, and PLM tracks parts, bills of materials and engineering changes. Each one made its function legible to the rest of the company, which is why a CFO can close the books and a sales leader can forecast with confidence.

Systems of record store state, and people have done the work around them: reading documents, reconciling records, deciding what to do and entering the result. AI is moving that work into the system itself. A system of action uses the system of record as its foundation, reads incoming information, interprets it against rules and context and takes the next step: updating the record, requesting a missing document or routing an exception to the right person. Customer support teams already use agents that resolve routine tickets end to end, and finance teams use them for invoice matching and reconciliation.​

The system of record becomes more valuable in this model, because every action depends on the quality of the data and rules underneath it. Leaders evaluating a system of action should ask which actions it takes on its own and which go to a person for approval, how each action traces back to its source and logic and how it handles cases where its confidence is low. In regulated work, those answers need to be reproducible and auditable.

​Compliance is the clearest example I know. A manufacturer has to show that its products meet requirements such as REACH, RoHS and PFAS reporting rules. The evidence for that lives everywhere. Supplier declarations arrive as email attachments. Safety data sheets sit in shared drives. A question about a substance gets answered in a Teams thread, and a supplier’s change notice shows up in Slack. Part data lives in PLM, supplier records in ERP and SCM and customer requests in CRM.​

When a customer asks whether a product contains a restricted substance, someone pulls the answer together by hand from all of those places. PwC’s 2025 Global Compliance Survey found that 85% of respondents say compliance requirements have grown more complex over the past three years, so that manual assembly is getting harder every year.​

Compliance went without a system for three reasons. It cuts across every other function, so no single system was a natural home. Teams treated it as a periodic project, which made spreadsheets seem good enough. Its data was also too unstructured for traditional software to handle. In an earlier article, I wrote about how AI-native software can work with data in whatever format it arrives. That removes the third barrier, and it means compliance can build its system of record and its system of action at the same time.

Compliance isn’t the only function in this position. Ashu Garg of Foundation Capital has argued that systems of record capture outcomes but not the reasoning behind them. A VP approves a discount in a Slack message, and the CRM records the final price without the approval or the rationale. The same is true of a waiver for a nonconforming part, an extension on supplier payment terms or an exception granted to a key customer.​

Those decisions shape how a company operates, and the precedent they set is often more valuable than the transaction itself. Today that context lives in chat threads, meeting notes and people’s memories. As AI agents take on more work, the absence of a record of why decisions were made becomes a practical constraint, because an agent can’t follow a precedent it can’t see.

The functions that lack a system tend to share three traits: the work crosses departments, the data lives in conversations and documents and the process depends on judgment. Those were the conditions that kept traditional software out. AI is making them workable.​

Where else in your enterprise is important work still happening without a system?​

Tech's slide has put losses on the books in some taxable accounts, and there are six weeks left to use them. Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a big reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

#3132. Why Physical AI Works In A Demo And Struggles In Your Business

Maria Zhang is the CEO and Co-Founder of Palona.

Physical AI must understand the operation and keep that understanding accurate as conditions change.​

A physical AI demo can make a difficult problem look solved. But it establishes what the system can do under the conditions shown. A business needs that capability to hold as workloads, layouts and routines change.

The gap between AI adoption and business value is familiar. McKinsey’s 2026 survey (login required) found nearly nine in 10 respondents reported AI use in at least one business function within their organizations. Only about 6% reported both significant impact and at least 5% of earnings before interest and taxes attributable to AI.

In my previous article, I explored a coding agent for physical businesses. Delivering that promise requires a reliable, continuously updated understanding of the operation.

In many knowledge-intensive applications, a foundation model needs specialized knowledge: a law firm’s precedents, internal policies or proprietary history.

Much of that context already exists in documents or structured records. Retrieval supplies relevant material, fine-tuning adapts models to specialized tasks and workflow integration connects them to the business.

Physical businesses need these capabilities, too. They also contain important information that has never been recorded.

An order system may record when work began and ended without showing where an employee waited or which handoff stalled. A language model cannot retrieve events the system never captured.

Physical AI must observe that activity and interpret its business meaning, drawing on knowledge of the operation. This is part of perception.

Consider measuring how quickly a restaurant line moves. Detecting people does not distinguish someone waiting to order from someone collecting food or waiting for a friend.

An experienced operator reads relationships and context. The AI must understand what people are doing, how interactions change and when the evidence is incomplete.

A staffing recommendation can be logically consistent with the reported queue while responding to a queue that does not exist. Strong reasoning can still produce the wrong decision from a mistaken account of the operation.​

Vision-language-action models, or VLAs, connect visual observations and language instructions to actions. World models learn how environments evolve to support prediction and planning. Simulation and digital twins provide virtual environments for training and testing; their usefulness depends on fidelity to relevant conditions.

These capabilities can support different architectures. An end-to-end system that observes, plans and acts may be appropriate for some applications.

A modular approach connects foundation models, domain knowledge, business rules and workflow systems through explicit interfaces.

I believe a useful boundary is the translation from physical observations into meaningful operational states.

The system might estimate that a customer is waiting, an order is ready or a task is blocked. Recorded events, such as an observed handoff, help track state changes.

For business decisions, this is more useful than object detections or generic captions.

Much of the business problem can then be expressed symbolically: as people, objects, events, relationships and rules. Language models, planners and workflow systems can use these representations to evaluate alternatives and coordinate action.

The representation must preserve timing, evidence and uncertainty. A robot may still require detailed geometry; an order-status decision can often use a more abstract description.

This boundary makes the system more modular. Changing an acceptable wait-time threshold need not require retraining the model that recognizes when service begins. It also helps teams distinguish observation or interpretation errors from failures in reasoning, planning or execution.

For operators, “The order is ready, but no handoff has been observed” is something they can check. If the handoff area was out of view, missing evidence cannot establish that no handoff occurred.

The goal is meaningful points of inspection, without requiring every internal neural representation to be explainable.

Camera placement, resolution and viewing angle affect what can be observed. Lighting, obstructions, connectivity and packaging changes affect whether the complete system keeps working. A strong model cannot reliably recover information its installation never captures. Even when the information is available, conditions that differ from training and testing can expose weaknesses.

Starbucks’s inventory-counting rollout illustrates the challenge. In September 2025, NomadGo announced deployment to more than 11,000 North American locations, advertising 99% accuracy.

Fast Company reported refrigerator reflections doubling milk counts, Wi-Fi failures erasing scan progress and packaging changes that could require weeks of adaptation. Reuters reported that Starbucks retired the tool in May 2026, citing standardization and consistency.

Reliable operation depends on the model, its inputs, software and workflow together.

A model can work, and the deployment can still fail.

Reliability requires good models, systems engineering and sustained work with customers. Operators reveal exceptions and environmental changes that should inform model development, evaluation and installation practices.

This is why we are developing Interaction Tracking as a primary modeling objective. Many meaningful changes in an operation are expressed through interactions among people and objects, within particular spaces and workflows. Tracking those interactions can estimate the business states that downstream reasoning needs.​

For buyers, the important questions extend beyond what the demo can do: What does the system actually understand, how can that understanding be checked and how will the vendor keep it reliable as conditions change? For investors, the company’s technical advantage deserves examination at the level of the complete deployed system.

A system can reason convincingly about the wrong situation and execute the wrong action precisely. Closing physical AI’s deployment gap means maintaining a reliable understanding of the operation as it changes.​

#3131. Is Altria's 5.6% Dividend Yield Too Good to Be True Heading Into 2027?

The company is doing well for a business selling highly unpopular products.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 20, 2026 at 12:56PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Altria Group ›

One of the great dividends of our age is paid by a company making products so unfashionable they're barely visible anymore. I'm talking about Altria (MO +0.86%), the latest iteration of a storied tobacco enterprise that created and still sells the iconic Marlboro brand in this country.

Several decades ago, it was rare to visit a household, office, or restaurant where at least one occupant wasn't lighting up. These days, it's normal to go days, weeks, even months without encountering any smokers. The cigarettes that remain the hard core of Altria's production to this day aren't a growing market. So it's worthwhile to explore whether the company's famously high-yield dividend -- which currently pays out at 5.6% -- is sustainable for much longer. Here's my take on that.

Given the many restrictions on traditional tobacco consumption in the U.S., plus the increasing health consciousness of its population, it's a wonder Altria ekes out any growth at all. In the company's third quarter, its net revenue only crept up by 1% year over year to $6.13 billion. If we strip excise (or "sin") taxes out of the equation, we get a meatier growth figure of 3.6%, with revenue net of such obligations of $5.44 billion. But that improvement was largely due to price increases, as total shipment volume of smokeables sank by 2.9%.

Revenue net of excise taxes, by the way, is considered the yardstick top-line figure for tobacco companies, so I'll stay with that throughout this piece without repeating the descriptor.

Of that $5.44 billion, smokeable products -- anchored by Marlboro -- pulled in $4.76 billion, or 88% of the total. Almost all of the remainder ($667 million) consisted of oral tobacco products, the revenue for which rose only marginally during the period. There's one bright spot there, however, and that's the company's promising on! and on! PLUS nicotine pouches, which collectively experienced a 13% increase in shipment volume.

Years ago, Altria sensibly tried to pivot toward products with a brighter future, specifically next-generation tobacco offerings seen as more innovative and (relatively) healthier. But its attempts to develop a vape in-house flopped, as did its acquisitions of stakes in existing vape manufacturers (most notably the spectacular flameout of the once-promising Juul Labs). These days, the company's "all other" category covers the tiny sales of such goods, which amounted to $12 million in the quarter.

Non-GAAP (adjusted) profitability, like revenue, didn't bounce sharply higher for Altria. It improved by 4% to $2.55 billion in the quarter. This, however, makes for a sky-high net margin of 47%. Most companies would be satisfied with a percentage in the low double digits. What's the secret sauce with Altria?

It's about the core product. Cigarettes are addictive, so users not only come back time and again to buy them, but they're also willing to put up with the frequent price raises by makers like Altria (and to fork over the always-high excise taxes to boot). Given that, there's little or no reason for a manufacturer to innovate the product, and to top it all off, cigarettes are cheap to make.

Put all of this together, and you have a good that generates high profits at very modest and steady costs. That's why, even in this day and age, tobacco companies continue to be cash-generating machines. Altria's statement of cash flows is always a thing of beauty, with high operating flows and tiny investments resulting in a mighty gush of free cash flow (FCF). This was only slightly down year over year in the third quarter, to almost $3 billion. That's far more than the under $1.8 billion the company needed to fund that high-yield dividend, plus stock-boosting share repurchases totaling $400 million.

American smokers aren't going to change their habits much, so Altria felt confident enough to raise its full-year 2026 earnings guidance. Adjusted net income should rise by 4.5% to 6% over the 2025 figure to $5.66 to $5.74 per share, the company believes. All that cash flow has to go somewhere, so the company's board authorized a $1 billion expansion of its existing share repurchase program, which had $265 million remaining. The initiative has also been extended, with the new deadline being Dec. 31, 2027.

Both of these moves strongly indicate Altria will keep its now 57-year (!) dividend raise streak alive, maintaining its status as a Dividend King (one of the few stocks that have raised their payout for at least 50 consecutive years). After all, its payout is one of the stock's great draws, and management is acutely aware of its importance. I predict, with the same level of confidence as Altria's leaders announced the guidance raise and the share buyback news, that it'll continue to deliver those high-margin profits and impressive levels of FCF.

And with that, this perpetually high-yield dividend is extremely safe, in my opinion.
