#3125. If I Could Only Own 1 Trillion-Dollar Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Through 2030, It Would Be Anthropic, Nvidia, or Alphabet. Here’s My Top Pick.

Nvidia's falling valuation and Anthropic's IPO may make them tempting buys right now, but Alphabet presents an interesting long-term investment opportunity.

By Adam Spatacco – Nov 20, 2026 at 1:00PM EST

The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has created some of the largest companies in stock market history. Nvidia (NVDA -10.69%) has evolved into an indispensable supplier of AI computing infrastructure, while Anthropic (ANT -10.16%) finally made its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) on Nov. 19. Meanwhile, Alphabet (GOOGL -0.83%) (GOOG -0.71%) is rapidly integrating AI services throughout its ecosystem of consumer and enterprise products.

All three companies offer exposure to the AI industry, but in different ways. This makes their respective risk profiles considerably different. Nvidia is facing an unprecedented leadership transition, while Anthropic must justify an enormous valuation while financing hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure commitments.

For investors looking to buy one trillion-dollar AI stock among this trio and hold it through 2030, Alphabet stands out as the most compelling choice.

Nvidia's financial performance makes it difficult to dismiss as an investment. During the company's fiscal third quarter, revenue surged 103% year over year to $115.8 billion while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 111% to $2.68. Management projected fourth-quarter revenue to land around $130 billion. This demonstrates how demand for Nvidia's accelerated computing platforms remains exceptionally strong.

Nevertheless, investing in Nvidia now comes with considerable uncertainty following founder Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation amid allegations involving ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang spent decades shaping Nvidia's technological roadmap, developer ecosystem, and relationships with critical supply chain partners. His departure raises legitimate questions about whether the company can maintain its founder-driven culture of innovation under new leadership.

Competition presents another challenge. Alphabet, Amazon, and other hyperscalers are developing custom AI accelerators to reduce their dependence on Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs). Although Nvidia's CUDA software platform creates switching costs, the expansion of custom silicon into the broader chip landscape could eventually pressure the company's market share and pricing power.

Although Nvidia could overcome these obstacles, its long-term investment thesis increasingly depends on a successful leadership transition and continued technological edge. For investors prioritizing durability through 2030, those uncertainties are difficult to ignore.

Anthropic presents a different investment proposition. The developer of Claude has experienced historic growth, with its annualized revenue run rate reaching $81 billion in October. As I write this (Nov. 19), Anthropic stock is trading around $95 and boasts a market cap around $1.2 trillion.

Anthropic needs to prove that accelerating revenue growth can actually translate into sustainable profitability. According to its S-1 filing, Anthropic has $900.9 billion in infrastructure requirements extending over the next two decades. These obligations create financial risks because developing and operating frontier AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, electricity, and capital.

Anthropic's disclosed arrangements include commitments of $121.3 billion to Google through July 2033, at least $110 billion to Amazon, and approximately $47.2 billion to Microsoft through June 2033. Many of these commitments require minimum payments regardless of actual compute usage, meaning Anthropic still needs to generate sufficient revenue and maintain access to financing to support its expansion, even if customer demand falls short of expectations.

Although Anthropic's growth is impressive, its business remains comparatively young and capital-intensive. Competition from Google's Gemini, OpenAI, and open-source models could pressure pricing and profitability. At a valuation already in the trillions of dollars, investors are already paying an enormous premium for financial results that have not yet materialized.

Alphabet's competitive advantages extend across Google Search, YouTube, Android, Chrome, Google Workspace, and Google Cloud. These products create a powerful distribution ecosystem for introducing new AI capabilities.

Importantly, Alphabet isn't simply defending its legacy businesses against the proliferation of generative AI. The company is incorporating its Gemini models into Search, productivity applications, smartphones, and enterprise software, creating unique opportunities to improve customer engagement and introduce new revenue streams.

Alphabet's latest financial results suggest the company's AI investments are already producing meaningful benefits. During the third quarter, total revenue increased 25% to $127.6 billion. The company generated $26.2 billion in net income and maintained a companywide operating margin of 32%. This underscores Alphabet's ability to fund AI development through existing profits.

Perhaps the most exciting opportunity is Google Cloud, which generated $30.7 billion in quarterly revenue, representing 103% year-over-year growth. That exceeded the growth rates of Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure. Google Cloud's growth demonstrates how Alphabet is increasingly becoming a formidable competitor in enterprise AI infrastructure.

Alphabet also has a technological advantage through its custom Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). These chips are helping the company optimize capacity costs for its own AI services while offering customers alternatives to Nvidia's infrastructure. Combining proprietary chips, Gemini models, cloud services, and consumer distribution gives Alphabet multiple levers to capture more value as AI adoption accelerates.

If only one trillion-dollar AI stock among this cohort could be bought today and held for the long term, Alphabet would be my strongest choice. While Nvidia and Anthropic could deliver outsize returns, Alphabet offers a particularly attractive combination of innovation, financial resilience, and durable competitive advantages.

#3117. How Often Do You Need To Scrub The Do Not Call List? The 31-Day Rule Explained

Phil Portman is a serial entrepreneur and the Founder & CEO of Textdrip — a small business SMS marketing tool to automate SMS campaigns.

​I see businesses repeatedly making the same mistake: They scrub their contact list once and then keep calling and texting from that list for months. That’s a risky habit, because every day new numbers join the Do Not Call Registry. A list that was clean in January can be full of problems by March.

After years of experience working in a regulated industry, I’m sure about one thing: Businesses rarely fail because the rules are unclear. They fail because their processes break down in practice. The Do Not Call rules are a crystal-clear example of this.

How often do you have to scrub the Do Not Call (DNC) list? Every 31 days. To keep safe harbor protection, you need to scrub against a version of the registry that is no more than 31 days old. In practice, that means every month.

The National Do Not Call Registry is run by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC). It lets people add their personal phone numbers to a list that tells telemarketers to stop contacting them. It exists to protect consumers who don’t want sales calls. It covers personal numbers, such as home and mobile lines. It doesn’t cover business-to-business calls to a company line. Knowing this difference helps you decide which numbers need a check.

Many teams assume it only covers voice calls, but it doesn’t. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) treats text messages as calls, so the same protections apply to SMS marketing. If you text prospects, those numbers also need a DNC check.

State lists exist as well. Some states keep their own Do Not Call lists, and some, such as Florida and Texas, have stricter rules than the federal registry. If you contact people in several states, you need to check each state’s rules before you launch.

Some calls are exempt, such as those to people who gave written permission or have an established business relationship with you. Even then, you must honor opt-out requests.

To qualify for safe harbor under FTC and FCC regulations, telemarketers must scrub their list against the National DNC Registry. Every call must be made using a registry version downloaded no more than 31 days earlier. Simply put, you must rescrub every month. If it’s day 32, you’re already at risk.

Suppose you scrubbed a list on the first of the month. On the 20th, a prospect joins the registry. Your team keeps working that same list. Any call made after day 31 relies on an outdated version. Many teams scrub only when they upload new leads. This sounds fine, but a campaign can run for weeks, and a number can join the registry halfway through. If you keep contacting that number, you’re working from outdated data.

Safe harbor is a defense that protects a business when a call goes out by mistake. But it only applies if you had a working process in place before the mistake happened. A written policy that nobody reads or follows won’t help. Training without a current list won’t help either.

The FCC rule lists what a DNC safe harbor process needs:

• An internal Do Not Call list that is kept up to date.

• Registry access used to scrub within the 31-day window.

• Logs (records) showing when each scrub happened.

Record-keeping is a common gap. Without records, you have no safe harbor, even if the scrub did happen. If a regulator or a lawyer asks for proof, saying “we did it” won’t be enough. You need proof (dates and logs).

Do Not Call violations get expensive quickly. Under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA), a consumer can sue for $500 per violation. If the violation was willful or knowing, a court can raise that to $1,500 per violation. A consumer generally must receive more than one call from the same business within 12 months to bring a DNC claim.

Some of these claims are filed as class actions. One outdated list can hold thousands of people, and each one may have a claim. A small gap in your process can turn into a very large bill. Legal fees and settlements add to that, along with damage to your business reputation.

I lead a company in a regulated industry, so I think about this often. Compliance works best when it is practiced as a routine instead of an event. We built Landline Remover to help teams make scrubbing a routine.

1. Scrub every time you upload leads, not just on launch day.

2. Rescrub active lists monthly, ideally a few days before the 31-day window closes.

3. Check your internal list and the national list together. Your internal do-not-call list holds people who told you directly to stop. The registry doesn’t know about them. Both lists matter.

4. Check reassigned numbers. Numbers change owners. The FCC’s reassigned numbers database can tell you whether a number has changed hands since you got consent.

5. Log every scrub with the date. That log is your proof if a court or regulator asks.

6. Automate the scrubbing process so it doesn’t depend on memory.

Do Not Call compliance is a monthly habit, not a one-time task. The rule is simple: scrub within 31 days, every time.

DNC scrubbing alone can’t protect a business. You need to keep proof that you followed the rule. Scrubbing only protects you if you can prove it. So build a regular scrubbing habit and keep the records. Remember that regulators don’t just look at your efforts—they ask for evidence.

#3115. Warriors finish winless road trip with lopsided loss to Grizzlies

It turns out that Steph Curry is pretty important to the Golden State Warriors success. When the Dubs head out on a five-game road trip just over a week ago, they did it with an eight-game winning streak and all the momentum in the world. And then, just a few minutes into the five-city trip, Curry suffered an oblique injury, and a few hours later, the Warriors lost to the Houston Rockets. What followed was brutal: a 38-point loss to the San Antonio Spurs, a 21-point defeat at the hands of the New Orleans Pelicans, a 22-point loss to the upstart Dallas Mavericks, and finally, on Thursday night, a 28-point loss to the surprisingly great Memphis Grizzlies.

The silver lining, if you're into that sort of thing, is that the Warriors looked the best that they have since Curry was injured, despite losing 126-98. The execution was the best it had been in a while, but ultimately, an astounding lack of shooting did the Dubs in.

As had been the case in all of the other Curry-less games, the Warriors got off to a comically slow start. They trailed 5-0, and then 8-2, and Steve Kerr's first timeout came when the Warriors trailed 13-4 just a few minutes in, as the team was racking up the turnovers. Even the good news was bittersweet: Charles Bassey scored the first seven points for Golden State, but also collected three quick fouls.

Still, the Warriors were executing well … mostly. They couldn't resist turning the ball over, with eight giveaways in the first quarter alone, but they were creating things on offense and getting good looks. Unfortunately, the good looks weren't falling, and they weren't able to do much on defense. Even with a nice run to end the opening frame, the Warriors trailed 31-24 after the first.

The Grizzlies came out firing in the second quarter, and quickly led 43-29 with an astonishing 21 points off of turnovers. That, combined with the Warriors' inability to make seemingly any jump shot, made it clear that unless there was a serious reversal of fortunes, the Warriors would not be winning. And there was, unfortunately, no reversal of fortune.

Memphis was turning Golden State's turnovers and missed shots into offens of their own, and used a 14-1 run to turn the game into a blowout at 47-30. But Golden State's response was impressive. The defense really stepped up late, and put the clamps on the Grizzlies with some of their best possessions in the past week (low bar, I know). That led to some much better offensive possessions, with the team getting significantly more aggressive to make up for the unsuccessful shooting. After trailing at one point by 18, the Warriors ran off a 10-0 run, and thanks to a strong defensive stand to end the half, only trailed 55-47 at the break. They had only made three shots from beyond the arc, they had no players in double figures, and Yaxel Lendeborg had yet to make a field goal, yet somehow they were in the game.

It wouldn't last long. For the third quarter in a row, the Grizzlies started the third hot, and quickly pushed the lead comfortably into the double digits. It felt like the Warriors were so close to playing well, but just couldn't quite get over the hump. They would execute well but miss shots, and then they would follow it up with some impressive individual plays supplemented by poor execution. The third quarter was ultimately defined by a distinct lack of easy shots … even when they scored, they simply couldn't get anything easy, and labored over every possession, good or bad. They still couldn't make any threes, and they still had too many turnovers, though credit where it's due: the energy and effort level didn't fade a bit, from opening tip until final buzzer. But energy and effort were no match for talent and execution, and the Grizzlies took a 92-73 lead into the final frame.

From there, it was just window dressing. The Grizzlies again were on fire to start the quarter, and quickly pushed the lead well into the 20s, making it clear that there would be no miraculous comeback for the Dubs. Both teams emptied their benches fairly early, as Memphis rolled to a 126-98 victory, their second win of the season against Golden State.

The Warriors had a serious talent deficit, playing without not just Curry, but also Draymond Green, Jimmy Butler III, Moses Moody, and Brandon Williams. Charles Bassey led the way with 16 points, and also grabbed 13 rebounds for a double-double, while Will Richard had another strong game off the bench, scoring 15 points and playing excellent defense. But Yaxel Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski once again struggled to carry the offense with Curry out, with the former scoring 11 points on 3-for-11 shooting, and the latter 15 points on 5-for-12 shooting. While Lendeborg struggled on offense, he played a good defensive game, and finished with eight rebounds, seven assists, one steal, and two blocks.

For Memphis, Jaylen Wells (22 points and seven rebounds on 8-for-10 shooting) and rookie Cameron Boozer (16 points, six rebounds, and five assists on 6-for-6 shooting) starred in a total team effort. But the biggest discrepancy, as it has been for much of the road trip, was the shooting. Golden State shot a miserable 5-for-29 (17.2%) from deep, while the Grizzlies went an excellent 15-for-35 (42.9%). That, along with 22 turnovers, is how you lose by 28 points.

The commercial space race is expanding as private enterprises take over roles once reserved for governments. Investors weighing Intuitive Machines (LUNR -10.89%) against Rocket Lab (RKLB -9.59%) are looking for the best long-term winner.

Both companies represent the growth of the modern space industry. Intuitive Machines focuses on lunar landing services and data infrastructure, while Rocket Lab provides reliable launch capabilities and satellite manufacturing.

Intuitive Machines provides lunar spacecraft, communication networks, and infrastructure-as-a-service. It serves a mix of civil and national security clients, including NASA and the U.S. Space Development Agency. NASA accounted for roughly 78% of revenue in 2025, and customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached about $707 million, representing revenue growth of approximately 220.9%. The company reported a net loss of $128.0 million for the period. This resulted in a net margin of negative 18%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was approximately negative 0.5x, indicating that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio of nearly 5.0x shows the company has sufficient short-term assets to cover its short-term debts. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was roughly negative $56 million, and many defense stocks are currently competing for similar infrastructure contracts.

Rocket Lab is an end-to-end space provider that designs rockets and manufactures spacecraft components. It serves diverse markets including NASA, the National Reconnaissance Office, and various commercial satellite operators. Its top five customers accounted for nearly 49% of 2025 revenue, which requires careful monitoring by investors.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $881.9 million, about a 59% increase over the prior year. Rocket Lab reported a net loss of around $226.9 million during this time. These results produced a net margin of negative 25.7%.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.1x, which compares total debt to shareholder equity to show reliance on borrowing. The current ratio of nearly 4.1x shows strong short-term liquidity, even as free cash flow for the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, was approximately negative $321.8 million. This cash consumption reflects the capital-intensive nature of building global launch infrastructure.

Intuitive Machines faces significant customer concentration, as a vast majority of its revenue comes from NASA. The company also deals with operational hazards inherent in space missions, including potential landing anomalies or mission failures. Additionally, the recent acquisition of Lanteris presents integration challenges and increased overhead costs.

Rocket Lab must manage development risks associated with its new Neutron launch vehicle, which recently suffered a tank failure during testing. The company is also exposed to operational hazards at its specific launch sites and relies heavily on key leadership. Finally, the pending acquisition of Iridium Communications (IRDM -2.95%) involves substantial financial risk and potential shareholder dilution.

Intuitive Machines appears cheaper, carrying a lower Forward P/E relative to future earnings estimates and a lower P/S ratio based on sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Intuitive Machines has been posting superb results in fiscal 2026, most recently posting sequential quarterly growth of 31%, to $269 million in the third quarter reported in early November. Management says they have an order backlog of $1.9 billion, up $1.2 billion from the end of 2025. NASA is moving toward steady access-to-space flights and deliveries, too, which bodes well for the company's longer-term sales. Revenue for fiscal 2026 is expected to more than quadruple to $935 million, though net loss is expected to widen to about $100 million. Analysts expect the business to turn a profit for the first time in 2029.

Rocket Lab, meanwhile, made a huge splash in the market with its pending $8 billion acquisition of Iridium Communications this year. The combination promises to make Rocket Lab a space powerhouse by combining its launch technology with the communications spectrum offered by Iridium. In short, Rocket Lab could very well be a serious competitor to Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SPCX -6.66%). Don't overlook Rocket Lab's expertise in sending small payloads into orbit, and it is closing in on the same reusable rocket technology that SpaceX has used to lower its customer prices.

Stand-alone Rocket Lab is seen boosting its revenue by more than 50% this year to $983 million, a figure analysts have raised throughout the year, with a net loss just about equal to 2025, at $199 million. The Iridium acquisition is a big meal to swallow, but the combined business should generate $1.8 billion in revenue in 2028, the first full year of the merged companies (The Iridium acquisition is slated to close mid-2027).

These are two exciting space-age stocks. Intuitive Machines, with its much more reasonable P/S and forward P/E ratios, gets the nod, under the adage of buying good companies at good prices for the long term, rather than paying extremely high premiums for future growth with Rocket Lab.

#3112. Your Employees’ Personal AI Agents Are Becoming Your Security Problem

David Goldschlag is co-founder and CEO of Aembit, an identity control plane for AI agents.

​Ahead of an important client meeting, a sales representative connects their personal AI agent to company email and files. The setup takes minutes and allows the employee to arrive prepared with considerably less effort, but that well-meaning shortcut may carry risks the rep never considered.

Personal AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots and Google’s Gemini Spark, are software assistants that can carry out routine tasks across connected services and continue working between conversations. It is early, and there is little data yet on how often employees connect these personal assistants to company accounts. But if the first numbers are any indication, the habit is forming quickly. Meta said Muse passed 10 million accounts within roughly six weeks of launch, and a Menlo Ventures survey found that 32% of U.S. adults who use AI have already let it act on their behalf without final sign-off.

For security leaders who remember the first requests to connect personal smartphones to company email, the arrival of these agentic deputies has a familiar feel. Employees found something useful and expected to use it, while IT and security were left to reconcile that enthusiasm with responsibility for company data.

Bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies and years of “shadow IT” disputes established an enduring reality: The rank and file would have a say in the technology they used. But the analogy has limits in the AI era. Traditional software generally follows predefined workflows, while an agent can choose which tools to use and which steps to take in carrying out an employee’s request, without the employee directing each action.

Permissions granted with little consideration during setup can later support a series of actions the employee never specifically contemplated. For CISOs, the difficulty is deciding how much authority should accompany that discretion and how to enforce those limits once an AI assistant begins working.

Consider the employee preparing for the customer meeting. The request of their agent sounds innocuous: Review recent correspondence, find the relevant account documents and prepare a briefing.

Yet the permissions available during setup may cover far more information than this assignment requires. Depending on the connection, the agent may receive access to a mailbox containing correspondence with hundreds of customers, along with internal discussions unrelated to the meeting.

Suppose the employee also asks the agent to prepare and send an external follow-up. An internal document contains useful background, including an unannounced pricing change. The agent could incorporate that information into a customer message because it appears relevant to the assignment. Every connection involved might be permitted, even though the resulting disclosure was never intended. Read-only access offers limited reassurance if the agent can send what it reads through another service.

Requiring employee approval before an agent receives access provides another safeguard, but its value depends on what the employee can reasonably assess. A consent screen can describe the permissions being requested without making clear how an agent could use them together. The employee may approve those permissions without anticipating the disclosure described above.

Company policy must establish which resources an assistant may access and which actions require further review. Employees should understand their responsibilities, but connecting an agent should not leave them to determine how much authority the company is willing to delegate.

The following practices can help security leaders establish those boundaries while giving employees a practical way to use personal AI agents.

Verify that records identify which agent acted and whose authority it used. Logs that name only the employee may leave investigators unable to distinguish direct actions from those taken by an agent.

Establish which accounts and resources it can access, whether it can act in the background and how the provider handles credentials and retrieved data. Approval of an assistant should not imply approval of every connection it supports.

Where controls permit, restrict access to relevant resources and separate retrieval permissions from permission to publish or send. Enforce those limits at runtime, when the agent requests access. If a service offers only broad access, weigh that limitation in the approval decision.

Reserve employees’ attention for consequential decisions. Before an external message is sent, for example, let them review its recipients, attachments and exact content, with another review required if material details change.

Ensure security can revoke an agent’s access without disabling the employee’s account. This gives security teams a way to intervene when an agent needs to be stopped. Here, that means access revocation: withdrawing the agent’s ability to use connected systems. Cutting off access, however, does not necessarily terminate the agent’s process.

Test it against background activity and previously issued credentials, and measure how long it takes for subsequent requests to fail. Depending on the implementation, previously issued access tokens may remain usable until they expire, or a revocation decision may take time to reach every system involved. Incident procedures should account for the behavior observed in testing, including any additional steps required to contain ongoing activity.​​​

These practices also expose limitations that a policy document alone cannot resolve. If a provider cannot support sufficiently narrow access or useful audit records, the company may need to restrict the information available to that agent or decline the connection.​

The BYOD experience offers a useful lesson about AI adoption. Employees’ preferences can influence company technology decisions long before a formal policy catches up. Security leaders should take seriously the reasons people want personal agents, including the convenience of using a tool they already know.

A workable policy should give employees a clear route to request access, explain which uses are permitted and offer alternatives when a requested connection grants more authority than the business can accept. Security teams, in turn, need evidence that the agreed restrictions hold during actual use.​​​

#3108. The Next Software Revolution After AI Is Efficiency

Itamar Syn-Hershko, Founder of NeverBlink AI and BigData Boutique, helps companies confidently operate and optimize data platforms at scale.

For decades, we’ve made software easier to write, even when it meant making it more expensive to run.​

We introduced programming languages, frameworks and layers of abstraction that allowed developers to move faster. Along the way, we accepted higher memory consumption, more CPU usage and increasingly complex infrastructure.​

For the most part, this made sense. Developers were expensive, hardware kept getting cheaper and getting products to market quickly was often more important than squeezing the most out of every server.​

I think we’re approaching a point where that trade-off no longer makes sense.​

AI is changing the cost of writing software, while the growing demand for computing resources is making efficiency more important than it has been in years. Together, these forces could change not just how we build software but also the economics of the entire software industry.​

Take Java, for example. Much of its success came from making developers more productive. Automatic memory management, a rich ecosystem and portability made it easier to build and maintain complex applications without worrying about many of the details involved in lower-level programming.​

The trade-off was additional runtime overhead. Garbage collection, managed memory and abstraction layers can require considerably more resources than a carefully optimized native implementation.​

This was often a perfectly reasonable compromise. If using Java saved months of engineering work, spending a little more on servers was easy to justify.​

But what happens when AI can write, maintain and optimize complex C++ or Rust code at a fraction of the previous engineering cost?​ We should start questioning whether some of the abstractions we’ve relied on for decades are still worth their price.​

I’m not suggesting we rewrite every Java application in assembly. There are good reasons to use managed languages, including their mature tooling, ecosystems and safety characteristics. AI-generated code also introduces its own risks and still needs careful review.​

But the argument that lower-level programming is too expensive or complicated to justify is becoming much weaker.​

​At the same time, the infrastructure side of the equation is changing.​

AI is creating enormous demand for computing capacity, memory, electricity and data center space. The International Energy Agency projects that global data center electricity consumption will roughly double by 2030.​

We cannot keep solving every software performance problem by adding more hardware. At some point, the availability and cost of that hardware become serious constraints.​

There’s also growing pressure to make software cheaper.​

AI is already reducing the time and effort involved in producing software, and we should expect some of those savings to reach customers. As it becomes cheaper to build competing products, companies will find it harder to justify high prices based on development costs alone.​

This puts infrastructure efficiency at the center of the conversation. If two products offer comparable functionality but one requires a fraction of the hardware to operate, the difference can be substantial. The more efficient product can offer lower prices, better margins or both.​

​Search engines and databases are good places to look for early examples.

​Traditional search architectures (Lucene-based especially, such as Elasticsearch and OpenSearch) often require continuously provisioned compute resources and substantial memory to maintain indexes and deliver low-latency queries. This can make infrastructure costs difficult to align with fluctuating workloads.​

​Companies such as turbopuffer and WarpSearch are challenging those assumptions. Both use an object-storage-first architecture for vector and full-text search, reducing the need to keep large indexes on expensive infrastructure. A Google Cloud case study reports search and storage cost reductions of 90% for its approach.

​There are examples outside search as well, including ClickHouse, Neon, Bun and more.

​These products aren’t necessarily the result of AI-assisted development. Many of their innovations started before today’s coding agents became widely available.

​What interests me is what happens when the engineering effort required to build systems like these drops dramatically.

​For engineering leaders, this should change how we evaluate technology choices.

​We spend a lot of time measuring developer productivity, feature delivery and time to market. We should be paying just as much attention to what our software costs to operate.

​That starts with measuring actual resource consumption. Cost per query, cost per transaction, memory per workload and CPU utilization are not just infrastructure metrics. They directly affect the economics of the product.

​It also means questioning architectural decisions we’ve come to accept. Does that service really need to run continuously? Does that dataset need to stay in memory? Are we using the right algorithms and data structures? Could a more efficient implementation eliminate entire servers?

​And perhaps most importantly, we should be using AI for more than producing code faster.

​AI can help investigate performance bottlenecks, evaluate alternative algorithms, rewrite expensive components and explore lower-level implementations that would previously have required too much engineering effort.

​There are still trade-offs. Reliability, security, correctness and maintainability matter. An implementation that saves 20% in CPU costs but introduces serious operational risks is hardly an improvement.

​The point is that we now have more ways to pursue efficiency without paying the same development cost we once did.

​I expect we’ll see more companies challenge established software categories by building products that achieve similar results with much less infrastructure.

​Some will use better algorithms. Others will rethink storage architectures, eliminate unnecessary compute or replace expensive runtime components. AI will make many of these approaches easier to implement.

​For established software vendors, this creates a real challenge. Their existing architectures may have been designed around assumptions that no longer hold, while newer competitors have the freedom to start from scratch.

​For customers, it should eventually mean more capable software at lower prices.

​We’ve spent decades making software easier and cheaper to write and accepting the infrastructure overhead that came with it.

​Now that writing software is becoming cheaper, it’s time to focus on making it cheaper to run.

#3107. Knicks eke out lucky win in Minnesota after fourth-quarter collapse

"For 'Dancing with the Stars,' " Karl-Anthony Towns said. "For us, at the end of the day, as long as we win, this team is just trying to stack the number on the left side."

The Knicks did stack another win in that left standings column. Perhaps they didn't deserve to.

They did just about everything they could to throw away that win amid a brutal collapse.

Karl-Anthony Towns goes up for a shot over Rudy Gobert during the Knicks' 102-99 win over the Timberwolves on Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. NBAE via Getty Images

Somehow, they escaped with a 102-99 win over the Timberwolves on Thursday night.

The Knicks led by 12 entering the fourth quarter and then quickly went up by 16 after Tyler Kolek's 4-point play to start the quarter. They had led since early in the first quarter and were in complete command.

But they proceeded to miss their next 13 shots and saw their lead dwindle to four. Target Center finally had life.

It appeared they had stabilized a bit when Towns' driving layup and Mikal Bridges' subsequent 3-pointer put the Knicks back up by nine.

But Towns, after a Timberwolves challenge, was handed a flopping technical for trying to draw a foul called on Rudy Gobert. A free throw, a Gobert alley-oop and an Ayo Dosunmu 3-pointer later, and the Knicks led by just three. Towns then was called for an offensive foul, and Bridges badly missed a jumper on the Knicks' next offensive possession.

The Timberwolves couldn't find a quality shot, though, with Dosunmu and Gobert both missing shots. Minnesota never got closer than three.

LaMelo Ball badly missed a potential game-tying 3-pointer with under 10 seconds left. Jonathan Kuminga got the rebound but threw it away to Landry Shamet, and the Timberwolves weren't able to foul as the Knicks tossed the ball up the court.

Miles McBride (left) and Jaden McDaniels battle for the ball during the Knicks' win over the Timberwolves on Nov. 19, 2026, in Minneapolis. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt

"It was hectic," Josh Hart said. "We gotta get better at finishing a game like that. But it's a win, 3-1 on the road trip. We'll take it."

Despite the ugly finish, the Knicks closed their four-game road trip with a win over a strong opponent. The Timberwolves have not missed much of a beat this season without injured superstar Anthony Edwards and possessed the league's best defense entering the game.

"Great to finish off a road trip, getting a win in a pretty tough environment by a well-coached team," head coach Mike Brown said. "It'll make the plane ride a little bit better going home."

Nobody has shot over 50 percent from the field against them this year. The Knicks could not change that, though they shot 57.1 percent by halftime as Towns — returning to Minnesota as an opponent for the third time since the Knicks' blockbuster trade to acquire him two years ago — was dominating his old team. He scored 17 points in the first half, and Jalen Brunson then erupted for 14 points in the third quarter. The Knicks' offense as a whole was humming.

It appeared the Knicks would cruise the rest of the way before the Timberwolves defense came alive.

"Our execution the first three quarters was at a pretty high level against this team," Brown said. "And then you give them credit. Fourth quarter, they did a phenomenal job defensively, kind of bogged us down. The ball and the pace offensively in the frontcourt wasn't popping like it was the first three quarters."

Towns shot 1-for-5 in the fourth. Brunson went scoreless in the period. As a team, the Knicks went 3-for-18 from the field and scored just 12 points over the final 12 minutes.

Brunson finished with 21 points. OG Anunoby added 15.

Kuminga led the Timberwolves with 23 points. The Knicks held Dosunmu, who has broken out in Edwards' absence, to just six points. Ball had 15 points on rough 6-for-21 shooting. The Timberwolves' 99 points were their fewest this season.

For three quarters, it was vintage Knicks — getting a little bit from everyone. Until it unraveled in the fourth quarter, where the Knicks had been so good in recent games.

"If you wanna win a championship, you gotta be ready to win in any way possible," Towns said, "because you never know what the game will be."

#3104. What Security Teams Still Get Wrong About Asset Visibility

Yochai Corem is GM of Exposure Management at Check Point Software.

Organizations have more asset data than ever, but turning that data into a reliable view of what they own, operate and expose remains difficult.

A server appears in three tools with different identifiers. A cloud workload has an owner who has left the business. A forgotten website remains online after the campaign that funded it has ended. Each leaves security teams with information they still have to investigate before they can act.

Security leaders should judge asset visibility by how reliably it supports a decision. A useful inventory helps teams establish what an asset does, who is responsible for it, how it is protected and what should happen when a problem appears.

Several familiar assumptions prevent organizations from reaching that standard.

An incomplete configuration management database (CMDB) should prompt a review of how records are created, updated and retired.

Start by defining its purpose. The CMDB should record the systems, services and dependencies needed to manage business operations, with accountable owners and lifecycle status. Detailed security telemetry can remain in specialist systems, linked through reliable identifiers. An impersonating website belongs in an external threat register connected to the affected brand.

Then identify which sources can reveal missing records. Cloud platforms, endpoint management, identity providers, vulnerability scanners and procurement systems can each expose inconsistencies. Buying a service should trigger registration; retiring it should trigger checks that access, infrastructure and records have been removed.

Reconciliation should reflect the pace of change. I would set a daily reconciliation target for cloud and endpoint feeds; use deployment and retirement events to trigger updates; and review unresolved discrepancies weekly. Quarterly ownership reviews can supplement those checks.

An asset without an owner needs an interim accountable team and an escalation deadline. “Unknown” should describe an investigation in progress.

The modern attack surface spans internal infrastructure, cloud workloads, software as a service (SaaS), internet-facing systems, supplier connections and the organization’s broader digital presence.

Those categories need different forms of accountability. Infrastructure teams may manage servers, cloud teams manage workloads and business application owners sponsor SaaS services. Marketing or regional teams may control domains and social accounts. Supplier relationships require a business sponsor alongside technical oversight.

Security should establish a review and response process across those boundaries. A newly discovered domain needs ownership verification and an assessment of what it hosts. An unfamiliar SaaS service needs checks on its users, data and access. A fraudulent social account needs investigation and a disruption process.

Review frequency should follow exposure and change, with continuous discovery where practical and scheduled reviews for ownership, supplier access and dormant services. This broader scope aligns with the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) inclusion of hardware, software, services and supplier services in asset management.

Leaders can test this assumption by following a newly discovered asset through the security process.

Does discovery trigger checks for required endpoint protection, vulnerability scanning and an accountable owner? Does an unmanaged internet-facing system reach someone authorized to restrict or remove it? Can the organization confirm that the resulting action occurred?

These outcomes show whether visibility operates as a security control. The Center for Internet Security’s (CIS) Control 1 connects inventory management with identifying and addressing unauthorized or unmanaged assets.

Useful measures include the time taken to assign ownership, the proportion of applicable assets covered by required controls and the age of unresolved discrepancies. A growing inventory count provides little reassurance when newly discovered systems remain unmanaged.

Additional tools introduce additional records, each with its own identifiers, timestamps and assumptions.

Effective reconciliation requires explicit rules. Stable cloud resource identifiers or device identifiers should take precedence over an Internet Protocol (IP) address that may change or be reused. Records need source and freshness information so teams can distinguish a current observation from a stale entry.

Organizations also need rules for conflicting fields. The identity system may establish who uses a device, while a service registry identifies the team accountable for the application it supports. Those relationships should remain distinguishable.

Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) can support this work. Organizations can also improve CMDB integrations, use cloud asset inventories and service catalogs, or build reconciliation workflows in their existing data platforms. The operational requirements remain consistent: reliable matching, clear authority for each field and a process for resolving exceptions.

Discovery should initiate a decision about management, protection or retirement.

A forgotten website needs an owner to confirm whether it still serves a business purpose. A vulnerable application needs assessment of its exposure, dependencies and operational constraints before a response is selected.

That decision should remain traceable through completion. If a service is retired, verify that it is no longer reachable. If a security control is applied, confirm that it covers the intended asset. Updating the inventory should accompany the operational change.

This ongoing connection between asset information and action also underpins continuous threat exposure management (CTEM).

CTEM depends on this discipline throughout scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation and mobilization.

An unknown asset cannot enter the prioritization process. A known asset without business context is difficult to rank. Missing dependencies weaken assessments of attack paths and change impact. An unknown owner delays action, while stale records undermine confirmation that an exposure has been reduced.

CAASM and external attack surface management (EASM) can support these stages by reconciling internal records and discovering internet-facing assets. Their value depends on the ownership, decision rules and response processes surrounding them.

Security leaders should expect asset visibility to connect discovery with accountable action. Every significant asset needs enough current context for someone to determine its protection requirements, address its exposures and verify the result. That is how a reliable inventory helps reduce the opportunities available to an attacker.​

Bloom was also added to the S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.91%) this September.

Bloom's SOFCs can convert natural gas, biogas, propane, and hydrogen into electricity without any combustion. Its systems can often be deployed in less than two months and bypass traditional utilities that often require years to set up new connections. Its new Power Connect System could further reduce its on-site installation time by over 40%.

A growing number of data center operators -- including Oracle (NASDAQ:ORCL), CoreWeave (CRWV -11.49%), Nebius (NBIS -14.02%), and Equinix (EQIX -4.36%) -- are using Bloom's SOFC systems to expand their AI infrastructure. That's why its backlog hit $20 billion at the end of 2025, and why it expects its revenue to more than double from $2.0 billion in 2025 to at least $4.4 billion in 2026. But will its stock head even higher over the next five years?

But from 2025 to 2028, analysts expect Bloom's revenue and adjusted EBITDA to grow at CAGRs of 73% and 126%, respectively. With an enterprise value of $50 billion, it still looks like a bargain at 25 times next year's adjusted EBITDA.

The Democratic sweep of the midterm elections could also throttle the construction of new data centers with tighter regulations.

Those challenges compressed Bloom's valuations, but its longer-term catalysts remain intact. The data center market is still growing, and tighter environmental restrictions could actually boost its sales of SOFC systems. Oracle should get Project Jupiter back on track, Bloom has directly refuted the short-seller's claims, and it's gradually expanding into more non-AI markets. Bloom's free cash flow -- which turned negative in the third quarter of 2026 after four consecutive quarters in positive territory -- should improve as those tailwinds kick in.

If Bloom matches analysts' estimates through 2028, grows its adjusted EBITDA at a 25% CAGR through 2031, and trades at a more generous 20 times its current-year adjusted EBITDA by the final year, its stock price could rise more than 145% over the next five years.

#3095. How To Teach Your AI Agent About Your Company

Frederik Riskær Pedersen, Founder and CEO of Maplith, a company brain for your AI agents.

For 16 years, I ran a translation company that grew from a handful of people into an international business. The most important thing I learned about knowledge is that it rarely lives where you think it does.

One customer shows it well. We had to fetch their files from their own system and deliver them in their own layout, and we could only invoice some of the repetitions. None of that was written down anywhere. It lived with one project manager. Anyone else would have done it the standard way and got it wrong.

That tailoring was not a side issue. It was the product. If the work had been standard, the customer could have run the model themselves. This is why a company’s rules never get standardized away: The exceptions are often exactly what customers pay for.

I think of this every time someone asks me why their AI agent isn’t delivering. The models are good enough. The problem is that the agent starts from zero every time. It does not know which systems you run, how they connect or which rules you follow without ever writing them down. So it guesses, and a confident guess in your accounts is worse than no answer at all.

Here are five things you can do this month before you let an agent work inside your business. None of them needs a new tool.

Book two hours with the three or four people who make most of the everyday decisions. Ask them one question: “What would a new hire ask you in their first week?” The answers are your unwritten rules: which customers get special terms, when a refund is approved, what can be invoiced and what cannot. Write each one as a short sentence, specific enough to check: “This customer gets files back in their own template.” “Refunds above 300 euros are approved by the finance lead.”

List every system you use and what each one is the source of truth for. You will find places where two systems describe the same thing differently. “Returned” in the ERP can mean the customer has sent the item back, while in the warehouse it means the item is back on the shelf.

The instinct is to make the systems agree. In my experience, that rarely works because each system was set up for the team that uses it, and that is why it works for them. Write the translation down instead. The same goes for numbers. In my company, the price did not sit in the same place from one customer to the next. Note where it lives for whom and which value to trust for which question.

Most useful answers need two systems joined: the order in the web shop and the invoice in accounting, or the support ticket and the customer in the CRM. Find the field that ties them together and test it by hand. Take 20 random orders and look for them in the other system. If you find 19, you can build on that link. If you find 12, you cannot, and an agent will rarely tell you it is guessing. The test takes an afternoon and saves months of wrong reports.

Split actions into four levels: read, propose, act after approval and act alone. Start with everything that changes something requiring approval from a named person. Set limits in money and volume, not in trust. When the agent has proposed the same action a hundred times without a mistake, move that one action up a level. That decision should be yours, never the agent’s.

For every action, record who asked for it, who approved it, what happened and when. It sounds bureaucratic, but it is the only way to answer when a customer, an auditor or your board asks, “Why did this happen?” Without a log, you also cannot tell when it is safe to give the agent more freedom.

None of this is about artificial intelligence. It is about making knowledge that lives in people’s heads, and in systems that do not talk to each other, available and trustworthy. Companies that do this get more out of their AI. They also become less fragile when a key person goes on holiday or leaves.

So start small. Book the two hours this week, write down 10 rules and test one link.

By Jack Delaney – Nov 20, 2026 at 1:15PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Costco Wholesale ›

Earlier this month, Costco Wholesale (COST +1.28%) declared a special dividend of $30 per share, payable on Dec. 4 to shareholders of record as of the close of business on Nov. 24. That payout will be double the $15 per share special dividend that shareholders received in 2024.

But rather than being a reason to buy the stock on its own, these intermittent bonus distributions point to a broader case for holding Costco as a long-term investment.

The special dividend payout is a way to reward its shareholders. But it's also an indication that Costco has more money than it can usefully deploy to grow the business at the moment, a situation many companies would like to be in.

For Costco, that situation has resulted from an increase in its income from membership sales, strong renewal rates, expansion, and improved profitability, which are all solid reasons to consider owning the stock. In its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended Aug. 30, Costco reported membership income growth of 7.3%. That’s the revenue stream that makes the entire business work. Its product sales have extremely thin margins; Costco makes the bulk of its money on the membership fees, so growth on that line indicates healthy demand from customers wanting to access Costco's warehouses.

In North America, Costco has a 92.3% membership renewal rate, while global renewals overall are just under 90%. This gives it a predictable high-margin revenue stream, and it also means Costco doesn't have to constantly replace large numbers of members who cancel. It also shows that, despite concerns about rising grocery and household costs, most members still see enough value in the warehouse giant to keep their memberships. And if the economy were to enter a downturn, Costco offers the kind of deals on bulk goods that people particularly desire when their budgets get tighter.

Costco can also generate more revenue and translate it into profitability by opening new warehouse stores. It chooses its locations selectively, as evidenced by the fact that it only opened 25 new warehouses in fiscal 2026. That selectivity is a positive, as expansion continues to drive membership fee growth without tying up all the cash Costco generates, giving it greater financial flexibility.

Finally, the company can pay out this latest special dividend because it's simply turning more of its sales into profits. For fiscal 2026, Costco reported $9.2 billion in net income, a nearly 14% increase from the prior year.

Costco's strong business model is what is allowing it to pay out that $30 special dividend, and it is one of the best consumer staples stocks on the market. But the clear strength of that business model has led the market to price high expectations into its stock.

Trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 48.6, there's little room for Costco to deliver any underwhelming or mediocre results in its earnings reports. I still like Costco as a long-term portfolio addition, but investors should buy in with the understanding that the company has high expectations to live up to.

#3092. Trust Is The New Battleground For Customer Engagement

James Garvert is the EVP of Fraud & Communications Solutions for TransUnion.

​Engaging with consumers has never been more essential, or more difficult. Amid the meteoric rise of AI-enabled scams, call spoofing and social engineering attacks, the challenges organizations face when trying to reach consumers seem insurmountable.

Every interaction depends on trust, yet consumers are more hesitant than ever to engage. Many of the traditional warning signs consumers were trained to recognize have disappeared—consumers are on edge.

And with good reason: It’s a jungle out there.

In our recent global study, “61% of business leaders ranked fraud among the risks with the greatest potential business impact, ahead of cybersecurity breaches, compliance, customer churn, operational cost and reputational risk. More concerning, 58% said they’re very or extremely concerned fraud is evolving faster than their organizations’ abilities to detect and prevent it.”

Historically, organizations have viewed fraud and engaging with customers as separate disciplines. But today’s threat environment makes it clear they’re deeply interconnected. In many cases, the communication channel itself—whether a phone call, text message, email or mobile app interaction—provides the first indication that fraud may be occurring.

Consumers don’t experience fraud, identity and communication challenges as separate issues. To them, it’s one experience, one problem. It’s a trust problem that’s reshaping the customer journey. In fact, 69% of consumers say they would switch vendors for stronger security.

Trust has become the foundation for both customer engagement and fraud prevention.

At our recent Fraud & Communications Summit in Chicago, keynote speaker Matt O’Neill, a former U.S. Secret Service Special Agent and recipient of Gold and Silver Awards for distinguished service, shared insights from years spent working undercover as a banker, broker, money launderer and other personas. In these roles, he led multinational investigations into crypto-laundering networks and dark web marketplaces.

According to O’Neill, fraudsters are winning because fraud has evolved into a highly organized industry. He explained that scam operations now function much like large multinational corporations. Scam compounds are similar to call centers, complete with organizational structures, performance quotas, shift schedules and human resources departments. Unfortunately, many of these compounds operate under sophisticated criminal networks and employ workers who have been trafficked.

At the same time, the barrier to entry into the fraud world has never been lower. AI enables fraudsters to create convincing scams at scale in virtually any language, including cloned voices, deepfake videos and personalized social engineering campaigns. And it’s cheap.​

The consequences of eroding trust extend well beyond fraud losses. Organizations often experience:

Ironically, the industries and brands most trusted by consumers are frequently among the most targeted by fraudsters, with the highest fraud instances related to auto lending, bank-issued and retail credit cards and unsecured personal lending.

According to Edelman, trust now rivals price and quality as a primary factor influencing consumer decision-making. Research shows that “77% of consumers cited confidence their personal data is secure as the most important feature when choosing whom to transact with online.”

Organizations can strengthen trust by approaching fraud prevention and customer communications as a unified strategy.

Traditional fraud controls were designed for predictable attacks. Today’s fraudsters adapt quickly, vary their tactics and coordinate attacks across multiple channels and sessions. Identity verification remains important, but it only confirms who someone claims to be. It doesn’t determine whether the current interaction should be trusted.

Here’s where identity verification falls short:

• KYC (Know Your Customer) controls are often strongest at onboarding, not throughout the customer lifecycle.

• Devices, behaviors and risk profiles change over time.

• Credentials can be compromised after verification.

• Synthetic identities can appear legitimate on paper.

The most important fraud signal is often not a single event. Any single signal can be manipulated or generate false positives. It’s the story that unfolds throughout an interaction. It emerges through relationships among users, devices, accounts, entities and sessions.

As if it wasn’t hard enough, AI has turbocharged fraud. In addition, labeling identified threats as AI-driven remains a challenge. That’s because it’s difficult to build comprehensive strategies with new AI fraud models evolving so rapidly.

While fraud practitioners know when an account was taken over, there’s currently no label for how it was taken over and whether AI drove the attack. As a result, the AI-attributed training set doesn’t exist yet for tracking that fraud, and detection stays anchored to heuristics and analyst judgment.

To be able to engage effectively with consumers and prevent fraud, organizations must adopt continuous authentication and layered risk strategies.

• Develop a comprehensive strategy—don’t address fraud in silos across your organization.

• Form strategic partnerships with your cyber teams.

• Correlate identity, device, behavioral and contextual signals in real time.

The process is straightforward: Collect. Correlate. Score. Decide.

Every phone call, text message, email and digital transaction represents a trust moment. Customers want confidence the organization contacting them is legitimate and their information and transactions are protected. Simply asking consumers to “trust us” is no longer enough.

Verified identity, authenticated communications and real-time risk intelligence are becoming the foundation of trust in a digital-first world.

The future isn’t reactive fraud mitigation. It’s proactive trust at the point of interaction, by orchestrating identity, risk and communications intelligence across every customer interaction.

In his social media post, Ives said the Democrats' midterm election victory is creating uncertainty for AI stocks, as investors worry that Washington will impose tougher restrictions on AI development and data center construction.

He also singled out the sudden resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang "in his black eye moment." Huang was forced out after the board began investigating his affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was spying for Beijing.

Meanwhile, regulatory concerns involving China, persistent inflation, and the prospect of additional Federal Reserve interest rate increases have weighed on technology stocks. Ives also pointed to forced selling and investment funds suffering losses that have reduced their ability to buy shares.

Ives even singled out Anthropic's (ANT -10.16%) successful IPO on Nov. 19, speculating that investors shifted money out of tech stocks and into the newly public AI company.

A perfect storm, indeed. But here's the thing -- none of those factors mean that customers are slowing their AI spending. And the demand for computing capacity remains sky-high.

That's why analysts, including Ives, have projected that capital expenditures and AI spending will reach $4 trillion.

Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue in its fiscal third quarter of 2027, up 103% from a year ago. And data center revenue was $107.6 billion, up 110%. But perhaps the most important thing is that Nvidia increased its forecast for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. And notably, that outlook came in the first earnings report since Huang's departure. Management expects demand to accelerate even faster.

Alphabet is seeing similar strength in cloud computing. Google Cloud revenue in the third quarter was $30.7 billion, up 103% from a year ago. Operating income more than tripled to $11.1 billion, and its backlog reached $561 billion.

Those figures suggest businesses are still signing contracts for computing infrastructure, even as investors question whether AI spending has gone too far.

And Anthropic's IPO prospectus offers another example. The Claude developer has committed to spending at least $110 billion with Amazon (AMZN -3.56%) and $121.3 billion with Google under long-term cloud computing arrangements.

That's an enormous amount of planned infrastructure spending from just one AI company.

Ives can't predict when the technology sell-off will end. But his central argument deserves attention: The market's enthusiasm for AI stocks has cooled considerably, while the companies supplying the infrastructure continue to report massive demand.

For investors, that means don't panic over this month's slide in tech stocks. And if you're feeling opportunistic, this could be an ideal time to add to positions while prices remain depressed.

#3086. Rapid Recap: Trail Blazers 124, Bucks 114

In a game with plenty of highs and lows, the Milwaukee Bucks lost to the Portland Trail Blazers 124-114. On the second night of their back-to-back, the Bucks came out lethargic, but frankly, so did the Blazers. Portland gave Milwaukee plenty of chances to blow the game open, but they refused to take them, and in the end, Portland's vets knew what to do when the game was on the line. On the positive side, Nate Ament dropped a career-high 18 points on 6/11 shooting, while the Blazers were led by old friend Damian Lillard, who scored a season-high 33.

Early on, this looked like a game where the Bucks were on the second night of a back-to-back and the Blazers were deep into a road trip, with intensity lacking on both sides. Tyler Herro looked rough, losing the ball and even missing free throws. Thankfully, Nate Ament was the spark, scoring seven of the first nine points as the Bucks took an early lead. Without Deni Avdija, the Blazers looked considerably less dangerous offensively but still stayed close thanks to their defence as they kept forcing turnovers. Of course, it didn't help that the Bucks, yet again, couldn't make a free throw to save themselves, going 2/7 (!) in the opening quarter. And to top it all off, Gary Trent Jr. went for one of his signature steal attempts on the final play and missed, leaving Scoot Henderson open for three to give his team a 24-21 lead—really disappointing stuff.

It was more of the same bad Bucks basketball to open the second: more turnovers, missed free throws, and bad fouls as the Blazers quickly upped their lead to double digits, 32-22. Thank goodness for Nate Ament, though, who poured in a quick five points—paired with triples from Tyler Herro and Kel'el Ware—to reduce Milwaukee's deficit to just one at the six-minute mark as they went on a 12-4 run, down 40-39. Both teams traded leads for the next few minutes, with Brayden Burries really starting to get in his bag, nailing a catch-and-shoot three and following it up with a smooth deceleration move in the lane for the and-one. The Bucks finally played with some verve as Kasparas Jakucionis began to make his mark, nailing a transition three and a put-back as the home side took a 55-47 lead with 3:30 to play. Of course, Scoot Henderson, who was shooting 20.0% from three coming into the game, went 4/4 in the first half as Portland closed on a 15-3 run to take a 60-58 lead into halftime.

The Bucks started the third with great energy on both ends. They opened with a perfectly run post-entry play where Herro got the ball off a screen for a three; then, a few plays later, Burries stole the ball, and Herro drained another three—this time from the corner—Bucks up 68-63 after two minutes. Portland brought Jrue Holiday in to stem the tide, and, like clockwork, the Blazers responded with a 15-2 extended run. Yep. HOWEVER, the Bucks didn't go quietly as the second unit came in and offered a real spark, cutting the deficit back to three with a few minutes remaining. Crucial late plays from Jakucionis and Rollins put the Blazers up 96-92 after three.

After playing his first minutes of the season last night and making a great impression, Caris LeVert opened the fourth with an elite defensive play, stealing the ball from Dame and converting on the and-one. A few plays later came the sequence of the night: Rollins flipped it to Ware for the baseline poster, then Rollins ripped Dame in the backcourt for the lefty finish, then Burries stonewalled Henderson in the backcourt to force the eight-second violation—Fiserv was rocking! The Blazers would fight back to extend their lead to six, but the Bucks answered with an 8-0 spurt made entirely off of buckets from Ware and Burries to take a 108-106 lead with six minutes to play! But of course, Jrue Holiday—who had made big shots all night—dropped consecutive buckets to give Portland back the edge, leading 112-108. At the three-minute mark, after buckets from Ament and Herro, it was a one-point game, but poor backcourt composure allowed Portland extend their lead to seven, which was enough in the end. Damn.

The Bucks won the possession game by a huge margin (91-77), but they just couldn't convert enough open shots. They were particularly horrid in the first quarter, shooting 8/21.

Trade Kel'el Ware. Trade Myles Turner. Trade Jericho Sims. Pete Nance is the only big you will ever need. Team-high +8 and one of just two Bucks with a positive rating.
