#3085. BJ's (BJ) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Membership growth and a litigation windfall shaped this quarter's results.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 20, 2026 at 1:26PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

BJ's (BJ -4.26%) reported third quarter results that surpassed internal expectations, primarily driven by a strategic decision to reinvest a onetime $240 million legal settlement into membership and stakeholder value. Management reported that the company utilized the settlement proceeds to fund its 42nd birthday event, which resulted in 6% traffic growth and the acquisition of 200,000 new members in October alone. The company stated that these investments were designed to accelerate the membership flywheel by driving shopping frequency and higher renewal rates. Furthermore, the company is executing a category management process to reduce SKU counts by 20% while reallocating space to high-growth areas such as snacks and protein. Management raised its full-year guidance for both comparable sales and adjusted earnings per share to reflect this operational momentum and the net benefit of the litigation settlement.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to BJ's Wholesale Club Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Diana Rashkow, Vice President of Investor Relations. Diana, please go ahead.

Diana Rashkow: Good morning, and welcome to BJ's Third Quarter Fiscal 2026 Earnings Call. Joining me today are Bob Eddy, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer; Laura Felice, Chief Financial Officer; and Bill Werner, Chief Development Officer. Please remember that we may make forward-looking statements on this call that are based on our current expectations. Forward-looking statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from what we say on this call. Please see the Risk Factors section of our most recent SEC filings for a description of these risks and uncertainties posted on our Investor Relations website for our cautionary statement regarding forward-looking statements and non-GAAP reconciliations. And now I'll turn the call over to Bob.

Robert Eddy: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Thanks for joining us today. I'm proud to say we delivered a terrific quarter that came in well ahead of our expectations. Net sales grew 18% and comparable club sales, excluding gasoline, were up 4.1%. Before I get into the details, let me explain how we approached this quarter. It starts with who we are. 42 years ago, we opened our first club in Medford, Massachusetts. The club model was a new idea at the time, but the core idea of leveraging cost savings to deliver value back to customers is a concept as old as retail itself. Today, we serve more than 8.5 million members in 271 clubs across 22 states.

A lot has changed since 1984, but what we do and why we do it hasn't. We take care of the families who depend on us. That purpose is how we run this business. It's how we show up for everyone who relies on BJ's, our members, our team members, our communities and our shareholders. Whether it's assortment decisions, a holiday promotional strategy or how we negotiate indirect costs, it is all with the goal of investing back into the member experience and pouring outsized value back into our members. These everyday decisions are what drive the lifetime value base of our business.

While we operate in that fashion every day, every so often, a moment comes along that calls for something bigger, a chance to do something our members, team members, communities and shareholders would remember. This quarter was that moment. As we announced in early September, we reached a litigation settlement that resulted in a onetime pretax benefit of approximately $240 million. We did not view the settlement as just an amount of cash. We viewed it as an opportunity to invest in BJ's stakeholders, and we chose to play offense with it. We built an ambitious plan to accelerate our strategy in ways that were fun and engaging, and we executed it on a tight time line.

I'm pleased to say it has been a resounding success. And what matters most is not the great results in the quarter. It is that results should build over time, more loyal members, an engaged team, connections to our communities and value for our shareholders. Let me take you through the investments in more detail. We started with our members, viewing the investment as a thank you for decades of loyalty. The centerpiece was our 42nd birthday event, where we offered 42% off featured items throughout the club. Our merchants chose those items carefully, focusing on what matters most to our members.

There were everyday staples that members buy week in and week out, like ground beef, chicken drumsticks and apples. There were Wellsley Farms favorites like hummus, deli ham and coffee, so members could try our own brands at an even lower price. There were fun and seasonal items like a kids' pedal go kart and outerwear, and there were a few splurges like Wagyu steaks and KitchenAid mixers, things that members might not otherwise buy for themselves. We supported it with the most ambitious marketing campaign we've ever run from traditional media like direct mail, TV and radio to a drone show over New York City. The buzz spread on social, too, with unpaid content generating millions of views.

We wanted our members to feel celebrated. That means great prices on the things their families love and a reason to treat themselves a little. Our members loved it. They showed up and filled their carts. Comp traffic increased by 6% year-over-year during the nearly 6-week promotion, levels we have not seen since 2020. We know that engagement drives loyalty. There is a direct link between trips and renewal rate. In fact, tenured members who shop with us once a month have a renewal rate of more than 95%. Comp units grew by 9% during the promotion. Members purchased more than 500,000 pieces of outerwear and enough ground beef to make more than 30 million burgers.

Both of those categories sold 3x their normal volumes. We also saw tremendous trial of new categories. For example, more than 100,000 members bought coffee from us for the first time. And just like trips, the more units and categories a member buys, the more loyal they become. Even better, the members who responded most are the ones with the most room to grow. The biggest jump in shopping frequency came from our newer and less engaged members and our most frequent shoppers who account for the bulk of the sales came in more often, too. Membership drives trips, trips drive renewals, and we've seen that flywheel work year after year.

In tandem with the birthday event, we made investments to accelerate our progress in a few key strategic areas. We ran a membership acquisition campaign with new programs and special pricing tied to the celebration. We offered targeted discounts to encourage members to try our own brands, and we gave members an incentive to get started with ExpressPay. I'll share what we're seeing from these initiatives in a few minutes when I walk through our strategic priorities. Next, I want to talk about our team members. We invested across the full organization because every great team member experience starts with our team. In particular, I want to highlight the awards we made to our more than 30,000 hourly team members.

In October, as part of celebrating our 42nd birthday, we surprised team members in our clubs and distribution centers with the largest recognition award in our company's history. The awards were based on tenure, which was our way of thanking our team members for their loyalty, just like we thanked our members for theirs. These team members are the lifeblood of BJ's. They are the most important team members in our company as they are on the front lines providing superior service to our members and delivering our purpose every day.

It was truly an honor and one of the proudest days of my career to be able to personally hand out BJ's gift cards to our team members to recognize them and thank them. There were more than a few tears shed when I visited our Royal Palm Beach, Florida club, and each member of our executive team had similar reactions in the clubs they visited. While I'm on this topic, I'd like to take this opportunity to say one more time to our team members in the clubs and distribution centers, we appreciate everything you do day in and day out in support of our members, our company and our purpose. Thank you.

Taking care of families doesn't stop at our club doors. It extends to the communities in which we live and work. This quarter, we also made significant contributions to support those communities just as we have throughout the last 4 decades. We will set a record this year for our community giving as we've supported hundreds of organizations and communities across our footprint. As we head into the holidays, I'm proud of how we're showing up in our communities. Just in the past few weeks, we funded weekend and school break meals for kids near our Fort Worth Club, and we've helped fund holiday meals in Buffalo.

We're also working to bring holiday cheer to patients and their families in children's hospitals across our footprint. Those are just a few examples of how we are taking care of the families who depend on us. Most importantly, the investments we made this year underscore our commitment to making a positive impact in our communities in the years and decades to come. Let me turn now to our shareholders. As you know, in November 2024, our Board approved a new $1 billion share repurchase authorization, which runs through January 2029. Year-to-date, we've repurchased more than $366 million of our shares, our largest annual amount since going public with a quarter still to go.

Taking care of the families who depend on us has always been how we build long-term value for our shareholders. Every added unit, trip, new member, own brands trial and ExpressPay adopter makes that engine stronger, adding to our membership base and the earnings it generates. And we expect the benefits to extend well beyond this quarter. As we closed out the birthday event on October 31, we moved right into the holiday season. Our early Black Friday event and free Thanksgiving turkey promotion are helping families prepare, host, and give. And we've added some fun surprises this season, new items members may not have seen before at BJ's. Turning to the broader environment. Our consumer remains resilient.

This quarter, more members shopped with us and spent more across every income level with a growing share choosing higher tier memberships. We also continued to gain share. Based on Circana data in the markets in which we operate, the rest of the market saw unit sales decline during Q3, while we saw unit gains. Our units grew more than 500 basis points faster than the market during the quarter. That includes the lift from our birthday event, but the lead isn't new. We've outpaced the market on units over the entire year. Our model is built to grow both sales and units by delivering value, and we're doing both faster than the market.

Gasoline continues to be a great share gain story with total gallons up 20% and comp gallons increasing by 11% during the quarter. This is one of the clearest ways we deliver value to our members, especially in times of elevated prices. We offer real savings when they need it most, and this offering is a big reason more of them are choosing BJ's. Now let me update you on our strategic priorities, which are how we deliver on our purpose every day. We invest in them with confidence because we know the results build over time. I want to focus on how our recent investments support these efforts.

Let me start with membership, the foundation of our business, which by all metrics remains extremely strong. MFI grew by 9.5% in the third quarter, which continues to track above our initial expectations for the year. As I mentioned earlier, in conjunction with our birthday event, we made a targeted push to attract new members. We signed up more than 200,000 new members in October alone, nearly 40% above our average month earlier this year. The combination of comp club membership growth of 2% to 3%, strong new member sign-ups, record renewal rates and higher tier penetration means we now expect MFI growth of approximately 7.5% as we exit the year.

Membership fee income is the highest quality revenue stream in our model. It's recurring, it's highly profitable, and it reflects our members' confidence in the value we deliver. Every member who joins, renews or moves up to a higher tier adds to a stream that builds over time. That's why we were so deliberate about bringing in new members during our birthday event and why the benefits extend well beyond this quarter. Our own brands were a big part of the story, too. In October, we ran our largest own brands trial campaign with discounts sent specifically to members who hadn't tried our own brands in the category before.

Members redeemed those offers about 670,000 times and 11% of the units we sold on those items went to members trying them for the first time. In addition to the coffee I mentioned before, members especially loved our Wellsley Farms products like our cashews and olive oil. We're confident that once members try a great product at a great price, they'll come back for it. Quality and value are what keep members engaged, and that builds loyalty and lifetime value. I also want to tell you more about our assortment work. Last quarter, I told you about our commitment to reduce our SKU count by about 20%. And today, I want to tell you how we will get there.

We've planned several waves of our category management process, or CMP, over the next 2 years or so. With each wave, we are reducing redundant SKUs and reallocating space to create room for innovation, more excitement and greater exposure to growing categories. We made meaningful progress repositioning several health and beauty aids categories and saw strong results in Q3. Late in the quarter, we also launched a grocery reset that reduced SKU count, introduced new items and made significant changes to space allocation, prioritizing high-growth snacking categories and high-protein options such as meat snacks. Initial results are encouraging, and we plan to deploy additional resets using this approach in Q1 and Q2 of next year and beyond.

We believe that in the next year or so, our members will see a notable improvement in the quality and the clarity of our assortment. That means an easier and more exciting shopping trip and more reasons to come back. Turning to convenience. Digitally enabled comp sales grew 38% in the quarter. In Q3, we made a targeted effort to drive ExpressPay adoption. We know that members who use ExpressPay shop more, spend more and renew at higher rates, and our efforts are working. ExpressPay order penetration increased by more than 200 basis points throughout the quarter. We're also building for the future.

Bev, our AI shopping assistant, continues to gain momentum and is becoming part of how members shop and get help, and she's now in our app. Those conversations also tell us what members want, which helps our team act on it. And as AI platforms evolve, we're meeting members where they are, building the capabilities to show up and shop with us in the AI assistants they're starting to use. And finally, our footprint. New clubs remain a key engine of our long-term growth. In Q3, we relocated our Rotterdam, New York, club and opened new clubs in Foley, Alabama, and Ocala, Florida, all with new gas stations.

So far in November, we opened our fifth Texas club in Mesquite as well as in Frankfort, Kentucky. We have 3 additional club openings in store for the rest of the quarter in Lecanto and Port St. Lucie, Florida, and Portage, Indiana, as well as 2 gas stations being added to existing club locations. The performance of our new club portfolio remains strong with ROICs in the high teens. We also have our strongest pipeline yet with nearly 30 new clubs planned for 2027 and 2028, including a new club coming to the Bronx next year. We are now running hard in real estate growth. And beyond 2028, we want to challenge ourselves to go even faster.

Before I hand it over to Laura, I want to say a few words about our team. This was a busy quarter with a lot of moving pieces, and it all came together because of the people in our clubs, distribution centers, supply chain and club support center who showed up every day to make it happen. I'm proud of what we accomplished together, and I'm grateful to every one of you. Laura, over to you.

Laura Felice: Thank you, Bob, and good morning, everyone. I'd like to add my thanks to our team members across the company for an outstanding quarter. Let me begin with our sales results. Net sales were $6.1 billion, up 17.7% year-over-year. Comparable club sales, including gasoline, were up 13.5% and excluding gasoline, they were up 4.1%. Traffic drove the majority of our comp growth during the quarter. Turning to our categories. Grocery, perishables and sundries comp was up 3.4%, led by grocery. General merchandise and services grew 9.1% with growth across home, seasonal, apparel, consumer electronics and services. Inflation was just under 1 point for the quarter after adjusting for the 42nd birthday promotional activity.

In gas, comp gallons increased 10.6%, and we continue to take share. Industry data indicates overall comp fuel gallons declined by about 5%. Membership fee income increased 9.5% to $138 million as we continue to grow our base of more than 8.5 million members, maintained strong renewal rates and drove higher tier penetration. As Bob noted, while we expect MFI growth to moderate as the impact of last year's fee increase fully normalizes, we now expect to exit the year at around 7.5% growth. Turning to gross profit. In total, we delivered $1.02 billion in gross profit dollars, up 1% over last year, even as we invested in our members.

Within that, merchandise gross margin rate was down 170 basis points year-over-year, driven by an estimated $56 million of onetime promotions related to our 42nd birthday, fully funded by the interchange settlement. Turning to fuel. Penny profit was approximately in line with our forecasted rate. Combined with strong gallon growth, fuel gross profit was just slightly ahead of our targeted level for the quarter. SG&A was $696 million on a reported basis, which includes $240 million of legal settlement benefit, partially offset by an estimated $95 million of in-quarter investments in compensation, advertising and labor that Bob described. As a result, adjusted EBITDA was $422 million. Our effective tax rate was 27.4%.

Adjusted EPS was $1.73, ahead of our expectation, driven by the great performance and aided by legal settlement benefit, partially offset by our in-quarter investments. Turning to our balance sheet and cash flow. Merchandise inventory ended the quarter at $1.84 billion, up 9% year-over-year, reflecting our new club openings and more normalized inventory levels compared to the prior year as we head into the holidays. Our comp inventory balance is clean with good in-stock levels. Our balance sheet remains strong with total debt of $469 million, cash of $29 million and net debt to adjusted EBITDA of 0.3x. Cash flow remained healthy. Year-to-date, cash flow from operations was $933 million, up from $639 million last year.

Capital expenditures, net of disposal, were $592 million, reflecting continued investment in our new clubs and our distribution network. Adjusted free cash flow was $455 million year-to-date compared to $141 million last year and $232 million in the third quarter. Our capital allocation priorities remain unchanged. First and foremost, we invest in the business, in membership, merchandising, digital capabilities and real estate. We also continue to return capital to shareholders. In the third quarter, we repurchased $35.6 million of our shares, bringing the year-to-date total to $366.3 million, and we have approximately $387 million remaining under our existing authorization. Now let me turn to the outlook for the full year.

We're pleased with our outperformance in the third quarter, and we've updated our guidance to reflect it. We are raising our full year guidance for comparable club sales growth, excluding gasoline, to 2.5% to 3%. For adjusted earnings per share, we are raising our range, and we now expect $5.10 to $5.30 for the full year. This range reflects our strong performance along with the net benefit of the legal settlement after the investments we made in the quarter. We're pleased with how the third quarter came together, and we entered the holiday season with a clear plan and a strong foundation.

As always, our outlook reflects our current view of the consumer and the broader operating environment, and we will continue to manage the business with discipline while investing for long-term growth. With that, I'll turn it back to Bob.

Robert Eddy: Thanks, Laura. Before we open the call for questions, I want to take a step back. This was a strong quarter, well ahead of our expectations. We were handed a rare opportunity, and we chose to play offense and invest in our future, and we're guided by our purpose in doing so. We celebrated our members. We honored our team. We stood with our communities, and we kept building long-term value for our shareholders. We did it the way we've always done it because that is our job. Our strategic priorities are working and the investments we made this quarter were designed to accelerate each of them. We're excited about the road ahead.

Thank you to our members, our team members, our communities and our shareholders for being a part of it. All of it comes back to why we are here. We take care of the families who depend on us. That's who we are. That's what we do, and we're still just getting started. With that, let's take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Kate McShane from Goldman Sachs.

Katharine McShane: I guess we were curious just with regards to the sustainability of some of this momentum that you saw during the third quarter. It does seem like a lot of the efforts did result in quite a bit of growth. What have you seen since maybe the ending of the anniversary sale in terms of response? And again, just how should we think about the sustainability of demand beyond the anniversary sale?

Robert Eddy: Kate, thanks for your question. We're pretty excited to share the results that we put out this morning. I'm really proud of the team for getting it all done. We've really never done anything of this scope and speed and maybe more importantly, impact on our company. And we really like the feeling. And I hope that these investments feel aggressive to you because that was our goal. We did terrific work on behalf of our members during COVID, but my opinion was we didn't invest enough of that unanticipated upside.

And so when we got this legal settlement this quarter, we really tried to do the right thing with that and invested over $150 million during the quarter to try and really get our company moving faster and to accelerate our strategy. So we drove unprecedented engagement with our membership with obviously, the comp upside and the traffic and the units that we talked about. We had the incredible engagement with our members and thanking them and rewarding them for their work and obviously, what we talked about from a community standpoint and from our shareholders as well. But your point is the best one. We did this not for any particular result in this quarter.

We did it for the long-term value of what these efforts do for us. And it's our belief that the gains made in this quarter will drive lifetime value and will drive our company to be better in the future. You think about investing in our members, not only did we sign up well over a couple of hundred thousand members. We talked about just 200,000 members in just October alone. So obviously, that benefit will persist into the future. But we know that increased engagement is a good thing from a lifetime value perspective.

The more units people put in their basket, the more times they come to see us, the more times they come to see us, the more they renew their membership. And obviously, the more they renew, the more they come to see us again. And so it's a virtuous cycle that we can invest in over and over. And in our past, maybe we haven't been so religious in doing so over time in response to whatever might be happening in a particular quarter or year. But I'm thrilled that we took the opportunity to really do that and build our company for the future. And so as we look forward, you can think about certain benefits that would persist.

Obviously, I talked about the number of members. We know there's a direct link between trips and renewal rates. So we've seen better results in renewal rates during and following the promotional period. We know that the traffic continues to give people reasons to think about us, and I believe will cause them to show up at increased rates in the future, both in this year and in the future and next year. And so I'm really bullish on our ability for these gains to be sustainable. Again, we didn't do it for 1 quarter's benefit here. We did it for that long term.

And that slide continues into some of the other things that we did, right, investing in own brands and investing in ExpressPay. We -- those benefits are harder to see in any one particular quarter, and really are meant to augur towards the future, right? I mean, we're giving somebody money to use ExpressPay as, for instance, their first time. But we know that once they get into that, they shop more, they spend more, they come to see us more. Their Net Promoter Score goes up quite considerably once they get into that franchise.

And so while that may look like not the best ROI in this particular quarter, it will definitely look like a great ROI in the future. And so we're pretty happy with what we did. And I think you can look for us to do more of that in the future if we have the opportunity.

Katharine McShane: And I just wanted to follow up with a quick question on your beyond 2028 real estate comment. Should we assume that you're contemplating opening more stores per year beyond 2028?

Robert Eddy: Yes. Look, I mean, I'll hand this over to Bill, but that's certainly our goal, right? We've gone from not opening any clubs to now reliably opening 10 to 15 a year. And we're experiencing fantastic returns. We talk about our returns on capital in the mid- to high teens. That's better than the S&P 500 average, right? Certainly better than our cost of capital. And so that just screams at us go faster. It takes a while to get the flywheel to go faster in this regard, but we'd love to open more if we can. So Bill?

William Werner: Yes. I think, Kate, what you saw, say, in the script, right, is a little bit of a signaling that we came out 2 years ago with a goal to accelerate to 25% to 30%. I think what you're hearing today is that we're trying to trend towards the top end of that range as we look -- range as we look out for the next 2 years, so '27 and '28 combined. And as a team, we're working hard on what '29 and forward looks like now. I've mentioned this on a couple of the earnings calls and in other investor meetings, it's -- the market is super dynamic.

And with the share gains that we're seeing and the share gains were amazing across this past quarter, especially during the birthday celebration, but notwithstanding like that 1 month across the board, we've seen crazy unit share gains, great dollar share gains. And every time we gain share, the models change in terms of opportunities for additional real estate. So it's just -- it's a really exciting time to be part of the real estate program here at BJ's, and the team is super engaged and excited to do everything we can to drive value for new prospective members and new communities.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Peter Benedict from Baird.

Peter Benedict: So a couple of questions. First, just can you help us maybe unpack the merch margin decline in the quarter? You gave some points. I think you talked about $54 million of reinvestment. But I was just curious what -- how you can kind of unpack kind of the full $170 million and how we think about the fourth quarter trends from a merch margin perspective? That's my first question.

Robert Eddy: Yes. Pete, thanks for your question. Maybe I'll start and Laura can fill in. I think our team did a fantastic job managing margin this quarter, particularly hard given all the different promotions and changes we are making, as you can imagine, the management was just a task in itself this quarter. We talked a little bit in the prepared remarks about the decline in margin rate being the result of all these promotions that we did, these onetime promotions. And so ex that, the margin rate was about where we thought it was going to be and similar to what it was in Q2.

I think what I would say is focusing on the rate loses the plot a little bit. We wanted to win by engaging the members with compelling merchandise with great values. And that means winning a little bit with margin dollars more than any one particular rate. And I think you should think about seeing us do that more and more as we go forward. This business is about membership and engagement and trips and units more than it is about any one particular rate. And we'd love to win through margin dollars more. It's better for our members and just fine for us. So maybe I'll hand it over to Laura so she can fill in.

Laura Felice: Yes. I think I would add on top of that, Pete, I think the question is a good one. Bob highlights, we continue to manage the business for margin dollar accretion. Rate is important, but it doesn't always give the full picture. And so driving healthy penny profit to our business is really the aim of what we're doing. And so we invested dollars in the quarter. We think that was important. Bob already talked about how we're thinking about that as we move forward and how it feeds the membership flywheel.

So that roughly $56 million that we talked about investing in the quarter, I think excluding that, our margin rates were healthy, and they were on target and ahead of the promotion, they were tracking where we thought they would be. You know onetime promotional investments are often hard to isolate because their impact extends beyond the onetime promotion and into the broader membership shopping behavior. And so again, we're really happy with the results we delivered. We're aiming at delivering gross profit margin dollars and holding together the whole P&L as we head into the fourth quarter and beyond.

Robert Eddy: Yes. And maybe I'll just finish up. I mean the legal settlement showed up in SG&A, Pete, but we viewed it as margin. We viewed it as our members' money, first and foremost. And so this quarter was really about giving them that benefit. And that's really what guided us when we knew the settlement was coming, we started crafting this program, how can we give this to our members for their benefit because we know that every time we give them a benefit, they in turn pay that back to us.

Peter Benedict: Yes. No, strategy makes total sense. My follow-up is really just around -- any way to assess like any pull forward that you may have had from the event. I mean, obviously, some great engagement there. Since it's closed out, any sense that you had any pull-forward impacts? I'm just curious kind of your read kind of on the early holiday trends, Thanksgiving, that type of thing.

Robert Eddy: Yes. Good question. Anytime you see volume increases like we saw in the quarter, that's a risk. I think our merchants did a phenomenal job selecting the items that we promoted to minimize that impact. And so maybe answer it in 2 different ways. From a general merchandise perspective, we absolutely pulled things forward. And our aim there was really to take sales out of the market before they went to [indiscernible] and so [indiscernible] about outerwear and KitchenAid mixers and things. We're thrilled that we got people in to buy those things no matter what quarter it comes in.

The fact that it came in Q3 gives us an opportunity to sell them something different in Q4 and may have stolen a sale from someone else. And in the food and grocery business, there's only so much you can put in your freezer. And so while we definitely sold a ton of ground beef, and I'm sure people froze some of it and that might be pull forward, you don't really do that with potatoes or apples or deli meat or some of the other things that we did. And so I'm sure there's some limited pull forward that will impact us going forward.

But the more important story is the engagement, the trips, the units, the reasons we've given them to come back and see us in the future. And that we think will overwhelm any pull forward.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Edward Kelly from Wells Fargo.

Edward Kelly: Bob, I guess my question is on investment. It's good to see smart investment in the business yielding returns. And when you say things like the biggest jump happening with your less engaged members and you talk about 200,000 sign-ups in October, which is really impressive. What is that telling you about BJ's and the pace of investment or what you should be investing moving forward? And then as part of that, what's the promotional cadence look like in Q4? Have you saved any dollars to invest in Q4? I think you're going to have probably a strong fuel margin quarter, so maybe you have money to spend there. But just curious as how you're thinking about Q4 as well.

Robert Eddy: Yes. Ed, it's a good question. I guess, let me start out by saying, again, we were thrilled with how our members reacted to this stuff. We were thrilled to have the opportunity to do it. And we've been talking for a while about this is clubs time, right, where members' wallets are pressured, consumers' wallets are pressured. We're among the lowest cost providers of grocery and general merchandise. And so we've been gathering share for a while. We've been a long-term share gainer and the club industry has as well. And so that's been the centerpiece of our strategy. How can we really take advantage of that? How can we build on that thought.

And so the idea of making these huge investments in the third quarter was just a fun thing to really think about because in a normal quarter, we're trying to make the investments that work within the construct of our P&L and our commitments to Wall Street and what's going on in the broader market. And we just had a greater pile of money to play with in this quarter. Importantly, we didn't really reduce what we were thinking about from a Q4 perspective. We didn't change that at all initially. We have been tweaking it based on some of the lessons that we learned in the Q3 promotions.

And this idea that our members really responded to some of these things and this idea that we can make longer-term bets than in any one quarter. And so I think you may see different types of promotions in the future, not necessarily more or less dollars put against them than we might have otherwise planned. But we learned a lot in how to engage our members, what they will respond to, what's important to them. And it's in things big and small, like what's the depth of a particular promotion that matters. What types of things matter?

I mean I think if you asked us 6 months ago, whether our members would buy Wagyu beef from us, we would probably have said no. And we decided to take a shot and see what happened, and they bought it in droves. And KitchenAid mixers, same thing. We've had many years where we've tried to sell those things and they haven't worked. And the fact that we got them in front of members at a great value put that in people's minds that we are a destination for those things. And so as we go forward, we'll just try and take those lessons and apply them judiciously.

And our whole aim as a team is about how can we invest in the member. And so we'll continue to do that, again, within the construct of the economy and our own P&L.

Edward Kelly: The flip side of all this investment and strong return on that is sort of like how do we think about 2027 and lapping a lot of this. And I don't envy you in terms of how you think about guidance for next year. But -- and I know it's early, but any thoughts on what does the real base year sort of look like in '26 as we think about like an algo or growth number for '27? Any early thoughts around that?

Robert Eddy: Yes. We kind of knew this question was coming. We had bets on how many questions we'd get to celebrate good results before we get into what happens next year. And so we're happy. This is a little bit of a champagne problem for us, right? We're coming off -- we'll be coming off the best year we've ever had as a company this year off of the best one we've ever had last year and the year before that. And so I dare say we won't have another once-in-a-career legal settlement. So it will be tough to have another quarter as profitable as this one in that regard.

We'll obviously not -- anniversary, the $150-odd million of spending we did in the quarter either. And that leaves aside the other benefits we've had this year, tariff refunds and excess gas income and the like. But that only contemplates the benefits that we've seen. We've also had some bad guys we haven't expected like $6 diesel and increasing medical costs and the unplanned investments in member value that we used tariff refunds to fund. And we took some of the fair winds in gasoline that we saw in Q2 and invested that as well. And so look, I think it's tough to give guidance at this point. We're not obviously not going to do that.

And each year in the recent past, at least since COVID, has been very dynamic and had good guys, probably more good guys and more bad guys than anybody has anticipated. So I've kind of stopped trying to anticipate what's going to happen every year. And rather, we just take what comes at us and try to make the best decisions that we can on behalf of our members and again, within the construct of the economy and our P&L. So as we always do, we'll work hard to mitigate any of the bad guys that come along, and we'll invest any winnings on behalf of our members, too.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Simeon Gutman from Morgan Stanley.

Simeon Gutman: So first question, this powerful impact that you've had on comp and MFI from maybe the 42nd birthday and other things. Can you talk about how well split the impact is across your footprint? Was it highest -- was it strongest in some of your highest market share markets? And I know you didn't speak to it directly, but have you seen more frequency since?

Robert Eddy: I don't know that there's really been any difference in terms of the impact of the promotions that we did from a geographic perspective. We saw terrific results across our chain in existing clubs, I mean, legacy clubs and in new clubs in super strong markets like New England and Florida or New York versus less dense markets. I think we put such good promotions out there and such good items, such relevant items out there that no matter where the members were, they reacted to them. And so that was terrific. We really -- we're proud of that. We weren't trying to target anything. We were trying to target every member and give them something to feel great about.

And I feel like we achieved that goal. And from a frequency perspective, it's a little early in Q4 to comment on anything, but I would imagine based on what we saw in Q3 that, that will help frequency in Q4 and beyond. And so we're pretty proud of what we accomplished in the third quarter and hope that will benefit us in the future.

Simeon Gutman: Okay. My follow-up, and if you were betting on how many of these base questions you're going to get, I'm going to give you another one, just basically the same thing. Thinking about you have this financial impact, and Bob, you've worn different hats, both financial and now full strategic and operational. I guess Wall Street is worried about what went into the mix this year, both from a financial perspective and now from a customer perspective. Customer, you have this lever in membership, which is unique, so an ability to retain the business that happened this year. And by the way, every retailer this week were contemplating what the base is.

And I think the operators don't sound that worried the way that you described it because you have offsets. I guess, is that the right way to look at it? You'll be able to lap it? Like you said, you'll be able to take other areas of expense out of the business, you're lapping gasoline, but there are some pretty big financial impacts that I think Wall Street is concerned about that operators are not as. So any more flavor to what you just spoke to would be helpful.

Robert Eddy: Yes. Look, I think it's going to be difficult to take -- for me to take every good guy and bad guy and sort of tell you how we'll mitigate those or deal with those because I don't know what's going to happen in the future from a good guy, bad guy perspective, right? So very simply, again, I feel like I'm repeating the last answer, but we're not going to anniversary the settlement, and we're probably not going to anniversary all the investment we did in Q3. So that's easy to think about. But what happens from a diesel perspective, not sure. What happens from a medical cost perspective, not sure.

What happens from a gasoline income perspective, not sure. And so it's very hard to answer that. I can tell you, we understand our commitment to our members to offer them great value. And so we will put that first and foremost. And we understand our commitment to ourselves and our shareholders as well. And so we will do our best to really find that base and improve against it. And I think the team understands the assignment for next year. I think we have some irons in the fire on how we will lap the stuff that is lappable. But again, we kind of don't know what's coming.

And I mean, I do think there is -- there will be considerable pressure coming from a price increase perspective out there if you take just one thing and talk about the diesel cost. Certainly, that is real. Every one of our competitors is experiencing that. We're experiencing that. We've offset that in our P&L with tariff refunds in some ways as a for instance, or with gasoline income. And so I think that could be a headwind next year. It could be offset by raising prices. It could go back down to $4 a gallon, and then it's not a problem.

And so again, I think we'll just take what comes at us and manage within the scope of what we can manage. We can't control everything, but we will control what we can control.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Chuck Grom from Gordon Haskett.

Charles Grom: Just now to Simeon's question, you talked about the potential for an uptick in frequency here in the fourth quarter and I guess maybe into 2027 from your actions that you took in the third quarter. So I guess, the question is that typically what you've seen? And I guess the million-dollar question, Bob, is there a way to quantify how much of a comp bump you saw in the third quarter from the 42nd event? And then, Laura, maybe you could just speak to the actual traffic increase in the third quarter.

Robert Eddy: Yes, sure. Thank you. So we talked about the 42nd birthday promos driving about 1 point of comp. It's a little bit of a messy math exercise to figure that out. And it's obviously impacted by the dollar impact of those promotions. And so it's probably not the best way to judge the performance of those promotions either. The units and the traffic being up 9% and 6% are better indications of how powerful those promotions were. I said in the prepared remarks, we haven't seen traffic increases like that since COVID, right?

To have that traffic over 6 weeks for us was very, very cool and very, very hard for our operations team to deal with and our supply chain team to deal with. But talk about champagne problems, we're thrilled to see that. And we know that, that comes back to us in the future simply through membership renewals. There's a linear impact between trips and renewal rate. And we're already seeing a renewal rate ticking up as a result of that, which means more trips in the future. And so I'm not going to give you a detailed answer to your question because we're not giving guidance for next year.

But we do know that we should have a pickup in Q4 and in next year because of it.

Laura Felice: Yes. And then, Chuck, maybe I'll jump in on specifics on your traffic question. I think there's 2 important things I'd point you to. The comp traffic during the promotion, which Bob already talked about, the plus 6%, which is incredible. Our members were showing up. They saw the value. They rewarded us with trips and basket. And then for the full quarter, not just the promotion, our comp was largely driven by traffic this quarter. And so you've heard us talk about it's either been a balance between traffic and basket as we progress through the year. This quarter, it was more traffic driven. We like that behavior.

Again, hanging on everything Bob said earlier, and we said in the prepared remarks, traffic drives the membership flywheel. Our members are seeing the value that we're offering, whether it's assortment or pricing or convenience with things like ExpressPay. And all of those should augur towards lifetime value benefit in the long term and our members continuing to reward us.

Robert Eddy: Maybe I'll just add on one thought, right? We plan to exit this year from an MFI perspective around 6%. And we just told you today we're going to leave this year around 7.5%. That's the result of signing up more members and engaging them, right? That's probably the best number we've had ex fee increase, right, as a company in a while. And so we had a terrific quarter within membership. Team has done a fantastic job. We talked about the 200,000 members in a month. We'll hit 9 million members during Q4.

There's all these things that we can talk about, but that simple change of run rate in MFI is a product of what we did in Q3.

Charles Grom: No doubt about that. My follow-up is just on the SKU rat a little bit. In the past, we've talked about some spotty history, and I know you don't want to go down that road again. So I guess what have you learned so far in wave 1? It doesn't sound like you've alienated any of your customers, but how are we thinking about the progression into next year? You talked about it being a 2-year process. Is there any reason why you couldn't accelerate that? So just any initial observations.

Robert Eddy: Well, you sound like me when I'm in these meetings. I wanted to go faster because I know it's important, and I know it's working. In the past, we simply deleted repetitive SKUs, and we didn't really change space allocation. We didn't add other categories or other items that are more relevant and growthy. And that is what we're doing now. So when we talk about a SKU reduction amount of 20%, we're really cutting more SKUs than that and adding some in. And so we have wave 1 on the floor now in our grocery business. And we're seeing fantastic results from it. We haven't alienated members.

We haven't lost sales dollars, and we're importantly getting people to buy these better, growthier products from us. And then we're experiencing the ancillary benefit of having a simpler assortment for our operators and our logisticians to figure out. And so look, we're super early in this. We've only got the first one on the floor. The second one will come in Q1. Third one will come in Q2 next year. It does take a while to figure out what we want to put on the floor, negotiate it all with our suppliers, get all the product and make sure we roll it out effectively to our members. We're going to go as fast as we can go.

Our merchants are excited about it based on what we've seen so far in the first wave. And more importantly, our members are excited about it. And look, we're just getting started. Our merchandising team is doing a fantastic job on this. And hopefully, as we go forward, we'll just see that impact built.

Operator: Your final question comes from the line of Michael Baker from D.A. Davidson.

Michael Baker: I'll ask 2 quick ones here to end. So what's the usual renewal rate of the discounted memberships that you offered during the event? In other words, that 200,000 new sign-ups, is there renewal -- do those usually renew around 90% or something different? And then I'll ask my second question. I wonder if you had a bet on how long it took for someone to ask this one. But as I look at my window, it's 65 degrees in Boston. You can't be selling a lot of fall apparel. It sounds like -- it seems like your guidance is looking for 2% to 3% or so in the fourth quarter on comps.

But if you could maybe talk about what you're seeing in terms of the weather. A lot of retailers have talked about it starting off slow because of the weather.

Robert Eddy: So listen, I think we talked about this in the past, discounted memberships come with easy renewal. Those folks have to renew. With that said, they're first year members, and so they don't renew at 100%. They renew at something less than that. But it's our job once we get them to sign up in that first year to engage them. And that was one of the cooler benefits of the stuff we did in the third quarter. And we haven't quite unbundled all the lessons from it as we look at the analytics.

But one of the things that we and I know our competitors have been fighting is more and more members come in to our franchise through digital means, and they don't just show up in our physical stores and make their first purchase on the day in which they sign up for our membership. And there's a really tight link between when they sign up and when they shop as you think about the quality of their membership. And so we've all been sort of fighting how do we engage these people that show up digitally.

They'll show up on a website or an app or whatever, sign up for a membership and then they don't make a purchase for a month. And that is a markedly different member than somebody who signs up and purchases on the same day. And pairing up these membership offers that we did in Q3 and the 42nd birthday party that gave people a tremendous range of promotions to react to at the same time they were signing up for membership and arguably probably drove many of them to sign up for membership really changes that dynamic in terms of the quality of the members that we get out of any particular promotion.

And so we're excited to get the read on the numbers on what did that better engagement model look like from a quality of membership perspective. I anticipate that it will look much better. I anticipate the renewal rate of these members will be better, but we haven't seen the read yet. It's just far too early. And look, as we think about the weather, it's certainly been favorable in Boston. We operate in 22 states now. So it's not quite just a Boston story. It's been a very nice fall here. And I think that probably has driven a little bit of a slower start to winter apparel.

But go back to what we talked about in the 42nd birthday with 500,000 pieces of outerwear, that's all winter apparel, right? So we really, I think, have done a fine job from an apparel sales perspective thus far, and we'll continue to try and put compelling products at great values in front of our members when the markets turn cold.

Operator: This concludes -- Sorry, go ahead.

Robert Eddy: No, I just want to thanks for your participation. Appreciate your support.

Operator: This concludes our Q&A session. Thank you all for attending today's call. You may now disconnect.

The Portland Trail Blazers made the trek to Milwaukee last year to play the Bucks. Damian Lillard was present, even though he was sitting out the entire 2025-26 campaign — his first season back with the Trail Blazers — as he recovered from the Achilles tear he suffered while playing for the Bucks in their 2025 first-round playoff series.

Fiserv Forum aired a video tribute to Lillard amid that November 2025 meeting, and the nine-time All-Star received a standing ovation after it played that night.

Thursday marked the 36-year-old guard's first time taking the court against Milwaukee since his injury and his two-season stint with the Bucks. Lillard was subdued talking about the matchup in the lead-up to tip-off, but he came away with his best performance in 624 days.

March 5, 2025, was the last time Lillard had a 30-point game. He scored a season-high 33 points on Thursday in a 124-114 victory over a reeling and rebuilding Milwaukee (1-15).

Portland (10-5) bounced back after dropping consecutive games to the Minnesota Timberwolves.

Lillard once again received a warm welcome from Bucks fans. Milwaukee ultimately waived him to sign center Myles Turner in the summer of 2025. The Bucks are still paying Lillard after they decided to stretch the remaining $113 million on his contract.

So, on Thursday, Milwaukee fans watched their team lose its 12th straight game and Lillard shoot 10 of 18 from the field, including 5 of 12 from the beyond the arc.

Plus, another former Bucks player, Jrue Holiday — part of Milwaukee's NBA championship team in 2020-21 — put on a show of his own. He logged 22 points, 7 assists and 4 steals.

Holiday stepped back to hit a crucial jumper with about 5 ½ minutes to go. Another 36-year-old guard, Holiday went on to help the Trail Blazers create separation late, even coupling a steal with a layup.

Portland also got 27 points and seven rebounds from a much younger member of its backcourt: Scoot Henderson.

Meanwhile, the Bucks fell again, a day removed from facing Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time.

Milwaukee had four players score 15-plus points this time out. Tyler Herro led the way with 19, Kasparas Jakučionis and Nate Ament had 18 apiece and Ryan Rollins chipped in 15. Turner, notably, was out with a shoulder injury.

The lead changed hands incessantly on Thursday. Herro drew the Bucks within one at the 3:18 mark in the fourth quarter. The Trail Blazers, though, scored the final nine points, with Lillard netting the last two at the free-throw line.

#3073. Preview: Jazz look to build scorching hot win streak against Phoenix

For the Utah Jazz, winning two games in a row might as well feel like 20. With an outstanding A+ road trip in Los Angeles, things could not be brighter despite a 3-13 record. The young core is finally showing its fruition. Keyonte is evolving as a facilitator; Darryn Peterson is a do-it-all guard; Brice Sensabaugh can apparently score from anywhere.

Back at the Delta Center, fans will have their first look this year at the inaugural Jazz NBA Cup court, in all of its purple glory. I don't think the bright painted floors will ever grow on me, but you have to admit its better than most.

They'll be taking on the Phoenix Suns, equally trapped in the whirlwind of the Western Conference with a 7-7 record. The Jazz have likely already been eliminated from the NBA Cup — taking two hits in both of the Cup Road games. Phoenix, on the other hand, still has a chance to claim a wildcard spot since they've only played one Group A match thus far.

I'll give the Suns their kudos; compared to the Jazz, they recovered from an abysmal 1-5 start to the season and have climbed all the way back to .500. There are still questions related to team chemistry and players' roles, but Phoenix still goes out there and shows effort every single night.

Spearheaded by Devin Booker in his 12th season, the Suns' biggest strength is their high-efficiency shooting. Their team shoots 47.5% from the field, placing them inside the top 10 in overall shooting efficiency. Young big men Khaman Maluach (60.9% FG) and Oso Ighodaro (58.0% FG) anchor most of the finishing, alongside Booker (48.0% FG). The Jazz likely won't have much of a footing against their bench unit either — Phoenix boasts one of the league's top benches, with players like Jordan Goodwin (9.8 PPG), Luke Kennard (9.4 PPG) and Collin Gillespie (9.3 PPG) regularly putting up double-digit nights. A victory over the red-hot Suns (victors of 6 of their last 8) would give Utah solid footing to build on, hopefully towards the NBA Playoff picture.

It should come as a given, knowing our Jazz, but Utah's two-game winning streak could have easily been a 14-game losing skid with a couple of swing possessions. The stat sheet may show a double-digit victory in the Jazz's triumph over the Lakers, but these teams were neck and neck all night. Utah could have easily blown the game open earlier, had it not been for their 20 turnovers through the first three quarters. That was shown in Inglewood too, where the same Jazz team coughed up 14 turnovers in three quarters against the Clippers.

Phoenix rarely beats itself — 5th lowest turnover rate in the NBA — and thrives off unforced errors led by Gillespie and Goodwin. With Lauri, JJJ and Nurkic still sidelined, the game will continue to be run exclusively by Utah's young backcourt. Keyonte George averaged 3.5 turnovers a game, while backup Isaiah Collier (2.0 turnovers) and Darryn Peterson (1.9 turnovers) also carry heavy ball-handling roles.

Utah can't count on miracle fourth quarters forever. Soon enough, they'll have to learn how to push through full-court coverage and slow down the pace on the scoring end. If Keyonte and DP can't take care of the rock, Phoenix's transition game will bury them early on.

LOS ANGELES, CA – NOVEMBER 18: Keyonte George #3 of the Utah Jazz handles the ball during the game against the Los Angeles Lakers on November 18, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Pantozzi/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Wednesday night, wings Josh Green and Josh Okogie hounded Luka Dončić into 10-of-28 shooting and nine turnovers. Green set the tone, staying glued to Luka while only committing one turnover in 28 minutes of action. Former Sun Josh Okogie stepped in whenever Josh #1 needed a breather, stepping in and giving Utah 43 combined minutes of relentless perimeter defense.

While Dončić dominates through size and slow-paced pick-and-roll manipulation, Devin Booker (24.8 PPG, 5.4 APG, 48.0% FG) attacks defenses with constant off-ball movement and a lethal mid-range game. The Joshs will have to fight through pin-downs and flare screens all night to prevent Booker from settling into his sweet spots. Booker enters Friday shooting a lethal 94.5% from the charity stripe on 6.1 attempts per game. If Green and Okogie get too aggressive, Booker will turn those whistles into free points.

Because Utah is missing its top frontcourt defenders, the Jazz saviour Mo Bamba plays a critical role behind Green and Okogie. With Bamba on the floor, Utah's defense improves by 3.8 points per 100 possessions thanks to his 4.5% block rate, giving Utah's wings confidence to crowd Booker's jumper without worrying about giving up uncontested layups if he drives past them.

Coming into this season as a third-string emergency big, Bamba has transformed into a starting-caliber NBA player. Bamba had his breakout game against the Spurs, exploding for 26 points (10-of-13 FG, 6-of-6 from three), 5 rebounds, 4 assists, 2 steals, and 1 block in 36 minutes—after not making a single three-pointer all season prior to that night. He followed that up with back-to-back double-doubles against his former LA teams and a combined 26 rebounds.

Phoenix ranks near the bottom of the league in controlling the glass and is missing starting center Mark Williams. Bamba averages 2.4 offensive boards per game in just 20.7 minutes—using his 7-foot-10 wingspan to tower over Phoenix's younger, lighter bigs, Maluach and Ighodaro, and create second-chance oppurtunities.

Bamba's biggest hurdle is staying on the floor. He fouled out in 20 minutes against Houston earlier this month and picked up four fouls against San Antonio. Against a savvy foul-drawer like Devin Booker, Bamba must contest vertically without biting on fakes so Utah doesn't have to lean too heavily on small-ball lineups, nor the Tony Bradley minutes.

#3071. AST SpaceMobile vs. Redwire: Which Space Infrastructure Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Redwire's revenue grew nearly 46% while AST SpaceMobile's sales soared over 670%, but one balance sheet gap separates these two space stocks sharply.

By Brendan Coffey – Updated Nov 20, 2026 at 1:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than AST SpaceMobile ›

The private space economy is rapidly expanding as satellite technology and infrastructure become more accessible. Deciding between AST SpaceMobile (ASTS -9.22%) and Redwire (RDW -12.29%) depends on your appetite for high-stakes disruption versus established hardware manufacturing.

AST SpaceMobile seeks to eliminate global connectivity gaps by providing cellular service from orbit. Redwire serves as a critical supplier of components, sensors, and microgravity research platforms. This comparison examines how their differing business models, financial health, and operational risks align with long-term investment goals.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached around $142.9 million. This represents a substantial revenue growth of roughly 671% compared to the prior twelve-month period as the company began its commercial rollout. However, the company still reported a significant net loss of approximately $628.3 million during this same time frame.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio stands at nearly 16.4x. This ratio measures liquid assets against short-term debts, indicating a strong immediate liquidity position. The company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 1.2x, meaning its total liabilities are 1.2 times its shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $1.1 billion.

Redwire functions as a diversified infrastructure provider for the aerospace and defense sectors. It supplies essential hardware, such as avionics and power systems, to NASA and various branches of the U.S. military. Beyond government contracts, the company has established commercial partnerships with leaders like Eli Lilly & Co. (LLY +0.04%) to conduct advanced microgravity research in orbit.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached approximately $431.9 million. This performance reflects revenue growth of about 45.8% over the previous twelve-month period. Despite the increase in sales, Redwire recorded a net loss of roughly $226.1 million during this cycle as it continues to scale its manufacturing capabilities.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.2x. This indicates that total debt is roughly 20% of shareholder equity, suggesting a conservative use of borrowed funds. The current ratio of 1.6x indicates the company has 1.6 times as many current assets as current liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $190.8 million.

AST SpaceMobile faces substantial liquidity risks because it must raise significant additional capital to complete its satellite constellation. It faces intense competition from established satellite systems like Starlink and traditional terrestrial providers like Iridium Communications (IRDM -2.82%), which is in the midst of a merger with Rocket Lab Corp. (RKLB -9.59%). Regulatory hurdles regarding spectrum usage and a pending class action lawsuit from investors add further complexity to its outlook.

Redwire relies heavily on a limited number of U.S. government contracts, which are subject to funding changes or immediate termination. The company must also navigate the risks of integrating acquisitions and managing intense competition from larger aerospace peers like Boeing Co. (BA -2.26%). Supply chain disruptions and a dependency on a small number of third-party launch providers could also impact its ability to deliver products.

Redwire appears much more affordable based on its P/S ratio, which compares market value to sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

In April, Redwire was selected as one of 14 vendors (out of a total of 32 bids) on the Space Systems Command $1.8 billion 10-year Andromeda Indefinite Delivery Indefinite Quantity, or IDIQ contract. That's a project to replace aging GPS satellites and upgrade the U.S. space infrastructure to counter emerging threats. The IDIQ win is something management feels moves Redwire up the food chain with the Department of Defense. It could mean significantly more revenue, since U.S. Space Systems Command provided a notice of its intent to raise the total shared ceiling for the Andromeda IDIQ to more than $6 billion to meet increased demand.

In the near term, Wall Street projects Redwire to post fiscal 2026 revenue of around $463 million, representing about 38% growth over the prior year. In addition, the business has an order backlog of $620 million. The business is still expected to post net losses for the foreseeable future, but they are trending in the right direction.

AST SpaceMobile, meanwhile, expects its space-based network to deliver significant business in a few years. Essentially, AST SpaceMobile is a direct-to-device play, providing full mobile phone compatibility with major carriers without the need for specialized equipment. Many of its potential clients are also equity holders in the company, including AT&T, Verizon, Bell Canada, Rakuten, Vodafone (VOD -0.67%), Alphabet Inc. (GOOG -0.71%), American Tower Corp,(AMT +2.14%) and Telus Corp. (TU +2.74%).

By the end of 2026, the company should have 45 satellites, which will allow it to fully service the U.S., and that should start to supercharge revenue growth. For fiscal 2026, Wall Street sees $166 million in sales, jumping to $586 million the following year, though the business is expected to still be unprofitable. Free cash flow appears much more manageable, with analysts expecting positive free cash flow and net income in 2029.

Both of these are exciting stocks for the space infrastructure age that is developing, but Redwire gets the nod for its quite reasonable P/S ratio for investors right now under the adage of buy good companies at good prices.

#3068. Forget SpaceX: This Stock Could Be the Real Winner of the Space Race

Autonomous driving technology is a beneficiary of today's space race.

By Ryan Vanzo – Nov 20, 2026 at 1:30PM EST

Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -6.64%) is arguably the top space stock on the market today. But it's far from the only one. There are dozens of companies directly profiting from today's space race. But there are hundreds more that will benefit in more indirect ways.

If you're also looking to profit from the space race, the best strategy may not be to invest directly in space stocks. Instead, look for companies with ways to benefit that aren't fully appreciated by the market. With this in mind, one trillion-dollar business stands out.

For decades, investors have considered Tesla (TSLA -6.91%) an automotive stock. That paradigm is no longer true. Tesla's $1.5 trillion valuation has little to do with making cars. Instead, that valuation is tied to future growth opportunities, with robotaxis at the top of the list.

At first glance, robotaxis don't seem to be directly related to space. But if you understand the value and limitations of autonomous driving technology, the connection becomes clear.

Robotaxis are widely believed to be a multi-trillion-dollar opportunity. With the ability to manufacture its own cars, Tesla has both a scaling and cost advantage over its competitors, many of which lack internal manufacturing capabilities.

Tesla plans on leveraging these advantages by launching its own robotaxi platform. In effect, the company could become the Uber Technologies (UBER -1.33%) of robotaxis, albeit while operating a closed ecosystem exclusively for Tesla models.

"Autonomous driving will increasingly demand more and more reliable network-based structures, requiring redundant, real-time architectures," concludes a report from the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. "Car manufacturers will be required to continuously increase bandwidths for both point-to-point data pipes and distributed network structures to meet new data demands. Level 5 cars will send 25 gigabytes of data to the cloud every hour."

In other words, robotaxis will require huge amounts of bandwidth to operate. If a robotaxi relies solely on terrestrial data networks, it creates connectivity vulnerabilities. That could cause service outages, customer experience issues, or even safety challenges. Network redundancy will matter. That's exactly the value that Starlink can provide for Tesla.

"We can't have Robotaxis getting stuck in these Bermuda Triangles of lack of cellular connectivity," Elon Musk warned investors earlier this year. "There are many places, even in Silicon Valley, where the cellular coverage is terrible or sometimes non-existent, which is surprising for Silicon Valley. I know when I drive to work, those first 10, 15 minutes, I can't actually do any calls because the cellular connectivity is so bad ... Starlink with its ability to do connectivity anywhere is actually quite important, so we don't have Robotaxis missing in action."

Robotaxis are a huge component of Tesla's current valuation. The total robotaxi opportunity could ultimately be valued at more than Tesla's market cap today. Robotaxi execution will therefore be critical, and the company's close relationship with SpaceX and Starlink should ultimately make it an unlikely winner of today's space race.

#3067. Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Knicks Cut Down Wolves

After couple great resume wins that included the first time in Minnesota Timberwolves franchise history where they defeated the same team, twice in a row, on back-to-back nights, the home stand continued with a familiar face back in town. Karl-Anthony Towns and the defending champion New York Knicks arrived at Target Center with hopes of toppling his old squad. KAT returning to Minnesota is always a big game and an emotional matchup for the fanbase and, as per usual, he was welcomed back with open arms.

The Timberwolves have been on a hot streak as of late, winners of seven of eight games with a single lapse in play against the Chicago Bulls. They looked to continue a successful home stand and take advantage of the early season uneasiness the Knicks have been experiencing.

While the Timberwolves still are dealing with a handful of injuries so far this season, they did get Jonathan Kuminga back to give a much needed boost to a team that had to grind out a win against the Blazers on Tuesday night.

The first quarter started at a breakneck pace as both teams kept finding the bottom of the net. Towns started the game well at his former home, while LaMelo Ball's aggression showed up early on as he was launching shots.

It was a game of runs early on, as each team had their stretch of dominance – Knicks had a 10-0 run early, and the Timberwolves matched pace with a 13-2 run of their own. The Knicks continued to be red hot as they shot over 70% from both the floor and from three in the first quarter. KAT led the way with 10 points while LaMelo held serve from the other side with nine of his own. New York took the advantage into the second by a score of 33-26.

Chris Finch started the quarter with a technical foul as he'd been in the referees ear for much of the start of the game. KAT and the Knicks continued their bucket-getting at an absurd clip as Josh Hart woke up from his season long slumber, draining a few threes.

During the middling minutes, the Timberwolves fell into too much isolation offense and struggled to generate good looks on the offensive end of the floor. New York went on a 9-0 run down the stretch and shot 10/16 from three in the first half which gave them a healthy 15-point lead heading into halftime. Jaden McDaniels was perfect from the floor in the first half and led the way with 11 points for Minnesota.

Jonathan Kuminga came out of halftime swinging, taking it strong to the basket and mixing in outside shots as he scored 14 points in the frame. Minnesota kept trying to claw back into the game, but the turnovers they committed made it hard for them to mount a run. They cut the lead a few times, but Jalen Brunson did a great job staving off runs with his shotmaking.

The Wolves continued to struggle to spur a fourth quarter run to start the final period. A Jaden three brought some wind into the sails as they went on to tighten up the defense as the Knicks had zero field goals over a seven minute span in the fourth.

Still, it wasn't enough. The Wolves had trouble getting over the hump, but a reviewed KAT flopping technical gave them life again.

Minnesota had their chances, but missed their final five shots of the game including a LaMelo Ball three that could've tied the game with seconds left. New York played keep away and took the close win, 102-99.

New York got greedy tonight even though Thanksgiving isn't until next week.

Second chance points are always backbreakers, and the Knicks took advantage in winning that battle 12 to four.

New York had hit their shots throughout much of the first half, which is already tough to deal with, and when that is compounded with multiple opportunities on the same possession it makes it feel that much worse.

Throughout the game, the score always seemed much closer than it felt. With Jalen Brunson denying any run in the third quarter, it started to feel like one of those games where the Timberwolves wouldn't be able to get the boulder rolling down the hill. It felt that way for much of the game, but then the Timberwolves started to gain some traction in the fourth.

This run was defined with their top ranked defense putting the Knicks in jail. Minnesota held New York to 12 points in the fourth quarter, including that aforementioned seven minute stretch where they did not score a field goal. The Timberwolves made it extremely hard on Jalen Brunson and navigated screens adeptly on defense to avoid the matchup hunting the Knicks were searching for.

Unfortunately, the Wolves wasted the great defense with tough turnovers that plagued them during the earlier quarters as well. They played extremely hard to get back into the game and rode the momentum that they created, but came up short in the closing minutes.

While they didn't deserve to win today, their best chance to tie the game was unfairly taken by an inadvertent whistle that Chris Finch was livid about in his postgame press conference.

Finch said, "The one that everybody in the arena saw hit the rim? … I mean it was clear that it hit the rim, it hit the rim and it went straight down to the floor… I mean were continually told that these are the best in the world and you know you can't miss that one". Credit to Andrew Dukowitz for the quote and video below.

The Timberwolves will take on the early season surprise Memphis Grizzlies in a Saturday night battle between two of the top teams in the Western Conference.

#3066. Here's What the Average Social Security Benefit Actually Covers

The average check is designed as a foundation, but senior households spend far more each year than most retirees expect.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:00PM EST

Most retirees lean on Social Security for much of their income, yet the average check was built to replace only part of a paycheck. As of October 2026, the average monthly benefit for a retired worker is $2,092.17, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA).

That amounts to $25,106.04 per year. While this provides a predictable stream of income, it's often significantly less than what you'll need to maintain your standard of living after you stop working.

A household headed by someone age 65 or older spends an average of $61,432 per year, according to the 2024 Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Expenditure Survey. While housing and healthcare are major line items, costs such as transportation and food also consume a large share of the budget.

The table below breaks down these annual costs for senior households. Note that these expenses are compared against benefit figures as of October 2026.

That $25,106.04 average annual benefit covers only 41% of typical senior household spending. This gap exists by design, as Social Security is built to replace roughly 40% of your pre-retirement income. The benefit formula is the same for everyone and is meant to be a foundation, not a full budget.

The SSA bases your benefit on an average of your 35 highest-earning years, where earlier wages are adjusted for inflation and run through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. This results in an average yearly shortfall of $36,325.96 that retirees must cover through savings, a pension, or other income.

For those without a pension or deep savings, part-time work may be the only realistic choice to bridge that gap. A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027, adding about $75 a month to the average benefit.

These adjustments are designed to help your buying power keep pace with inflation, though they aren't intended to close the structural gap between your benefits and your total expenses. The average check remains a foundation for your retirement income, but the challenge for most is finding the right way to cover the rest.

Personal savings are the best option to pay for what Social Security won't cover. It doesn't matter whether you keep these funds in a 401(k), an IRA, or even a health savings account (HSA), so long as they're accessible to you when you need them.

If you qualify for a pension through your employer, this may also go a long way toward covering your remaining expenses. Talk to your employer to get a rough idea of how much your pension might offer you in monthly or annual income in retirement.

When personal savings aren't enough, and a pension isn't an option, you might have to explore alternatives, like working in retirement. It might not be ideal, but there are plenty of flexible options these days that enable you to work from home or set your own hours, so you should still have plenty of time to enjoy some of the freedoms of retirement.

For more on how Social Security affects your retirement, see this guide.
