#3059. Cerebras Stock Looks Like a Buy as Customer Base Expands

Cerebras stock climbed after adding Microsoft as a customer.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Cerebras Systems ›

Cerebras Systems (CBRS -1.84%) continued to rebound from its lows, climbing 11% on Nov. 13 after the stock reported soaring revenue and announced a deal with Microsoft (MSFT -2.24%). However, the semiconductor stock is still down more than 40% from its $185 IPO price in May, and more than 70% off its highs.

Cerebras, which makes systems built around its wafer-scale chips the size of an iPad, has thus far been more of a niche provider of high-end artificial intelligence inference (AI) systems with a small customer base. As such, the deal with Microsoft is important, as Cerebras continues to expand its client list, which now includes OpenAI, Amazon (AMZN -3.71%), and Oracle (ORCL -7.93%). As the company's systems move into the mainstream, it still looks like a good time to buy the stock.

In addition to the big deal with Microsoft, Cerebras also addressed rumors around OpenAI, which is set to become its largest customer. It noted that it didn't have enough capacity to provide the system behind OpenAI's ultra-fast mode for its latest models, and that this was why its solution wasn't used, not for technical reasons.

Cerebras has a take-or-pay contract with OpenAI worth more than $20 billion for 750 megawatts of capacity, accounted for in its remaining performance obligations (RPOs), which total $26.1 billion as of the end of September. Notably, the Oracle and Microsoft deals were signed after the quarter and are not in that amount. Due to delays, Cerebras may owe OpenAI delay credits, which were deducted from its RPOs.

Despite some hiccups with OpenAI, Cerebras saw its revenue jump 55% to $210.8 million. Its core sales figure, which strips out revenue distortions from customer warrants and pass-through accounting, soared 70% to $230.9 million, topping the $214.7 million consensus, as compiled by LSEG.

Customers continue to prefer renting its systems, leading to its cloud revenue climbing 265% year over year to $141.9 million and its core cloud revenue surging 287% to $144.9 million. Hardware revenue sank 29% year over year to $68.9 million, while core hardware revenue slipped 11% to $86 million.

Gross margins have been an issue for Cerebras. Its core gross margins came in at 41%, up 30 basis points versus a year ago. Core gross margin for its cloud operation was 46.9%, a big improvement from 16.5% a year ago. However, its core hardware gross margin was 31%, down from 50.5% a year ago. The company said this was due to the continued ramp of its manufacturing capabilities and the final shipments of hardware to early customers under special pricing. Its long-term target for hardware gross margins is 60%. Meanwhile, its cloud gross margins were impacted by Cerebras renting back some equipment from a customer.

Management projected Q4 core revenue of between $310 million and $330 million, with core gross margins between 47% and 49%. Cerebras also raised its full-year guidance, taking its core revenue forecast to a range of $940 million to $960 million, up from a previous outlook of $880 million to $890 million. It now sees its core gross margins coming in between 42% and 44%, up from an earlier projection between 41% and 43%.

For 2027, management expects core revenue to more than triple, with strong growth for both cloud and hardware. The Microsoft deal will contribute revenue starting in the first half of the year, and Oracle's will start in the summer. Cerebras anticipates substantially increasing its data center capacity next year.

Cerebras has the fastest inference solution, which is growing faster than the AI model training market and is expected to become the larger of the two markets in the coming years. In fact, Bloomberg Intelligence projects the inference market will be double the size of the training market by 2032.

Cerebras has arguably the best inference solution; the issue is that it's expensive. Still, the company is making inroads and gaining big, new customers. While it's seen some hiccups with capacity, it has a long runway for growth.

While I consider Cerebras stock speculative, I think it looks like a buy at these levels, given its potential to disrupt the chip market in inference.

#3055. Archer Aviation Trades Near $4. Could a $5,000 Investment Set You Up for Life?

Archer is trading near its 52-week low. Could this be a once-in-a-generation opportunity, or a trap?

By Steven Porrello – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Archer Aviation ›

At the time of this writing (around noon on Nov. 16), Archer Aviation (ACHR -9.06%) stock is trading below $4 a share. That's a seemingly remarkable price for a company with ambitions to revolutionize urban transportation, especially considering its stock was flying high in the double digits just last year.

But is today's share price really a bargain? And if so, could a $5,000 investment today be enough to set you up for life?

Archer is developing an electric air taxi, which it calls Midnight. It doesn't have regulatory approval to fly its eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) commercially (no one has that certificate in the U.S.), but it is widely considered one of the frontrunners in this nascent industry.

What the heck is an air taxi? Basically, a cross between a helicopter, an airplane, and a drone. This feat of engineering can take off vertically like a helicopter, then switch to forward flight like an airplane, cruising at speeds of up to 150 mph. If it gets all the necessary approvals, it could radically change how people travel, turning hour-long traffic jams into urban hops that last minutes.

How close is Archer to getting its approval ducks in order? Closer than ever, but not quite ready for takeoff. Indeed, the company has entered the fourth and final phase of the FAA's type certification process. "Final" sounds encouraging, but this phase is not for the faint of heart. It involves rigorous testing to prove that Midnight can carry passengers safely, with regulators scrutinizing everything from the flight's performance to its safety systems. The process could take years. There's no guarantee Midnight will make it through.

If Midnight does make it through, the long-term opportunity could be enormous. Morgan Stanley (MS -4.83%) has estimated that the global eVTOL market could reach $255 billion by 2035 and $1 trillion by 2040. Archer doesn't need to capture the entire market to grow substantially; even a small slice could translate into billions in annual revenue.

Let's play with some numbers. At $4 a share, a $5,000 investment would buy you 1,250 shares. If the stock were to climb tenfold, that investment would be worth $50,000. A 20-fold increase would make your shares worth $100,000, and a 50-fold increase would be worth $250,000.

So, yes, on paper, the potential returns are enormous. On the other hand, all of them would require Archer to develop into a major player in the aviation industry, with a thriving air taxi business, substantial revenue, and, eventually, consistent profits.

Can Archer do that? Maybe, maybe not. And it's precisely the uncertainty behind that "maybe" that helps explain why Archer trades at $4 a share, not, say, $14. Risk-tolerant, intrepid investors might be interested in Archer at this price, but those averse to risk might want to avoid the eVTOL industry for now.

#3052. The Stock Market Is Flashing a Warning Seen Just 6 Times in 156 Years, and History Is Clear What Comes Next for Stocks

A time-honored valuation metric is flashing a warning, but history suggests the real danger for investors might not be another market crash.

By Steven Porrello – Nov 20, 2026 at 2:43PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

History doesn't repeat itself exactly, but sometimes it comes pretty close. And right now, one of the stock market's most reliable valuation tools is flashing a warning seen only six times since 1871.

The warning comes from the Shiller price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, one of our most time-honored valuation tools. This handy metric divides the current price of the S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.91%) by its average inflation-adjusted earnings from the previous 10 years, helping us gauge how expensive stocks are. Over 156 years, the Shiller P/E has averaged nearly 18. Only six times has the metric crossed a threshold of 30; in five of the last six, it was followed by a significant market decline.

Today, the Shiller P/E clocks in at around 40. On the surface, that seems concerning for investors. But there might be a catch to this seemingly ominous warning, and it might change how we interpret what history is signaling to us.

First, let's start with the historical record. Fair warning: It's not particularly encouraging.

The five previous periods in which the Shiller P/E rose above 30 for two consecutive months during a bull market did not end well for investors. That's an euphemism. It ended badly, very badly. One only has to mention the crash of 1929, or the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000, or the COVID-19 crash of 2020, to get a mental picture of the damage. The S&P 500 also dropped nearly 20% in late 2018 and roughly 25% during the 2022 bear market.

From this perspective, the Shiller P/E looks like a crystal ball. Jump above 30, so it goes, and a market crash will follow. But there's a problem with this interpretation, and it could be making the Shiller P/E look far better at predicting crashes than it actually is.

The problem could be that we're looking at these six occurrences separately when at least four could be considered as one extended period of unusually expensive stocks. This is the argument of former Federal Reserve economist William Emmons, who has pointed out that the Shiller P/E hasn't fallen below 24 since October 2013.

Why would this matter? Simply put, it means we have fewer truly independent examples of the Shiller P/E predicting a market crash. Instead of six separate warnings, we might be looking at just three periods of extremely high valuations, with the third still ongoing. That doesn't change the fact that market crashes occurred. But counting each episode separately could make the Shiller P/E look more reliable at predicting crashes than it actually is.

That said, Emmons doesn't discredit or dismiss the Shiller P/E. He thinks it's a valuable metric. But its real value, he suggests, doesn't lie in predicting market crashes; rather, it helps investors understand the long-term returns stocks might deliver over the next decade. And when valuations are unusually high, Emmons argues, those returns are historically disappointing. Which brings me to my next point.

Again, it's easy to look at the history of the Shiller, and assume that a market crash will end this period of unusually expensive stocks. But a stock market crash isn't the only way high valuations could level out. Indeed, stocks could simply go nowhere for years while earnings remain strong, and a similar result would occur.

Here's what I mean. Let's say that the Shiller P/E drops from 40 to 30. Well, that could mean stock prices dropped 25%, assuming average inflation-adjusted earnings stayed the same. But it could also mean that stock prices stayed relatively flat while earnings increased by a third or more. These are totally different investing experiences -- a market crash versus years of stagnant returns -- but either way, the market comes out looking less expensive.

In this way, the warning from history isn't that stocks are about to plunge even more than they have recently. They might, they might not. Either way, it's a good reminder to pause, take a hard look at our investments, and reassess how much risk we're taking. After all, the stock market could avoid a crash, corporate profits could continue growing, and investors could still earn disappointing returns. That might sound paradoxical, but at today's valuation it is entirely possible.

Tonight is the third game of Houston's NBA Cup journey. A loss here eliminates Houston from moving to the next round (I think technically it doesn't but in reality it does). The Rockets will probably be without Alperen Sengun, who has a corneal abrasion in one eye and swelling in his other eye. The Rockets have two days off after tonight, so it behooves Houston to rest their star center even if he's able to go.

When these teams met last week, the Denver Nuggets were coming off a trip to Mexico City and had to spend an extra night south of the Texas border. Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Frontline (FRO +2.38%) reported record financial performance driven by unprecedented freight rates and significant geopolitical disruptions that have altered global oil trading patterns. The company maintains a modern fleet of 51 vessels with a low average age of 6.9 years, positioning it to capture elevated spot rates while maintaining a fleet-wide cash breakeven of $23,600 per day. Management expects record-breaking earnings for the fourth quarter based on high booking levels across all vessel classes, supported by shifting trade routes and the ongoing energy security narrative.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q3 2026 Frontline plc Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to hand the conference over to your speaker today, Mr. Lars Barstad, CEO. Please go ahead.

Lars Barstad: Hello. Thank you. Dear all, thank you for dialing in to Frontline's quarterly earnings call. We continue to operate in an uncharted territory as there is no playbook for the events this market has seen over the last 9 months. And Frontline is steaming ahead and the recent correction in rates only moves us from interstellar earnings to astronomical, we are running at a profit margin of about 90% with revenues 10x our running costs.

Before I give the word to Inger, I'll run through our TCE numbers on Slide 3 in the deck. For Frontline's third quarter of 2026, we made $148,500 per day on our spot trading VLCCs, $102,500 per day on our spot trading Suezmaxes and $67,800 per day on our LR2/Aframaxs. So far in the fourth quarter of 2026, 68% of our VLCC days are booked at $562,600 per day, 69% of our Suezmax days are booked at $324,300 per day and 68% of our LR2/Aframax days at $190,800 per day. Unprecedented numbers and all up in the 6 digits.

I need to remind the audience that these numbers are still on a load-to-discharge basis with the implications of balance days at the end of the quarter that may occur. We face -- that even with all this, we face a record-breaking fourth quarter. Now I'll let Inger take you through the financial highlights.

Inger Klemp: Thanks, Lars, and good morning and good afternoon, ladies gentlemen. Let's then turn to Slide 4 and look at the profit statement highlights. The adjusted profit in the third quarter decreased by $49.3 million compared with the previous quarter, primarily due to a decrease in our TCE earnings.

The ship operating expenses decreased by $2.1 million from previous quarter, and that was mainly due to sale of 2 Suezmax tankers in the second quarter and 2 VLCCs in the third quarter, but also to a decrease in general running costs for the remaining fleet, which was then partially offset by a decrease in supplier rebates. The administrative expenses decreased by $1.6 million from the previous quarter, and this excludes synthetic option revaluation loss of $1.2 million in the third quarter and the gain of $5.3 million in the second quarter. The adjusted interest expense decreased by $1 million from previous quarter, primarily due to lower interest rate margins.

Depreciation increased by $4.4 million from the previous quarter, and that was due to the delivery of 6 newbuildings in the second and third quarter, partially offset by sale of vessels. Let's then look at the balance sheet on Slide 5. Frontline has a solid balance sheet and a strong liquidity of $1.4 billion in cash and cash equivalents. And that is including undrawn amounts of revolver capacity of $1.1 billion in marketable securities and minimum cash requirements at the end of September. We have no debt maturities until 2028, and we have no meaningful maturities until 2031. And this is supported by increased tenure across the portfolio, as shown in the maturity chart on the slide.

The remaining newbuilding commitments at the end of September was $288.7 million, and that relates to the acquisition of the 9 newbuildings from affiliates of Hemen earlier this year. The company has secured newbuilding financing of up to $737 million for all the 9 newbuildings as we have set out in the press release. Let's then turn to Slide 6. And let's look at the financing optimizations that we have been doing recently. From June to November 2026, we lowered the weighted average interest rate margin by 60 basis points from 178 basis points at the end of the first quarter of 2026 to 118 basis points at the date of this presentation.

That was made through margin reductions on existing facilities and also through the refinancing of selected facilities. The reduction was driven by amendments with 23 basis points, refinancings with 27 basis points and newbuilding financing and asset sales with 10 basis points. The total RCF capacity increased from $473 million at the end of the first quarter of 2026, and then up to $2.27 billion at the end of the third quarter of '26 of which then $1.2 billion was drawn and $1.1 billion was undrawn. This RCF structure allows the company flexibility to manage liquidity actively without holding excess cash on the balance sheet.

Let's then move to Slide 7 and look at the fleet composition and the cash breakeven and OpEx. Upon delivery of the remaining VLCC newbuildings and the sale of 2 VLCCs, our fleet consists of 14 VLCCs, 19 Suezmax tankers and 18 Aframax/LR2 tankers and has an average age of 6.9 years, consists of 100% eco-vessels where 69% are scrubber fitted. We estimate an average cash breakeven rate for the next 12 months of approximately $24,100 per day for VLCCs, $25,200 per day for Suezmax tankers and $20,600 per day for LR2 tankers, with a fleet average estimate of about $23,600 per day. This includes dry dock costs of 10 VLCCs, 6 Suezmax tankers and 7 LR2 tankers.

The fleet average estimate excluding dry dock cost is about $21,800 per day or $1,800 per day less. We recorded OpEx, including dry dock in the third quarter of $8,400 per day for VLCCs, $10,600 per day for Suezmax tankers and $13,400 per day for LR2 tankers. Cash generation, Frontline has a substantial cash generation potential with about 28,000 earnings days annually.

And as you can see from this slide, the cash generation potential basis current fleet to TCE rates and spot market rates as of November 19, is $4.4 billion or approximately $19.70 per share, providing a cash flow yield of 44% basis current share price. A 30% increase from current spot market will increase the cash generation potential to about $5.8 billion or $26.10 per share. And likewise, 30% decrease from current spot market will decrease the cash generation potential to $3 billion or $13.30 per share. With this, I leave the word to Lars again.

Lars Barstad: Thank you, Inger. Let's move to Slide 9 and look at the market highlights. Middle East continues to be the focal point and although we almost forget that during the summer months, we had an MOU in place between U.S. and Iran, and we actually started to see risk premiums leaving the market. This quickly changed as the summer came to an end. And during the third quarter, the risks of trading, both in the Black Sea, in the Red Sea and in and around the Gulf of Oman increased. The big kind of step change as far as we saw it, was that the Middle East-based national oil companies started to take control of their own logistics.

The market started to run out of shipowners that were willing to take the risk even despite the highly -- high-paid routes, they basically stopped accepting taking the risk of passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The only way for the Middle East exporters to arrange for freight of their oil. We have to remember, this is like a national security issue was to actually buy the tonnage themselves and move the oil. This way, they managed to reduce the rebates they had to offer to the market in order to get the oil exported. Secondly, it also reduced the freight costs, and they didn't have to pay third parties astronomical numbers in order to get the oil moving.

And this is the situation we basically have now is that the mother lode of the oil being moved through the Strait of Hormuz is actually on tonnage controlled by the exporters themselves. This created further growing shuttle traffic in the Gulf of Oman with lengthy ship-to-ship transfer activity, increasing the sailing inefficiencies as we proceeded, kind of, towards the end of Q3 and the start of Q4. Then further, we've had the Yanbu pipeline disturbance and also the risk situation, specifically in the Red Sea adding to these challenges. You load about 3/4 of a ship, take it through the Suez Canal, top-up at Sidi Kerir and then you sail all the way around African continent. And we now have 3.5 years lead time, if you go to the market to order virtually any ship at this point. We still believe that what's happening around us and what has transpired over the last 9 months are going to have long-term implications for the market. We're going to have inventory refill. We're going to have energy security scrutiny and also, we're going to see refiners diversify how they source their feedstock. If you look at the market charts on the bottom of this chart, yes, we have corrected quite substantially.

But one has to peek over to the left-hand side of this chart and look at what levels we're actually talking about. Bottoming out on VLCC is around $250,000 a day. Suezmax is around $175,000 a day. And also, you might notice that Aframax is out of the U.S. Gulf is straight back up to almost $200,000 per day. So by no means this is not a freight crisis. Let's move to Slide 10 and discuss a little bit more around the flows. So we already mentioned that global crude oil exports have surpassed the heights of September 2025. Part of this is, of course, caused by Middle East crude oil exports back to pre-conflict levels.

But it's also the addition or the incremental barrels coming out of the Atlantic Basin that adds to this. And also, it's important that despite the hits on Yanbu, flows have resumed and added a lot of output from the region as we can see on the top right-hand chart. What's also very interesting to observe, and this is the bottom chart is that the Asian imports, excluding China, is extremely firm and is well beyond seasonal patterns. And then we can only imagine what will happen when or if China resumes full import volumes. They're still lagging about 2 million barrels behind the average of Q4 2025. We've also seen some positive moves on the products trade.

This trade has been laggard largely due to protectionism amongst producers, but also the lack of kind of ample exports, particularly from China. But now we are starting to see from the Middle East at least, it's a huge refining region that the clean trade is starting to drizzle through despite the disturbance in the Strait of Hormuz. Again, this is data into October. I think everybody who has followed the recent events in the Strait of Hormuz, we should probably expect a little bit of reduction here. But this is a firmish long-term trend that of course, depending on activity, we think is going to continue.

I think one thing that's very important to remember, and I mentioned it on the previous slide, the EIA expects world inventory builds to the tune of 4 million barrels per day in 2027. This comes on top of their expected consumption of 104.5 million barrels per day. Since the inventory builds are happening primarily then in U.S. and also in Asia, particularly the Asian part of this is going to be crude transported. But again, the recent deterioration in the security situation in the Strait of Hormuz will have an impact short term, particularly on the U.S. exports trade.

But this is going to be a positive one because we're already seeing that with the current kind of very prompt lack of oil coming out of the Strait of Hormuz, we're already seeing arbs from the U.S. starting to work into Europe. And secondly, it would start to work to Asia. Let's move to Slide 11. And this is a slide we wanted to show basically to kind of show you how sensitive this market and particularly so the VLCC to small changes in, kind of, how the population of tankers are positioned.

If you assume we have around a bit north of 900 VLCCs in the market, and I think it's better to read it on the right-hand slide -- chart, sorry, the left and the right slide actually show more or less the same, but it's probably easier to see on the right side. So if you assume we have about -- a bit over 900 VLCCs globally, currently, 241 of them are either about 20 years of age, they are dark or sanctioned. We believe China controls a bit north of 100 VLCCs. These are all being utilized for the existing import of Chinese crude.

We have not seen Chinese charters active in the market for the last 6 months, you can say. And they take care of China's import from primarily West Africa, but also the other cargoes that come out. And then you have a fleet of about 200 vessels, which is controlled by national oil companies and other kind of major oil companies. And then you have to look at the orange kind of last column here, which is actually the independent traders and of course, Sinokor, which is a fleet that's almost -- is below 400 vessels. This is the fleet that gets affected by the ever-changing trading patterns and arbs opening and shutting.

And this is also why any kind of disturbance to the trade becomes quite violent in the freight rate terms. As far as we can analyze currently, there is about 70 VLCCs involved in the shuttling of crude in and out of the Hormuz Strait. This is a mixture of the column, which we call national oil companies and the pure spot players. But this is almost 10% of the fleet that is below 20 years, not dark and not sanctioned, but looking at the actively traded fleet, it's nearing 20%. We also know that this fleet is constantly being exposed to disturbance by way of being -- by way of attacks.

And there are certain market sources that are putting into the numbers that between 1% and potentially 2% of the VLCC fleet is currently either under repairs or in some cases, becoming a total loss. Then I would like to move to Slide 12 and look at the order books. This is an alarming picture for anybody that's been in shipping for a long period of time. And kind of historically, we would say that the party is over. But there is some granularity here. These are the vessels that will come to age as the order book delivers. And this can, and we hope will cushion the impacts of the very large delivery years we are approaching. To further exemplify this, we have a slide on Page 13, where we're trying to do kind of an indication or show you the net fleet developments as the order books look right now. We'll come up with a new term, and this is the deadbeat fleet. So this is the fleet that under normal circumstances, probably wouldn't be around.

And this is kind of going to form a cushion as we move forward because it's likely to be expected that the debit fleet is going to be starting to move to recycling yards if this market breaks in any kind of severe manner. And if you keep that into consideration, at the same time, we look at kind of how the fleet age as we move forward into 2030. We're actually only -- well, only, we're looking at the peak fleet growth of between 6% and 7% in 2028, the way the order book looks right now.

And this is all due to the simple fact that although we have a very high order book, we also have the highest observed age of the -- average age of the global tanker fleet that we've had for decades. Then I'd like to move on to Slide 14 and a quick summary. And we question, are we currently trading low in the mother of all cycles? I actually did this headline on Monday or Tuesday. And I can say that we're already in a situation where freight rates are actually starting to move north again after having kind of a fall for the last 2, 3 weeks.

But we still have historically high freight rates, and they are, to some extent, also challenging the oil trading complex. This is a development that will ebb and flow because the trade needs to have room for the freight. So it means that the arbs need to widen in order for oil to be transported. We have seen that when we reach the peaks back in October, oil actually stopped moving. With the levels we are now, the oil can start to move again. And I think we'll be in -- will be very high, but will also be ebbing and flowing depending on the supply of oil coming to the market.

As we already mentioned, global crude exports is beyond September '25 heights. And I don't think any of you had that on your bingo card back in May, June. Asia imports ex China is recovering beyond historical and seasonal highs, which is a positive. And the energy security and inventory situation is likely to dominate the narrative. The long-term implications as fleet aging inefficiency and expanding trade patterns will cushion the impact of the order books as far as we see. And Frontline continue to be center stage with our modern VLCC heavy fleet. And we also need to note that the long-term period market implies lasting disruptions and fairly high tanker markets.

And with that, I will open up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And the first question comes from Jon Chappell from Evercore ISI.

Jonathan Chappell: Lars, I'm going to start where you finished the long-term period market. I think it's in the press release, you have 17 ships on time charter right now, which is pretty elevated given Frontline's history of being more exposed to the spot market. You've talked about a lot of the uncertainty, a lot of the volatility, that recent pull down the last couple of day tick-up. Is this an opportunity for you to maybe continue to tweak the Frontline operating model and take advantage of the maximum inefficiency and disruption and lock in more cash flow? Or do you think you still want to be kind of full hilt to the spot market?

Lars Barstad: Well, it's a good question. And as you perfectly well know, but for the audience, most of the TCE cover that we have on is fairly short dated so it means that a lot of these time charter contracts were done early in the year. With the lack of a crystal ball, we actually didn't see this happening when these were concluded. So this will come off kind of starting in Q1 and during Q1, which means we have an opportunity to reload kind of time charter cover at higher levels.

When we decide to do that is difficult to say because the challenge in this market is that the near-term, kind of, cash generation you can do on spot means that these time charter curves are steeply backwardated. So it kind of hurts to make those decisions. But I think as a general note, you should expect Frontline to have a much higher degree of time charter coverage as we proceed compared to previous years. So I hope that answers your question.

Jonathan Chappell: It does. And it segues to my follow-up, too. I mean, obviously, it does hurt given the spot market levels right now, but as you kind of insinuated if didn't say directly, there is some fragility to those numbers. I thought this first bullet point on your last slide was really interesting in the commentary around challenging the oil trading complex. Do you think what we saw in October is somewhat of a perceived ceiling on how high rates can go before it starts to change the global trading patterns.

And within the context of possibly a higher floor given the inventory restocking, the continued inefficiencies, geopolitical uncertainty and now maybe potentially a ceiling that we can identify, is it more violent within maybe a tighter incredibly elevated, but still a tighter range? Do you think over the next 12 months?

Lars Barstad: It's very hard to say. This is -- these are not kind of fixed boundaries, right? What we saw and which will propel the rates into the stratosphere was, I think, kind of more desperation than economics, kind of, refiners facing having to shut in refinery runs, which is far more costly than what any freight can be. But then I think also kind of why we dived, kind of, off the peaks was probably due to far more volume oil. The oil market in general became far more or far better supplied as the trade through Hormuz became fairly efficient.

So I think to answer that question, at the end of the day, it's going to be how much oil volume is going to be available to the market as oil products have indicated, kind of, at least for a few weeks now, it's been plenty. But if the export or the challenges to oil exports out of the inner kind of Middle East Gulf persists going forward for weeks, maybe we'll have a situation where the marginal barrel will be much harder to get a hold of. And where both traders and refineries will have to account for the increased freight cost.

So this is a little bit whether if it's the dog or the tail or whatever the expression is. But I think kind of the -- so it's a fact that freight to some extent, stopped the yards. But it's also a fact that, that happened at the same time as far more oil volume than people expected started to flow through, particularly in the Middle East. So it's difficult to say. I think the one to watch, of course, is this volume or the reduction of the volume that we might have observed recently being able to come through the Strait of Hormuz.

Operator: We are now going to take the next question. And this question comes from Greg Lewis from BTIG.

Gregory Lewis: Lars, I'd love to get more thoughts around Slide 11 in those 70 Vs that are kind of in that shuttle trade. Really, what I'm trying to understand is you mentioned some of those are like captive fleets. Did we see vessels maybe that had been used to store oil enter the shuttle trade kind of like as we think about those vessels, what's kind of the utilization because those vessels would be moving through any way kind of like, I guess, maybe like what are the wait times on the other side of the Strait that's kind of hampering or extracting utilization. As we think about those 70 Vs, how inefficient do we think that is to the market?

Lars Barstad: It's a very good question and also very difficult to answer. I would like to answer it may be potentially in a different manner. There are actors in this market that we are also public that we have performed the Hormuz trade and if you look at some of the numbers that they are making public, it's about half of what the TD3C index has implied. So that basically means that, although your headline number is more than $1 million per day, what you can actually churn out of it in TCE terms due to inefficiencies due to the waiting that you just mentioned.

And it's not like you say it's a 10- to 11-day voyage to go dip in and out of the Strait of Hormuz. Obviously, it takes much longer because of changing security situation attacks, you don't want to sail kind of the minute, there is activity. The STS activity takes time as well. And maybe a way to load at the terminals and all that stuff. So it looks like the inefficiency is fairly high in that trade and what you're actually able to capture in money as a shipowner is a little bit less in a TCE equivalent than maybe what the market has anticipated.

As Frontline, we don't participate in that trade, but of course, we note the headline numbers. But I think that maybe answers some of your questions. Secondly, we were just in Dubai a couple of weeks, sorry, a week back, met kind of all our key clients in the region. And we understand that kind of the incidents in the shuttle, kind of, market is kind of quite underreported. So it's been an increasing threat and you have incidents happening 2, 3 times a day. Of course, not necessarily severe, but enough to make meaning that the vessel needs to go -- undergo some sort of repair before it can, kind of, partake in the trade again.

So -- but mind you, the 70 vessels, this is also a floating target. But I think this is probably a good point to mention how kind of U.S. have opened up for that you can get an amnesty or get pulled off the OFAC list if you kind of apply. And in that application process, you actually have to explain what is the purpose or what will be the purpose of the ship. And as far as we understand, the only purpose you can have is to partake in this shuttle trade.

So that 70 number might actually increase as we move forward because that's the only possibility you have to capitalize on vessels that are heavily sanctioned by U.S.

Gregory Lewis: Okay. Super helpful. And then I did have my second question I wanted to ask is around the order book. Obviously, you lay it out in the chart, but it's just -- as you think about digging deeper into those numbers, clearly, everybody sees the 60-ish vessels that are scheduled to deliver next year, then there that massive ramp the following year. I guess my question is kind of around this. I feel like in average years we've seen some shipyards or ships get pushed back into the following year. It seems like there's 5% to 10% slippage in an average year. So -- and I'm curious your thoughts around that.

And then the other question is, I imagine you've done a lot of diligence on a lot of these shipyards and probably visited most of them. What do you think the actual ability is of these yards to go from saying, making 60 ships as an industry to 130, i.e., as challenging as '28 looks, could we see a scenario where maybe '28, '29 and '30 kind of smooth out.

Lars Barstad: Yes. Both 2 good questions. And slippage was kind of a keyword in our presentations kind of pre-2020. And you're right, it was ranging between 5% and 15% actually for any year. And I think it's important for you and the audience to understand that. I don't think we can introduce 60 or 100 VLCCs to the market any year really without actually seeing the markets come under some pressure. The idea here is, are we going into pressure that's going to really put a dent in the market? Or will it just kind of put a slight pressure on rates during kind of the peak delivery period.

As far as we understand, most of the 2027 vessels are actually coming in the second half of the year, which could be a challenge, of course. But it all depends on where we are kind of market-wise at that point in time. What's the situation between U.S. and Iran and what's the, kind of, energy complex in general. But with that, kind of moving over to the yards. What we understand and we've actually seen this, is that some of the most expensive yards, the yards that have added a lot of capacity in the last couple of years are actually starting to struggle with getting skilled workforce.

So it means that the way these yards work is that you have an existing yard, you add the docks and then you can build, kind of, a new series of ships, right? But you need a lot of people to work in that dock. You need a lot of skilled welders and other sorts of quite highly qualified people. And we are at the point now where even in China, they're struggling to get hold of this to the point where certain shipyards are standing outside their competitors, offering people as they leave work, a job with their kind of setup. So this is creating some sort of inflation also in the -- in how you remunerate the workers.

So I think, kind of, even in China, you might be kind of getting close to where -- there is a limit to how much it can grow from here. So that makes us quite comfortable that we're not going to see an aggressive increase in the capacity to build ships. And also, I think it's important to note that -- it still show that other segments, non-tanker segments are also ordering ships at the various yards. So it's -- there is no margin pressure for these guys as of yet.

Operator: We are now going to take the next question. And this one comes from Rohit Sah from Makalu Fund Management.

Rohit Sah: I have 2 questions. First question is about inventory plans. As you know, many countries have announced plans to increase their crude oil inventory over and above what it was last year. So of course, the freight rates play a big role in when those inventories are refilled, right, because they'll have to be exported. So can you give us a sense of where freight rates have to be before countries can start thinking about rebuilding their crude oil inventories.

Lars Barstad: That's a hard one, Rohit. But I thank you for picking up on the points, which is a very good one. when this situation happened in February, there were some big consuming countries, I can name India, I can name Korea, Indonesia, Vietnam that find themselves in a situation where they actually didn't have sufficient -- neither strategic oil nor commercial storage which created an issue for them. And you rightfully say there are plans to expand this -- their capacity to store oil, both commercially and strategically. But I don't necessarily think it's a freight question. I think it's an oil price question.

So at least what we've seen historically is that for China, they seem to be motivated by low oil prices. That's when they go in and replenish their inventories. And freight is not really what's making it, kind of, making them stop to build that way. But again, we also believe that we are not going to have like this October super market for extended period of time. If you really want an answer, right now, we seem to have pretty normalized markets. We see the trade working, but we're still kind of between $200,000 and $300,000 per day on a VLCC. So maybe that's the answer.

Rohit Sah: Okay. My second question is that the Atlantic ocean exports have picked up considerably this year. And structurally, it looks like the Atlantic will become more and more important for crude oil exports. So as this shift moves from the Middle East to the Atlantic slowly over time, how much of an impact do you see this having on the tanker market?

Lars Barstad: I think it's going to be very positive. And if you look at it, and India has already kind of said they will, Korea has already committed to taking more barrels from Atlantic Basin exporters going forward. But the interesting part here is what will then happen to the Middle East barrels because they will have to then find another one. And so I think kind of you can have a very interesting trade developing here where you'll have increased flows from the Atlantic Basin to the Far East. But then you'll have actually also an increased flow from Middle East to the continent. So which is the perfect kind of storm for us as shipowners.

So -- but I think as a general, we will see ton miles gradually increase whenever this comes to fruition.

Rohit Sah: Do you have a -- can you give us a sense of how much impact that would be, let's say, you had to shift 1 million barrels from the Middle East to Asia from -- instead from Atlantic to Asia, how much would that increase in VLCC demand?

Lars Barstad: Well, it's 30% just there on the voyage length.

Operator: We are now going to take the next question. And this one comes from Audrey Zong from China Securities.

Audrey Zong: This is Audrey Zong from China Securities. Actually, I think you have touched a little bit about this question. I want to know, looking at 2027, there are 3 key variables: growing cargo volumes, shorter average voyage distances as Middle Eastern barrels replaced Atlantic supplies and additional vessel days absorbed by shuttle operations and STS transfers. How do you assess their net impact on vessel demand with newbuilding deliveries, adding supply under what conditions do you -- will you expect average VLCC Spot TCEs in 2027 to exceed the already strong levels of 2026.

Lars Barstad: Well, thank you, Audrey. If I had the answer to that, like an exact one, I will probably not work here. But this is like an equation with many unknowns, right? And I think if you assume that we're going to be continuing like we are doing now with kind of time-consuming trade out of the -- or day consuming trade out of the Middle East, the Atlantic basin doing what it does right now, and you add a lot of modern efficient ships to the market. We are certainly not going to have the market that we observed in October because there is more capacity coming to this market.

And I don't think -- it's not like the Middle East are going to surpass their volumes materially from what they did earlier in October. So maybe that answers a little bit of your question. But then again, I think the situation is going to be very fluid, and it's going to be fluid going forward. So I would like to kind of maybe answer it differently. There are extremely smart charterers they're willing to pay $100,000 per day for a 3-year time charter for a VLCC so -- and the backwardation in the curve tells us that this is the market we have now and the market we had a month ago, it's not going to last forever, right?

But the floor is going to be far higher than what we have observed in previous cycles. I think that's how I would answer it.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] There seems to be no further questions for today. I will now hand the call back to Lars Barstad for closing remarks.

Lars Barstad: Thank you very much, and thank you for listening in. Very interesting times, exhausting times to some degree. Let's hope for some sort of solution in the Middle East situation. And let's see how this plays out. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3044. Warriors vs. Grizzlies player grades: Charles Bassey posts a double-double

Well, that was yet another dud. The Golden State Warriors completed a winless five-game road trip by losing 126-98 to the Memphis Grizzlies, suffering their fourth consecutive defeat of 20 or more points. How fun!

I thought the Warriors played better than the score would suggest, and just couldn't overcome a 5-for-29 three-point shooting night, but still, one thing is painfully clear: this team will need a miracle just to tread water while Steph Curry is sidelined.

With that, let's speed run some grades. As always, grades are based on my expectations for each player, with a "B" grade representing the average performance for that player.

Note: True-shooting percentage (TS) is a scoring efficiency metric that accounts for threes and free throws. Entering Thursday's games, league-average TS was 57.5%.

33 minutes, 11 points, 8 rebounds, 7 assists, 1 steal, 2 blocks, 3 turnovers, 2 fouls, 3-for-11 shooting, 1-for-4 threes, 4-for-4 free throws, 43.1% TS, -31

It was unfair to expect Lendeborg to carry the Warriors in Curry's absence and, unfortunately, we're seeing why. He's been the team's first option, and the opponent's focal point, in all four games since Curry was injured … and he's shot just 19-for-67 in those games.

I did love the way that he stayed committed to other elements of the game in this one. He was so active on the glass, and had some of his best passes. It was honestly a solid all-around game for Lendeborg, save for the lack of scoring (which really hurts his grade), and he didn't have his best defensive game, either.

Grade: CPost-game bonus: Led the team in assists; worst plus/minus on the team.

23 minutes, 8 points, 3 rebounds, 3 turnovers, 1 foul, 3-for-9 shooting, 0-for-2 threes, 2-for-4 free throws, 37.2% TS, -11

I'm glad that Bob Fitzgerald and Kelenna Azubuike highlighted Santos' energy and effort levels, because they really do deserve praise, and the team would be better off if everyone followed Gui's lead there. Unfortunately, the effort outpaced the execution for Santos in this one.

25 minutes, 16 points, 13 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 steal, 2 blocks, 2 turnovers, 5 fouls, 6-for-7 shooting, 4-for-5 free throws, 87.0% TS, -19

Bassey as easily one of the best players on the court for the Warriors, and one of the only ones who could score reliably. He shot 6-for-7, while his teammates combined to go 27-for-73. He got into foul trouble early, as fouls and turnovers continue to be the thing he is struggling with the most as he steps into a bigger role. But can't argue too much with someone having a highly-efficient 16 and 13.

Grade: A-Post-game bonus: Led the team in points and rebounds.

32 minutes, 15 points, 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 2 turnovers, 1 foul, 5-for-12 shooting, 0-for-5 threes, 5-for-6 free throws, 52.2% TS, -27

The Warriors had one of the worst shooting performances from deep that you'll ever see and, unfortunately, Podz was the biggest culprit. He just couldn't buy a jumper, though it didn't stop him from trying. He had a few brilliant passes in this game, but otherwise it was just a really rough outing from him.

25 minutes, 9 points, 1 rebound, 5 assists, 2 steals, 2 blocks, 2 turnovers, 5 fouls, 3-for-10 shooting, 1-for-4 threes, 2-for-2 free throws, 41.4% TS, -14

Melton slid back into the starting lineup with very mixed results. He was once again extremely disruptive on the defensive side of things, as he has been on so many occasions this year. And he did a good job setting up his teammates. But he was a bit out of control for far too many possessions: he swiped a little recklessly on defense, drawing five fouls; he had some careless passes, some of which went for turnovers and others that he was lucky didn't; and he took some ill-advised shots early in the shot clock.

Melton showed a lot of talent in this game, but not as much veteran poise as the Warriors need.

27 minutes, 15 points, 5 rebounds, 2 turnovers, 1 foul, 5-for-8 shooting, 1-for-3 threes, 4-for-4 free throws, 76.8% TS, -13

Another game where Richard was both an absolute terror on defense and way more impactful on offense than we expect him to be. He didn't technically register any steals in this game, but his defensive excellence was the primary reason behind multiple Grizzlies turnovers. And for the second game in a row, he was one of the only Warriors who could do anything on offense.

He's endearing himself to his teammates and coaches by playing through the UCL tear in his thumb, but even more importantly, he's proving that he's a player who deserves a big workload even when the team is healthy.

17 minutes, 3 points, 2 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 1 block, 2 turnovers, 2 fouls, 1-for-5 shooting, 0-for-3 threes, 1-for-1 free throws, 27.6% TS, -6

Horford was back on the court after sitting during Wednesday's loss, though unfortunately, he couldn't make much of an impact in this game. He had a few mighty impressive rebounds and some nice defensive possessions, but couldn't do much on offense, and was beat on plenty of occasions by Memphis' speed.

15 minutes, 5 points, 2 rebounds, 1 steal, 2 turnovers, 1 foul, 2-for-8 shooting, 1-for-4 threes, 31.3% TS, -16

Niang didn't play well. It happens. No need to dwell on it. Or at least, no need to write about it.

12 minutes, 9 points, 1 assist, 1 foul, 3-for-6 shooting, 1-for-3 threes, 2-for-2 free throws, 65.4% TS, -4

I liked that Cryer wasn't as reliant on his three-point shot in this game as in past games. He was quicker to attack, looking for ways to beat down the defense and get to the rim for easy buckets or free throws. If he wants to be a reliable scorer off the bench, he'll need to keep doing that.

24 minutes, 2 points, 1 rebound, 1 assist, 3 steals, 1 turnover, 1 foul, 1-for-2 shooting, 0-for-1 threes, 50.0% TS, 0 plus/minus

If you're a fan of single-game individual plus/minus, Payton is your guy, as he played half the game with a plus/minus of 0 … meaning the team was outscored by 28 points in the half of the game where he sat. GPII is responsible for some of that, as he had a great defensive game, but he really didn't do anything at all on offense.

4 minutes, 0 points, 2 rebounds, 1 assist, 0-for-1 shooting, 0.0% TS, 0 plus/minus

Some good possessions in a little bit of garbage time for Leons.

4 minutes, 5 points, 1 turnover, 2 fouls, 1-for-1 shooting, 3-for-4 free throws, 90.6% TS, +1

With Horford back, Ike just played some garbage time in this game, but he made the most of it by dropping in five points, and being the only player on the team to have a positive plus/minus.

Grade: IncompletePost-game bonus: Best plus/minus on the team

Thursday's inactives: Jimmy Butler III, Steph Curry, Draymond Green, Moses Moody, Kristaps Porziņģis, Brandon Williams

#3035. Top Wall Street analysts are upbeat about the prospects for these 3 stocks

September ended on a mixed note, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 0.5% and 4.3%, respectively, while the Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.9%. Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud company CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

Chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

"CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," said Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

#3018. Clippers vs. Spurs takeaways: Victor Wembanyama adds to highlight reel

Victor Wembanyama and the San Antonio Spurs remain the standard in the Western Conference and will continue to get everyone's best shot this season.

The Spurs served as a tough test for the Los Angeles Clippers. They gave the Spurs their best shot in a 124-112 loss in San Antonio on Thursday, Nov. 19. Wembanyama led the game with 32 points and 11 rebounds for the Spurs.

It was a bounce-back win for San Antonio, which had a 12-game win streak snapped against the Detroit Pistons earlier in the week.

The Spurs were missing Dylan Harper, who was out with a hip rotator strain, on Thursday. He avoided serious injury but is expected to miss at least a week.

Here's some takeaways from Thursday's game:

Wembanyama can simply do things that others can't.

His latest example came with 3:36 left in the fourth quarter against the Clippers on Thursday. Rui Hachimura's missed shot was rebounded by Stephon Castle, who threw the ball right down the court to a wide-open Wembanyama.

While Wembanyama could've dunked the ball, he seemed to settle for a jump shot inches from the rim.

Wembanyama laughed when asked about the play and stated that dunking has led to a blister on his hand.

"I'm not going to lie, I've had this blister forever and it's killing me," Wembanyama told reporters after the game. "Every time I dunk, it kills me. … It's actually so painful."

While the Clippers still have a lot of work to do if they want to be in a position to compete for a play-in spot later this season, coach Tyronn Lue's team showed some promise and potential against the West's best on Thursday.

L.A. shot the ball well for most of the game and kept the game close behind the effort of veterans Darius Garland and Brook Lopez. Both scored 23 points each.

Garland's had high-scoring performances early this season, but turnovers have been a problem for the guard. He managed to limit his mistakes Thursday, having just one turnover on a big stage against the Spurs.

Max Strus went 5-for-10 from the field, including 5-of-9 from the 3-point line for 18 points.

Clippers center Yanic Konan Niederhauser made his season debut. The second-year player was dealing with a right foot Lisfranc injury and was limited to 11 minutes against the Spurs due to a minutes restriction. He went 1-for-4 shooting and finished the game with two points, three rebounds and a steal. He did find himself in foul trouble with a team-high five personal fouls.

While the Clippers will have to figure out the center rotation following Niederhauser's return, Lue has encouraged Isaiah Jackson to stay ready.

"Nothing (Jackson) has done wrong," Lue said before the game. "You want to try to reward him for what he has done since Yanic has been out. We will see how the flow of the game goes."

Jackson shot 3-for-5 from the field, finishing with six points, four rebounds and three steals in nine minutes of play. He also recorded two blocks against Wembanyama, once at the rim and the second at the 3-point line at the end of the third quarter.

San Antonio managed to get the best of one of Los Angeles' NBA teams, but a meeting with the other still looms.

The Lakers will head to San Antonio next week for an NBA Cup showdown. The Spurs sit at the top of the NBA Cup Group C standings with a 2-0 record. The Lakers are third after splitting their first two games.

A win for the Lakers would not only place them in a tie for the top spot in the group but also provide a glimpse at where things stand in the conference.

The Lakers are tied with the Spurs and LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers for the best record in the league at 13-3. Los Angeles has played well throughout November but had its nine-game winning streak snapped against the Utah Jazz on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

The upcoming Spurs-Lakers matchup will provide a glimpse at two of the league's early MVP front-runners on the court together. Luka Doncic is averaging a league-leading 38.1 points per game along with 7.6 assists and 7.0 rebounds. Wembanyama is averaging 28.4 points, 12.0 rebounds and a league-best 4.1 blocks per game.

The Miami Dolphins have really struggled this season, as they've put together a 1-8 record through their first nine games, while their opponents have outscored them 224-148.

#3013. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3012. Spurs use strong fourth quarter to put away Clippers at home

The San Antonio Spurs overcame a season-high 21 turnovers, using a strong fourth quarter to defeat the Los Angeles Clippers 124-112 at the Frost Bank Center on Thursday night in the penultimate game of their three-game home stand.

The victory is the 13th in the last 14 games for San Antonio, who bounced back from a loss on Tuesday against the Detroit Pistons. The game was the first of several without guard Dylan Harper, who was officially diagnosed with a left hip rotator strain that he suffered at the end of Tuesday's game. He is expected to miss between two to four weeks.

As a result, Julian Champagnie replaced Harper in the starting lineup, and the transition was smooth, considering his starting position last season. Carter Bryant was the first one off the bench for Spurs coach Mitch Johnson, replacing De'Aaron Fox at the 8:54 mark of the period. Johnson said pregame that Harper's injury would cause the Spurs to play around with the rotations a bit more, so that is something to keep an eye on as the week go by.

"We still made some mistakes here and there, but the main thing is we were all connected," Spurs forward Victor Wembanyama said after the game. "And we were mostly on the same page tonight, so that compensated for some of the mistakes."

A low-scoring first quarter saw the Spurs take the 24-21 lead into the second. The Clippers tried to pull Victor Wembanyama away from the paint and it led to a few easy Clippers points at the rim. Wembanyama and Stephon Castle finished the period combining for 14 of San Antonio's 24 points.

The Spurs took a three-point lead into the second half. San Antonio led by as many as 14 points in the second quarter and went on a 21-7 run, but turnovers and poor coverage on the perimeter allowed Los Angeles to stay in the game going into the third quarter.

Los Angeles took that momentum into the second half and opened the quarter on a 11-4 run as San Antonio's defense struggled to get back as the Clippers hit back-to-back three-pointers. That led Johnson to call timeout and talk things over with his team. Johnson's message finally sunk in the fourth quarter as the Spurs outscored the Clippers 34-22 in the final period to pull away for the win.

San Antonio won the game despite a season-high 21 turnovers, something Johnson said has also contributed to the team's shooting woes.

"I actually don't think our passing has been very sharp this year," he said after the game. "I think we've had a lot of passes that have not been on target and I think it's affected our shooting at times."

Of those 21 turnovers, Stephon Castle committed seven of them. Per ESPN, Castle became the first Spur with 7+ turnovers in a single half since Tim Duncan in 2003.

"I don't think it was anything they were doing," Castle said of his turnovers. "I think for me, I was getting probably just one dribble too deep into the paint… So, being able to make the adjustment at halftime, I think, kind of opened it up for me."

Wembanyama led the Spurs with 32 points and 11 rebounds, while Castle and Champagnie combined for 41 points to pace the San Antonio starting unit.

Jordan McLaughlin had a solid outing with five assists and three steals in 11 minutes. He also did not turn the ball over once, which prompted praise from Coach Johnson and McLaughlin's teammates after the game.

De'Aaron Fox had just one shot going into the fourth quarter and took five on the night. He finished with 10 points, but he will need to be more aggressive in the coming games with Harper out.

Keldon Johnson turned back the clock to last season's Sixth Man of the Year run as he had 10 points, 5 rebounds, and 3 assists off the bench. San Antonio will need that contribution from him more consistently to take the load off the starting unit as Harper and Tobias Harris get set to return next month.

The Spurs are now 13-3 on the season and will wrap up their three-game homestand on Saturday night at the Frost Bank Center against the New Orleans Pelicans at 7 p.m.

#3008. Standout rookies Cameron Boozer, Yaxel Lendeborg battle in Grizzlies-Warriors game

Cameron Boozer and the Memphis Grizzlies earned a dominant victory over Yaxel Lendeborg and the Golden State Warriors on Thursday, Nov. 19.

Memphis outscored Golden State 71-51 in the second half in a 126-98 victory at the FedEx Forum.

Boozer, the third overall pick in the 2026 draft, finished with 16 points, six rebounds and five assists in 27 minutes of play. He went 6-for-6 from the field and 4-for-4 from the free-throw line. His fourth made field goal was a pull-up jumper with the shot clock winding down. That make drew a reaction from his father, former NBA star Carlos Boozer, who was sitting courtside.

Lendeborg, the 11th pick in the draft, produced 11 points, eight rebounds and seven assists in 33 minutes for the Warriors. The forward struggled from the field, making just three of his 11 shots.

The Warriors have been playing without Stephen Curry, who suffered an oblique abdominal tear in the first quarter against the Houston Rockets on Nov. 11.

Entering Thursday, Boozer and Lendeborg were cited by the NBA as being the first pair of rookies to average 16-plus points, 7-plus rebounds and 3-plus assists per game through their first 15 games since Larry Bird and Magic Johnson during the 1979-80 season.

More: Cameron Boozer grabs top spot in NBA rookie rankings as Grizzlies surge

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Standout rookies Cameron Boozer, Yaxel Lendeborg battle in Grizzlies-Warriors game

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced an enforcement action against American Express Company to address, among other things, the firm's failure to sufficiently detect and report certain suspicious activity related to money laundering.

The Board also identified significant deficiencies in how American Express Company's enterprise-wide anti-money laundering program was implemented, in particular at the firm's subsidiary national bank. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the primary federal regulator of the firm's national bank, has issued a separate enforcement action against the bank.

The Board's action will help ensure that the firm operates in compliance with all U.S. laws and regulations.

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

Key findings from the 2025 survey include:

In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here.

The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 10 â 2 vote:

The Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability.

Voting against the monetary policy action were Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack, who preferred to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point at this meeting.
